No licence covers bakery machinery itself; four routes bind every job.
MOIAT, the Ministry of Industry and Advanced Technology (https://moiat.gov.ae), absorbed ESMA in 2020 and owns UAE standards, the Emirates Conformity Assessment Scheme (ECAS); low-voltage machines also need the GSO Gulf Conformity Mark, G-Mark (https://www.gso.org.sa).
Dubai Municipality Food Safety Department (https://www.dm.gov.ae, permits via Food Watch, https://foodwatch.dm.gov.ae) approves the establishment, the one-directional layout, food-contact materials, hygiene. ADAFSA (https://www.adafsa.gov.ae) does the same in Abu Dhabi; Sharjah and Ajman run their own.
Dubai Civil Defence (https://www.dcd.gov.ae) enforces the UAE Fire and Life Safety Code of Practice: hood suppression, fire dampers, gas. MOCCAE (https://www.moccae.gov.ae) covers imports and refrigerants; DEWA (https://www.dewa.gov.ae) sanctions load.

Premium European: Pavailler and Bongard (France), Bertrand Puma (mixers, dividers, moulders), MIWE, WACHTEL and DEBAG (Germany), Sveba Dahlen and Revent (Sweden), Polin (Italy), RONDO and Fritsch for laminating, CFI for retarder-provers.
Mid-tier: Sinmag and Chanmag (Taiwan), Esmach, Tecnodom, Logiudice Forni, Fagor; Turkish Kumkaya, Fimak, Inoksan, Ozti. Budget: Chinese OEM stock rebadged by Dubai traders.
UAE presence to verify: TFB Bakery Equipment, Ras Al Khor (Pavailler, Bertrand Puma, CFI); Paramount, Sharjah Industrial 12 (Chanmag, Tecnodom, Fagor, Rational); Rio Dubai, Al Diwan.
What genuinely differs: steel gauge and deck insulation, steam generator mass, burner and control brand (Siemens/Riello vs unbranded), parts availability. Demand the CE Declaration of Conformity, wiring and gas diagrams, food-contact declaration, serial-numbered warranty, parts price list.

They say "a good bakery oven". They mean predictable crust and colour on their own recipe, that an inspector passes and a technician can fix within 24 hours. Sourdough at 250 degC with heavy steam on a deck is a different machine from 5,000 croissants a shift.
Real constraints: ceiling height (a rack oven with hood needs 2.9-3.2 m), door and lift width, DEWA sanctioned load, piped gas versus an LPG manifold outside, landlord fit-out rules in a mall unit, the Ramadan clock.
Capacity is the functional need; labour skill, cleaning time, parts lead time and energy cost decide five-year cost. For expansion, size hood and panel for the second oven now - retrofitting after DCD sign-off means a fresh submission.
Trade-offs to say out loud: European reliability and resale versus 2.5x capex; automation cuts headcount but adds technician dependency; used saves 50% and voids the CE file.

Pre-quote: site plan, equipment schedule/BOQ with capacities, electrical single line or DEWA load letter, tenancy contract or Ejari, trade licence showing the food activity.
With the quotation: itemised BOQ with model numbers, datasheets, dimensional and utility drawings (kW, phase, gas type and mbar, water and drain points), warranty terms, payment terms.
For approvals: 2D layout showing one-directional flow for DM Food Safety; hood, duct and wet-chemical suppression drawings for Civil Defence; DEWA load approval; gas drawings with an approved contractor.
On delivery: invoice, bill of lading or AWB, certificate of origin, CE Declaration of Conformity, ECAS/G-Mark certificate for low-voltage machines, food-contact declaration for trays, moulds and belts, refrigerant charge.
After installation: method statement, commissioning report, O&M manuals in English, parts list, AMC schedule.

Technical: oven undersized for the real recipe - the buyer quotes daily kg but cannot state bake time per product. Refrigeration derated by ambient - a plant room with no ventilation drawing.
Commercial: currency and freight moving between quote and order - a EUR price with no validity date. Scope gap - a BOQ with no installation line.
Legal: importing with no CE file or G-Mark - the supplier cannot produce a Declaration of Conformity.
Financial: 50% advance to an unstocked trader - no showroom, mobile-only.
Operational: no local parts - the agent cannot name the last three shipped.
Schedule: DM or DCD rejection after equipment lands - the buyer never started the layout submission; or a Ramadan deadline against a 14-week lead time.
Supplier: an expired or invented agency letter. Customer: no trade licence or landlord NOC - the classic reason a paid order sits in a warehouse for months.

Four archetypes. Appointed OEM agent: manufacturer agency letter, factory-trained engineers, local parts stock, quotes on the OEM sales drawing, 10-16 weeks ex-works Europe. Multi-brand kitchen house: sources Italy, Turkey, Taiwan; strong on turnkey fit-out and DM submittals, weak on bakery process advice. Sharjah/Ajman fabricator: tables, hoods, troughs, trolleys and racks in 304 to drawing in 2-4 weeks, owns no imported process machines. Trader: Chinese stock off the shelf in Deira, 3-7 days, thin after-sales.
Verify before trusting: trade licence with the correct activity; an actual agency letter, not a website screenshot; a showroom you can visit; engineers resident in the UAE; a parts store you can walk into; three UAE installations you can phone; whether commissioning and gas connection are in-house.
Red flag: a quoted lead time shorter than the OEM's own published lead time.

Size from output, not catalogue. An 18-tray rotary rack oven on 600x800 trays gives 90-110 kg baked bread per hour at a 20-25 minute bake; a 4-deck 12-tray gives 40-55 kg/h. Mixer: bowl at 55-60% fill, dough weight = flour x (1 + absorption + additions), so a 130 L bowl takes ~50 kg. Match mixer batch to divider hopper and one oven load or you build a queue.
Key variables: kW and phase (400 V, 50 Hz), gas type and burner pressure in mbar (LPG vs piped natural gas), steam generator mass, tray pitch, trolley footprint, door width, feed-water hardness, condenser ambient rating.
Specify EN 1672-2 and EN ISO 14159 hygienic design, IEC/EN 60335-2-42 and -2-46 for electric ovens, AISI 304 contact surfaces, 316 near brine.
Failure points: undersized steam generator, condensing unit rated 32 degC in a 48 degC plant room, unbalanced trolley bearings, burner jetted for European gas pressure.

Pale crust, no oven spring: check steam first - water pressure and hardness, then generator temperature and scale, then burner or elements. UAE feed water scales a generator within months without softening.
Uneven bake in a rack oven: trolley rotation motor and bearing, then hood extraction pulling one side, then tray overloading.
Refrigeration tripping in July: condenser cleanliness, then plant-room ambient, then charge and superheat, then whether it was ever rated for 45-48 degC.
Mixer overheats dough: recheck DDT - UAE flour and mains water sit above 30 degC - then belt slip, then bowl fill over 60%.
Divider weight drift: dough temperature, oil level, knife wear.
Escalate to the OEM when a control board, burner or compressor fails in warranty, or a fault repeats three times. Prevent with quarterly AMC, a water softener from day one, monthly condenser cleaning and a spares kit.
Industrial lubricants and greases in the UAE must comply with MoIAT regulations, requiring a GHS-compliant MSDS and a Certificate of Conformity for legal importation.
To verify a tapered roller bearing equivalent, one must match the bore diameter, outside diameter, and total assembly width to ensure proper fitment and load distribution.

Checklist before quoting or fitting. Capture the full designation including cage, seal, clearance and heat-treatment suffixes. Confirm sleeve, nut and washer as a set. Measure the shaft and housing rather than trusting the drawing. Specify fit class against load and rotation. Confirm clearance against operating temperature. Name the lubricant, fill percentage and relubrication interval. State the mounting method, induction or hydraulic, never hammer and drift. Require laser alignment with a signed report.

Best practice: standardise on one clearance and one grease per plant area, hold critical spares on consignment for 12 to 30 week lead times, and freeze the shutdown parts list 12 weeks before the window.

Frequent mistakes: reusing a worn housing bore; greasing past 40 percent fill; heating with an open flame; buying genuine-priced goods at a Naif cash counter; letting a storekeeper cross a designation from memory; quoting free zone stock for a mainland site with no customs entry.

Models: unit price per line against an LPO, annual rate contract at a discount off list, consignment stock at large plants, day rate for alignment work, call-out plus parts.

Cost drivers ranked: brand tier first, a two to sixfold spread between SKF and a Chinese generic on the same designation; bore size, with anything over 200mm and 230 or 240 series stepping up sharply; special clearance or cage grade; certification, where 3.1 certs and ATEX add weeks; freight mode; quantity.

Budget tiers: AED 300 to 3,000 for small bearings and belts; AED 5,000 to 60,000 for a spherical roller with housing and seals; AED 60,000 to 400,000 a gearbox.

Terms: 30 to 90 days for known accounts, post-dated cheques still normal, LC for new buyers, 5 to 10 percent performance bond on ARCs, VAT 5 percent, corporate tax 9 percent over AED 375,000. Levers: consolidate lines, accept sea freight, commit volume.

The trade splits into rolling bearings, mounted units, seals and lubrication, and power transmission: belts, chain, couplings, gearboxes, motors. Language is designation-first: 6205-2RS1/C3, 22315 EK/C3 with H2315, SNL 3134, UCP 210, SPB 3550, 08B-1. MRO is maintenance, repair and operations; ARC an annual rate contract.

Buyers are maintenance planners and storekeepers, not procurement alone. Heavy end: ADNOC group, Borouge Ruwais, EGA Jebel Ali and Al Taweelah, Emirates Steel Arkan, DEWA M-Station, Union Cement, Stevin Rock quarries. Volume end: district cooling under Tabreed and Empower, pumping stations, food plants, ports.

Cycles: break-fix same day, planned shutdowns October to April, ARCs on one to three years, project builds via EPC. Q4 budget flush is real. Ramadan and the summer midday work ban compress site hours; Chinese New Year stretches generic supply four to six weeks.

Ask in order. One, full designation with suffixes, or OEM number plus machine make, model and serial. Two, quantity per line. Three, required-on-site date. Four, delivery emirate, mainland or free zone. Five, brand policy: genuine only or interchange. All mandatory. Six, certification: 3.1, ATEX or IECEx. Seven, buyer entity and whether ICV applies. Eight, shaft and housing sizes, speed, temperature, VFD, lubricant. Skippable on straight resupply, never on a repeat failure.

Rules. If the designation is partial, get a photo of the bore face before fanning out. If the bore exceeds 200mm or the series is 230 or 240, warn on 12 to 30 week lead times and price air freight separately. If the site is an ADNOC hazardous zone, force the ATEX question. If the buyer is ADNOC or EGA, require ICV. If the same bearing failed twice, route to a scoping call, not another quote.

Rolling bearings: deep groove 62 and 63, angular contact 72 and 73, self-aligning 12 and 22, spherical roller 222/223/230/231/240, tapered 302/320/322, cylindrical NU/NJ/NUP, needle, thrust and rod ends. Mounted: SNL and SAF plummer blocks, split blocks, UCP/UCF/SY units. Accessories: H adapter sleeves, AH withdrawal sleeves, KM nuts, MB washers, taconite and labyrinth seals, V-rings.

Power transmission: classical A/B/C and wedge SPZ/SPA/SPB/SPC belts, ribbed PJ and PK, timing HTD 8M and 14M, taper-lock and QD bushes, pulleys, ANSI and BS roller chain, sprockets, chain, jaw, tyre, grid, gear and disc couplings, torque limiters, shaft locking devices, helical, bevel-helical, worm and shaft-mounted gearboxes, IE3/IE4 motors.

Services: induction and hydraulic mounting, laser shaft alignment, dynamic balancing, vibration surveys, oil analysis, gearbox rebuild, ISO 15243 failure analysis.

Mandatory to quote: full designation with every suffix, or the OEM part number plus machine make, model and serial; quantity per line; required-on-site date; delivery emirate and whether the site is mainland or free zone; brand policy, genuine only or interchange; certification needed, meaning 3.1, ATEX or IECEx; and the buyer entity for VAT and ICV.

Strongly wanted: a photograph of the old bearing bore face and box, housing type and bore condition, measured shaft and housing diameters, speed, temperature and load, lubricant in use, and whether the drive runs on a VFD.

Providers reject an inquiry when the designation is partial, such as 22222 bare; when one piece is wanted with a free site survey; when there is no delivery address; when the brand is open but a target price is attached; when it is urgent with no PO authority named; or when genuine SKF is demanded at a counterfeit price.

Ministry of Industry and Advanced Technology, https://moiat.gov.ae, holds standards, conformity assessment and the conformity body register, the functions formerly under ESMA, plus ENAS accreditation and the Industrial Registry (Decree-Law 25 of 2022). Its In-Country Value programme at https://icv.moiat.gov.ae decides ADNOC and EGA awards.

Ministry of Economy and Tourism, https://www.moet.gov.ae. moec.gov.ae now redirects here. It registers commercial agencies, runs the Commercial Agencies Committee on exclusivity disputes, and takes trademark complaints against counterfeits.

Trade licences come from Dubai DET, Abu Dhabi via TAMM, or the free zone. Dubai Customs, https://www.dubaicustoms.gov.ae, covers import codes, duty and IPR seizures. Federal Tax Authority, https://tax.gov.ae, covers VAT and corporate tax. Law text sits at https://uaelegislation.gov.ae. The category is unlicensed.

Bearing tiers actually stocked here. Premium: SKF, Schaeffler with FAG and INA, Timken, NSK, NTN, Koyo. Mid: NKE, ZKL, URB, Nachi, Asahi, FYH, plus LYC and HRB from China. Budget generics fill Naif counters and are where counterfeits enter. Housings: SKF SNL, Cooper split, Dodge.

Power transmission: Gates and ContiTech for belts and Poly Chain, Optibelt, Fenner for taper-lock, Renold and Tsubaki for chain, KTR Rotex, Lovejoy, Falk Steelflex, Voith fluid couplings, Ringfeder and Tollok locking devices. Gearboxes: SEW-Eurodrive, Nord, Bonfiglioli, Flender under Siemens, Sumitomo. Motors: ABB, WEG, Siemens.

Verification that matters: OEM distributor locators and authenticity apps, EN 10204 3.1 certificates, ATEX or IECEx numbers checked on the issuing body register, MOIAT conformity registration at moiat.gov.ae, ICV certificates at icv.moiat.gov.ae.

They say they want the cheapest equivalent. They actually want the line running today with no repeat failure in six weeks, and a paper trail that survives an audit. Storekeepers optimise for shelf match, planners for shutdown dates, procurement for unit price. Those three fight and the quote gets blamed.

Real constraints: shutdown windows fixed months ahead, HSE induction and gate passes, crane bookings for heavy lifts, budget locked by cost centre, ICV scoring on large tenders.

Trade-offs to name out loud: a genuine premium bearing at four times the price with warranty and failure support against a generic that runs but voids OEM claims; air freight at AED 1,500 to 6,000 against 30 to 45 days by sea; the exact OEM designation against an interchange with a different cage or clearance; a full SNL housing set against reusing a worn housing bore that kills the new bearing in weeks.

Commercial: quotation with 7 to 30 day validity and Incoterms, proforma invoice, buyer LPO, delivery note signed at the gate, tax invoice showing the TRN, and a bank details letter for vendor registration.

Technical and compliance: EN 10204 2.1, 2.2 or 3.1 test certificates, manufacturer authenticity and warranty letter, authorised distributor letter, certificate of origin attested by the chamber of commerce, packing list, MSDS for greases, ATEX or IECEx certificate with a readable number, and a third-party inspection release note where the tender demands one.

UAE-specific: trade licence and TRN copies, an ICV certificate from MOIAT for ADNOC and EGA tenders, a customs import entry when free zone stock moves to mainland, site gate pass, HSE induction records.

Services: scope of work with acceptance criteria, method statement, alignment reports, failure analysis citing ISO 15243.

Counterfeit supply. First sign: price over 40 percent under authorised net, seller absent from the OEM distributor locator, laser etch inconsistent across one batch.

Wrong part. First sign: a quote that drops suffixes, offering 22222 where the machine needs 22222 EK/C3 with an H322 sleeve.

Grey import. First sign: genuine goods, no regional warranty, no authorisation.

Free zone to mainland. First sign: a price with no customs entry line, and the buyer later hit with duty and VAT.

Credit. First sign: a buyer pushing 120 days on a first order.

Schedule. First sign: a large spherical roller or gearbox with no confirmed factory slot; 12 to 30 weeks is normal and shutdown dates do not move.

Technical. First sign: repeat failures inside 90 days, meaning fit, alignment, sealing or lubrication, not the bearing.

Legal. First sign: exclusivity claimed with no MoET agency registration.

Four archetypes. Authorised distributors holding an OEM agency letter: real catalogue net pricing, factory backing, warranty honoured, but they will not touch a competing brand. Multi-brand stockists in Al Quoz, Ras Al Khor, Sharjah Industrial 1 to 18 and Mussafah ICAD: broad shelf, mixed provenance, fast. Deira Naif and Murshid Bazaar counters: cash, no traceability, highest counterfeit exposure. Engineering service houses: mounting, alignment, rebuild.

Free zone traders in JAFZA, Hamriyah and SAIF hold bonded stock for re-export. They cannot deliver to a mainland site without a customs import entry, 5 percent duty and 5 percent VAT.

Verify first: trade licence with an activity covering machinery spares, TRN, an OEM authorisation letter dated within a year, a warehouse you can visit, an ICV certificate for ADNOC or EGA work, and that the quoted suffix matches the shelf.

Standards in daily use: ISO 15 boundary dimensions, ISO 492 tolerance classes Normal to P4, ISO 281 dynamic rating and L10 life, ISO 76 static rating, ISO 5753 internal clearance C2 to C5, ISO 15243 damage classification, ISO 21940 balancing, ISO 20816 vibration severity, ISO 606 chain, ISO 4183 pulleys, ATEX and IECEx.

Scoping logic: shaft and housing diameter, tolerance and fit such as k5 shaft to H7 housing, load type and direction, speed against reference limit, operating temperature, sealing, lubricant and relubrication interval, service factor.

Failure points seen weekly: C3 replaced with CN on a hot fan and it seizes; interference fit on a rotating outer ring; an adapter sleeve driven up by feel instead of measured clearance reduction; VFD motors without insulated drive-end bearings, producing fluting; grease filled past 40 percent of free volume; belt tension set by thumb.

Recurring: repeat bearing failure at four to twelve weeks, almost always fit, alignment, sealing or lubrication, not the bearing; belts shredding in Al Quoz and quarry dust; gearbox oil over-temperature in July at 50C ambient; fluting on VFD-driven motor bearings; false brinelling on standby pumps beside running machines; moisture corrosion on coastal sites.

Diagnostic sequence: photograph the failed bearing, classify damage against ISO 15243, measure shaft and housing bore, check housing roundness and shoulder squareness, take a laser alignment reading, check soft foot, verify grease type and interval, set belt tension by frequency, then review load and speed.

Escalate to OEM engineering when damage is subsurface fatigue well inside calculated L10, or when two identical failures follow proven fit and alignment. Prevent with standard clearance, induction heaters and taconite seals.

Checklist before quoting: licence copy in hand; site survey with photographs of the distribution board, drains and access; treatment menu agreed; device class checked against the licence; registration route named; MEP loads issued in writing; delivery date tied to the inspection date; payment milestones and warranty in the contract. Best practice: never order a medical-class device before EDE authorisation is confirmed; put cost per shot in the quote; commission with the client present and sign a training record; hand over O&M manuals and calibration certificates on day one; book PPM before the warranty expires. Customer mistakes: buying on Instagram price, no floor drain, no trained operator, a landlord-set deadline. Provider mistakes: no site survey, an expired authorisation letter, a verbal warranty. Documentation mistakes: unattested origin certificates and missing conformity papers park goods at customs. Compliance mistake: energy devices bought against a beauty salon licence.

Models: supply-only CIF, supply-and-install lump sum, turnkey priced per treatment room, placement or rental against consumable minimums, lease-to-own, and annual maintenance at 8-12% of capex. Cost drivers ranked by impact: device class and brand origin; medical registration plus agent margin; wet-area civil and MEP works; handpiece and consumable cycles; freight, 5% customs duty and 5% VAT; out-of-hours mall or hotel access; training and warranty length. Bands: four-station salon fit-out AED 45k-120k; mid-market spa AED 250k-700k; hotel wet area AED 800k-3m; diode laser AED 90k-350k; HIFU AED 60k-180k; Class B autoclave AED 9k-22k. Terms: 50/40/10 across advance, pre-shipment and commissioning; letter of credit above AED 500k; credit only for hotel groups. Negotiate consumables, ex-demo units, training days and warranty, never list price.

Trade shorthand: front-of-house stations, back-of-house wet area, backwash units, pedicure spa jet versus pipeless, hammam, rasul, vichy, Class B autoclave to EN 13060, IPL, diode, HIFU, RF, EMS, fluence in J/cm2. Who buys: independent salon owners, hotel spa and FF&E procurement at the Jumeirah, Atlantis, Rixos and Address groups, gym and wellness chains, aesthetic clinic groups, and the fit-out contractor buying on the client's behalf. Supplier tiers: EDE-registered medical distributor, brand-agent spa specialist, Deira or Al Quoz general trading importer, Instagram direct-from-China reseller. Cycles follow fit-out, not the calendar: enquiry to install runs 4-12 weeks, hotel refurbs booked against low-season June to August closures. Peak buying September to January. Ramadan kills install labour, not orders. Beautyworld Middle East at DWTC resets pricing every spring.

Ask in order. 1 Emirate and exact address. 2 Which licence do you hold, and can you send a copy? Mandatory, never skipped. 3 Salon, spa or clinic, and the treatment menu. 4 Rooms and stations. 5 New fit-out or replacement. 6 Site condition: drainage, DB capacity, ceiling height, access. 7 Target date and licence inspection date. 8 Budget band. 9 Supply-only or turnkey. Rules: if the device is a Class 4 laser, medical IPL, HIFU or injectable-adjacent and the licence is a DED salon, stop and route to a clinic-licence conversation. If the buyer holds no EDE registration, tag the RFQ agent-required. If it is a wet area on a bare shell, route to a scoping call. If the budget is under AED 40k for a laser, expect grey market and say so. Fan out only at 80% confidence with licence, room count and date confirmed; below that, book the scoping call.

Four families. Salon: styling and barber chairs, backwash units, trolleys, nail bars, pedicure spas, dryers, reception joinery. Spa wet area: hammam and rasul rooms, vichy showers, sauna and steam cabins, hydro tubs, floatation. Treatment: three-motor electric and hydraulic massage tables, facial beds, wet tables. Devices: IPL, diode and Nd:YAG laser, HIFU, RF, EMS body sculpting, hydradermabrasion, cryolipolysis, skin analysis, plus Class B autoclaves and UV cabinets. Scope splits three ways: supply-only, supply-and-install, or turnkey with civil works, MEP coordination, commissioning and training. Alternatives: refurbished European, rental or placement against consumable minimums, lease-to-own. Lifecycle: brief, site survey, shop drawing, quote, 50% advance, 4-10 week shipment, 3-10 day install, commissioning, training, then annual maintenance contract.

Mandatory before anyone quotes: emirate and exact address; which licence the buyer holds, DED salon or spa versus DHA, DoH or MOHAP clinic, with a copy attached; the treatment menu; room and station count; new fit-out or replacement; site condition covering drainage, DB capacity, ceiling height and access; the licence inspection or opening date; budget band; supply-only or turnkey; and whether the buyer already holds EDE registration or needs the supplier to act as registered agent. Price and lead time move on device class, brand origin, registration status, civil and MEP scope, sea versus air freight, and install hours. Suppliers bin an enquiry with no licence copy, no room count, a request to put a Class 4 laser behind a salon licence, a sub-two-week deadline on indent goods, or shipping under someone else's registration.

Emirates Drug Establishment, https://www.ede.gov.ae/, is the sole federal regulator of medical and pharmaceutical products including medical devices and medical cosmetics under Federal Decree-Law 38/2024; marketing authorisation and establishment registration sit there, not MOHAP. MOIAT, https://moiat.gov.ae/, holds the conformity functions formerly at ESMA: certificates of conformity, Emirates Quality Mark and ENAS-designated assessment bodies. Facility licensing is emirate-level: DHA https://www.dha.gov.ae/, DoH https://www.doh.gov.ae/, MOHAP https://mohap.gov.ae/. Dubai Municipality https://www.dm.gov.ae/ permits salons, spas and health clubs and, under Dubai Law 7 of 2025, runs a unified contractor register. Add TDRA https://tdra.gov.ae/ for RF approval and Civil Defence for sauna and steam. Federal Decree-Law 25 of 2025 replaces the 1985 Civil Transactions Law from 1 June 2026.

Energy devices you will actually meet: Alma (Soprano), Candela (GentleMax Pro), Lumenis (M22, Splendor X), Cynosure, Cutera, InMode, BTL Emsculpt Neo, Venus Concept, Lutronic, DEKA and HydraFacial. UAE distribution runs through EDE-registered houses such as Al Zahrawi Medical, Gulf Drug and Dyna Trade, plus brand branch offices in Dubai Science Park and Dubai Healthcare City. Spa and wet area: Klafs, TyloHelo, Effegibi, Starpool, Gharieni, Lemi, Living Earth Crafts. Salon furniture: Takara Belmont, Maletti, Gamma & Bross, REM, Pietranera, Belvedere. Sterilisers: W&H Lisa, Melag, Tuttnauer, Getinge. What genuinely differs is whether the UAE agent holds a current manufacturer authorisation letter, stocks handpieces locally and employs biomedical engineers. Booking platforms like Fresha and Zenoti are not an equipment channel.

They ask for the best laser; they want the lowest cost per session on a brand clients recognise. The real constraints are the landlord fit-out window, the licence inspection date, ceiling height, an absent floor drain, distribution board capacity and mall night-work rules. Buyers price the machine and ignore cost per shot, engineer response time and operator training, which is exactly where the money leaks. Risk tolerance splits sharply: hotel spas buy brand plus a service SLA and pay for it, independents chase capex and end up orphaned. Name the trade-offs out loud. Chinese OEM saves 50-60% capex with no registration route, no parts and near-zero resale. Refurbished European saves 30% on six months warranty. Placement removes capex but fixes consumable pricing for three years. Pipeless pedicure spas cost more and pass hygiene inspection.

Commercial: quotation with technical submittal, LPO or supply contract and warranty certificate. Regulatory: manufacturer authorisation letter renewed yearly, CE certificate and Declaration of Conformity, Certificate of Free Sale, ISO 13485, EDE marketing authorisation and establishment registration for medical-class devices, MOIAT certificate of conformity for mains equipment, TDRA type approval for RF or wireless handpieces, plus IEC 60601 and 60825-1 test reports. Import: attested certificate of origin, commercial invoice, packing list, bill of lading, customs bill of entry. Site: shop drawings, MEP load schedule, method statement and risk assessment, Civil Defence NOC for sauna and steam, contractor third-party liability insurance. Handover: commissioning report, laser safety and calibration certificate, training record, maintenance contract. NDAs appear only on hotel FF&E tenders.

Technical: the device fails commissioning on power or water; the early sign is a supplier who skipped the site survey. Commercial: a 50% advance paid to a general trading importer with no service arm; the early sign is a quote with no warranty clause. Legal: a Class 4 laser installed behind a salon licence; the early sign is a buyer who cannot produce the licence copy. Financial: consumable pricing unfixed after year one; the early sign is a suspiciously cheap machine. Operational: no trained operator on opening day; the early sign is training left out of scope. Schedule: goods held at customs pending EDE authorisation; the early sign is a CIF quote with no registration line item. Provider: an expired manufacturer authorisation letter, so read the date. Customer: a budget anchored on an Instagram price for a grey-market unit.

Archetypes: the EDE-registered medical device distributor with biomedical engineers and stocked parts; the spa and wellness specialist with its own install crew and MEP draughtsman; the Deira, Naif or Al Quoz general trading importer selling furniture ex-stock with no service arm; the direct China or Korea importer selling on Instagram with no warranty path; and the brand's own UAE branch. Tell them apart by the trade licence activity line, not the website. Verify before trusting one: licence activity covering medical equipment trading for energy devices, EDE establishment registration and device authorisation, a current-year manufacturer authorisation letter, a named biomedical engineer, spare parts stock, three maintenance-contract references and a VAT TRN. Turnaround: ex-stock 3-10 days, Europe 6-10 weeks, China 4-7 weeks plus clearance.

Standards that decide acceptance: IEC 60601-1 and 60601-2-22 for laser systems, IEC 60825-1 for laser classification (hair removal is Class 4), IEC 60335 for commercial appliances, EN 13060 Class B for small steam sterilisers, ISO 13485 for the manufacturer's quality system. Scope room by room: 220-240V 50Hz single phase for chairs and beds, 380V three phase for sauna heaters and large hydro tubs; spare capacity at the distribution board; hot water volume and pressure; 50mm floor drain plus tanking in wet rooms; local extract at nail stations; ambient temperature and chiller load around lasers. Failures that recur: pipeless pedicure spas with no dedicated drain, undersized DB, laser thermal cutouts in a 26C room, wrong IP rating in a wet zone, hammam table set with no fall to drain, and 60Hz US-spec units sold as European.

Problems that recur: laser cutting out mid-session, pedicure spa backing up, steam room failing to hold temperature, autoclave failing its Class B cycle, handpiece counter exhausted mid-package. The diagnostic order a veteran follows: confirm the fault is reproducible; measure supply voltage and phase balance at the board; check ambient temperature and airflow around the unit; check water pressure, drain fall and filters; read the machine error log and shot counter; verify handpiece and consumable life; only then call the engineer. Root causes cluster in site services, not in machines. Resolutions: re-commission, upgrade the DB or drain, replace the handpiece, or claim warranty with serial number and commissioning report. Escalate to the manufacturer when a fault repeats after two visits or a safety interlock trips. Prevent with quarterly PPM and logged water quality.
CAT A refers to the base building standard provided by the landlord, whereas CAT B refers to the interior fit-out customized by the tenant to meet their specific operational needs.

Checklist before recommending any operator: trade licence current and showing the correct activity; head lease or Ejari in the operator's own name; written landlord consent to sublicense; permission to issue Ejari or the free zone equivalent; Civil Defence certificate for the floor; TRN on a sample invoice; deposit payable to the entity that signs; a written reinstatement scope; a seat cap for shared areas.
Best practice: align the end date to the licence anniversary, take the space one desk short and add later at a pre-agreed rate, negotiate free months instead of a lower headline, and cap the annual uplift at signature.
Customer mistakes: paying twelve months upfront to an unverified centre, and assuming a free zone flexi desk supports a mainland licence.
Provider mistakes: overselling visa quota and quoting ex-VAT silently.
Documentation mistake: a verbal fit-out promise and no exit condition on paper. Compliance mistake: signing before the licensing authority confirms the address.

Dubai 2026 ranges, monthly unless noted. Hot desk AED 500-1,500. Dedicated desk AED 1,200-2,800. Serviced office AED 2,500-4,500 per desk in Business Bay, Barsha Heights and JLT; AED 4,000-7,000 in DIFC, One Central and ICD Brookfield. Abu Dhabi runs 10-20% above Dubai for grade; the northern emirates 30-50% below. Virtual office AED 4,000-9,000 a year, or AED 9,000-20,000 with Ejari. Free zone licence plus flexi desk packages run AED 12,500-25,000 a year at IFZA, Meydan, SHAMS and RAKEZ, and AED 35,000-60,000 at DMCC or DIFC. Meeting rooms AED 120-450/hour.
Cost drivers ranked: licence and visa quota, location and grade, term, headcount, fit-out and reinstatement, after-hours HVAC, parking at AED 500-1,500.
Terms: 1-3 months deposit, 1-4 post-dated cheques or autopay, 5% VAT on everything.
Levers: term, prepayment, low-floor units, free months rather than a cut headline, capped uplift.

Vocabulary a buyer throws at you: flexi desk, hot desk, dedicated desk, serviced office, managed or office-as-a-service, virtual office, Ejari, Tawtheeq in Abu Dhabi, Establishment Card, NOC, CAT A and CAT B fit-out, reinstatement, chiller-free, service charge, BUA versus NIA, cost per desk, visa quota.
Buyers split four ways: a new licence needing only a compliant address; a 5-40 person SME wanting turnkey, no capex; a corporate placing a project or country-entry team on a 6-24 month horizon; and a landlord or free zone appointing an operator to run a floor.
Tiers run global brands, regional platforms, landlord-operated centres, free zone in-house workspaces, and independent one-floor centres. Seasonality is real: enquiries peak September-November and January-March, collapse through Ramadan and July-August, and renewals cluster on the trade licence anniversary, not the calendar year.

Ask in this order. 1 Must this space carry a trade licence and residence visas? Mandatory. 2 If yes, which authority - DET mainland, DDA/TECOM, or a named free zone? Mandatory. 3 Emirate and preferred districts. Mandatory. 4 Headcount now and at month 12. Mandatory. 5 Start date and term. Mandatory. 6 Open desks or enclosed office. Mandatory. 7 Budget band. Skippable once, then required. 8 Parking and meeting hours. Skippable.
Rules. If a licence is required under mainland DET, exclude every free zone flexi desk and route only to centres that can issue Ejari. If visas are needed, compute area against the zone rule before fanning out. If headcount is 1-2 with no visas, route to hot desk and virtual office providers only. If headcount exceeds 25 or term exceeds 24 months, this is a managed office - book a scoping call. If the buyer will not name emirate or headcount, do not send the RFQ.

Taxonomy, cheapest to heaviest. Virtual office: registered address, mail handling, and where permitted an Ejari or flexi desk supporting the licence and a fixed visa allocation. Hot desk: unassigned seat, business hours. Dedicated desk: named seat, lockable pedestal, 24/7 access. Serviced private office: 1-30 pax, furnished, all-in monthly including reception, cleaning, internet, utilities and meeting-room credit. Day office and meeting room by the hour. Managed office: a bespoke floor built and run under the client's brand, fixed rate per desk over 24-60 months.
Coworking is not a lease: no rent-free period, no leasehold interest, rarely an Ejari. Alternatives are a fitted Grade B lease or a sublease.
Lifecycle: brief, shortlist, viewing, licence check, proposal, agreement, deposit and cheques, onboarding, renewal or exit. Selection turns on address validity first, cost per desk second.

Mandatory before any operator will price: emirate and preferred districts; headcount now and at month 12; whether the space must carry a trade licence, and under which authority; how many residence visas are needed; start date; term; open desks versus enclosed office; budget band; and whether an Ejari or Tawtheeq document is required.
Skippable at first pass: building brand, parking bays, meeting-room hours, IT specifics.
Price and turnaround move on: visa quota, term, enclosed versus open, floor level and view, after-hours HVAC, and any partition work that triggers Civil Defence approval.
Operators drop an enquiry when the buyer will not name headcount or start date, asks for an Ejari the centre cannot legally issue, wants a one-month term with three visas, or demands a mainland licence address inside a free zone. Anonymous is fine here; vague is not.

Dubai mainland licensing sits with the Department of Economy and Tourism, DET, at https://www.det.gov.ae, which ties each licence to a registered address. Ejari and RERA lease oversight sit with Dubai Land Department, https://dubailand.gov.ae, which runs the Dubai REST app for registration, renewal and disputes. Fit-out permits are Dubai Municipality at https://www.dm.gov.ae. TECOM communities including Dubai Internet City, Media City and d3 fall under Dubai Development Authority at https://www.dda.gov.ae, which licenses by cluster and permits its own fit-outs. Abu Dhabi mainland is the Department of Economic Development at https://added.gov.ae. Free zones self-regulate: DMCC, https://www.dmcc.ae, and IFZA, https://ifza.com.
Federal Tax Authority at https://tax.gov.ae covers 5% VAT and corporate tax. No accreditation exists for running a business centre; the licence activity is the gate.

Operators active in the UAE: IWG under the Regus, Spaces and HQ brands; Servcorp, strong in Emirates Towers, ICD Brookfield and Abu Dhabi's Etihad Towers; WeWork Middle East; The Executive Centre; Compass Office; and homegrown names including Nook, Nasab, A4 Space, AstroLabs and Bureau, plus Letswork, which aggregates day-pass access.
Landlord and government-backed workspaces: DIFC Innovation Hub, One Central by Dubai World Trade Centre, in5 by TECOM, Dtec in Dubai Silicon Oasis, Hub71 in Abu Dhabi, Sheraa in Sharjah, and the in-house flexi desk products of RAKEZ, SHAMS, Meydan, IFZA and DMCC.
What genuinely differs: whether the centre can lawfully issue an Ejari or free zone address, the visa quota attached, and whether the operator holds the head lease or is itself a sub-tenant.
Platforms quoted: OfficeRnD, Nexudus, Yardi Kube, Cobot, Optix, Kisi or Brivo for access.

What they say: I need a cheap desk. What they mean, three questions in: a licence address that survives renewal, visa slots for two or three staff, a Metro-adjacent postcode a client will respect, and no capex. Price is rarely the binding constraint; certainty of the licence and visa outcome is.
Real constraints: the licence must sit with a specific authority; the package caps visas; the CFO refuses a balance-sheet lease liability; the parent needs a named-brand building.
Trade-offs to name aloud: a cheap free zone package buys a licence but not a desk anyone can work at; a prestige address doubles cost per desk without changing productivity; a 12-month lock earns 15-25% off but blocks a pivot; an independent centre saves 20% and carries sublease risk; open coworking is unusable for a team on calls.
Risk tolerance is low on compliance, high on aesthetics. Sell certainty, not photography.

From the operator: licence or membership agreement with a schedule of services, house rules, and their own valid trade licence showing a business centre or coworking activity. For any licence-bearing deal: an Ejari certificate in Dubai or Tawtheeq in Abu Dhabi, or the free zone lease and facility agreement, plus the landlord's written consent to sublicense where the operator is a sub-tenant.
From the client: trade licence copy, passport and Emirates ID of the signatory, memorandum or certificate of incorporation, and a signed authority letter where a PRO acts.
Money papers: deposit receipt, post-dated cheques or a direct debit mandate, a VAT-compliant invoice carrying the operator's TRN, and a mutual NDA on managed deals.
Building papers: Civil Defence certificate, fit-out approval and as-builts, contractor insurance, and a reinstatement scope agreed in writing at signature, not at exit.

Legal: the operator is a sub-tenant without landlord consent. Early sign - no head lease or Ejari in their own name. At renewal that means eviction and a licence with no valid address.
Commercial: the quoted rate excludes VAT, service charge, chiller or parking. Early sign - one all-in number with no line items.
Compliance: promised visa quota exceeds what the zone allows. Early sign - the salesperson quotes visas without asking the square metres.
Financial: the deposit is payable to an entity other than the one signing.
Operational: chronic overselling of hot desks. Early sign - no seat availability data and no disclosed cap.
Schedule: fit-out promised in six weeks with no Civil Defence submission date named.
Customer-side: a buyer who hides the licensing authority, or wants a mainland address at free zone pricing - that dies at document stage.
Provider-side: no TRN on the invoice.

Five archetypes. Global branded operator: consistent SLA, strongest meeting-room network, least flexible paperwork, highest price. Regional platform of 3-15 sites: decent product, negotiates hard in the last week of a quarter. Landlord-operated centre: best security of tenure, weakest service culture. Free zone in-house workspace: only viable if the licence sits in that zone, quota fixed by package. Independent single-floor centre: cheapest and often good, but frequently a sub-tenant itself, the biggest hidden risk in this trade.
Verify before trusting anyone: the operator's trade licence and listed activity, head lease versus sublease, written landlord consent to sublicense, permission to issue Ejari, and Civil Defence certification for the floor.
Turnaround: hot desk same day; serviced office 2-5 working days; Ejari and licence address 5-10 days; managed fit-out 8-16 weeks.

Scope on density first. Plan 8-12 sqm gross per person for serviced offices and 6-8 sqm in dense coworking; under 6 sqm fails comfort and often the area-per-visa test. Mainland visa quota is assessed on usable area, historically around 9 sqm per visa, and is confirmed by DET and GDRFA, never by the operator.
Variables that decide feasibility: HVAC capacity and after-hours chiller availability, occupancy load and egress width, sprinkler and detector layout after any partition change, acoustic separation for call-heavy teams, Cat6A cabling, one wireless access point per 8-10 desks, 200-300 VA per workstation, and access control that logs by individual.
Failure points repeat: partitions built without a Civil Defence-approved drawing, sprinkler heads blocked by new ceilings, single-ISP buildings with no diverse route, base-build cooling shut off at 18:00, and a landlord NOC never obtained.

Licence renewal rejected on address: check the Ejari is live and matches the licence, then that the unit number is identical on both, then that the operator's own licence and master lease are current. Fix by re-issuing the Ejari or relocating before the grace window closes.
Visa refused: verify area-per-visa against the zone rule, then the establishment card and immigration file, then quota consumed.
Internet outages: establish whether the centre buys wholesale from the building or holds its own carrier account, and whether a second route exists.
Overcrowding: request weekday occupancy logs from the access system before accepting a denial.
Escalate to the landlord when consent cannot be shown, and to the Rental Dispute Centre or free zone authority when deposits are withheld with no reinstatement scope. Prevent all of it by verifying the paper chain before the first cheque clears.

topic: Field expertise — UAE codes, standards & specs
content:
CARPENTRY & JOINERY — UAE FIELD KNOWLEDGE BASE

GOVERNING AUTHORITY & APPROVALS: Carpentry/joinery itself is largely unlicensed at point of installation, but context drives approvals. Any fit-out inside a building (new joinery, partitions, false ceilings with wood elements, kitchens) in Dubai typically needs a Dubai Municipality (or Dubai Development Authority for DDA-jurisdiction plots, Trakhees for free-zone/ports areas like JAFZA, Palm, TECOM) fit-out permit obtained via the landlord/main contractor before works start. If joinery affects fire escape routes, fire-rated doors, or combustible material use in corridors/lobbies, Dubai Civil Defence (DCD) approval per the UAE Fire and Life Safety Code of Practice is required — timber species, veneers, and adhesives near escape routes must meet fire-rating/flame-spread requirements. Contractors must hold a valid UAE trade license (carpentry/joinery or general contracting/fit-out classification) with DED or free-zone authority; larger commercial jobs require an approved main/fit-out contractor to sign off. Custom furniture for export or with electrical components (lighting in cabinetry) may need ESMA conformity marking on integrated fittings.

STANDARDS: BS and EN standards for timber grading, plywood/MDF (moisture and formaldehyde emission class — E1/E0), door sets (fire door ratings referenced against DCD-recognized test standards), and BS EN standards for hardware (hinges, locks) load/cycle testing. ISO 9001 quality references are common in tender specs. ASTM standards sometimes referenced for panel products in imported US-spec projects.
