Electrical Work & Contractors in the UAE operates under a layered regulatory framework. **DEWA** (Dubai Electricity and Water Authority) is the primary authority for all electrical installations in Dubai: contractors must hold a valid DEWA-approved contractor registration, and all LV/MV designs require DEWA NOC and final connection approval. Drawings must be submitted via DEWA's SMILE portal. For free zones and port areas (Jebel Ali, DAFZA, Dubai South), **Trakhees** (PCFC Engineering) issues the equivalent permits. **Dubai Municipality** (DM) oversees building electrical compliance under the Dubai Building Code. **Dubai Civil Defence (DCD)** approval is mandatory for any fire-alarm, emergency-lighting, or fire-rated cable installation, referencing the UAE Fire and Life Safety Code of Practice. For solar PV and grid-tied systems, **Shams Dubai** net-metering regulations under DEWA govern system sizing, inverter approval, and export-tariff agreements. Abu Dhabi installations fall under **ADDC/AADC** and **ADCD** equivalents.

Core technical standards include **IEC 60364** (low-voltage electrical installations), **IEC 60947** (switchgear), **BS 7671** (IET Wiring Regulations, widely referenced by UAE consultants), **NFPA 70** (NEC, used on some US-aligned projects), **IEC 61439** (switchboard assemblies), and **IEC 62305** (lightning protection). DEWA's own **Distribution Code** and **Technical Standards** documents are binding for utility-side work. Cable specifications typically reference **IEC 60502** and **IEC 60228**. ESMA conformity marking applies to imported electrical equipment and fittings sold in the UAE.

Scope discussions cover: LV panels (MCCs, DBs, MDPs), MV switchgear (11 kV/33 kV), cable sizing and routing (XLPE, SWA, LSZH, fire-rated FP200), earthing/bonding systems, busbar trunking, UPS and standby generators (AMF panels), lighting design (lux levels, LED drivers), EV charging infrastructure, solar PV (on-grid, off-grid, hybrid), power factor correction capacitor banks, and structured cabling interfaces.

**Price drivers:** cable quantity and cross-section (copper vs. aluminium), panel complexity and brand (Schneider, ABB, Siemens, Legrand), conduit type (GI vs. PVC vs. cable tray), DEWA/DCD approval fees, civil works for trenching, specialist labour (DEWA-certified electricians), material lead times for MV equipment, and project location (free zone vs. mainland adds permit cost).

**Compliance pitfalls and qualifying questions:** Unlicensed contractors risk DEWA blacklisting and DM stop-work orders — always confirm the contractor holds a current DEWA-approved contractor card and a valid DED/DM trade licence. Red flags include

In Dubai, electrical design and installation work must be done by contractors/consultants enrolled with DEWA (Dubai Electricity & Water Authority). All consultants and electrical contractors must enrol with DEWA to undertake works on any premises in the emirate, and are classified into categories based on capability. Contractors must employ DEWA-certified electrical engineers and technicians who pass DEWA's technical examinations.

The governing technical document is the DEWA Regulations for Electrical Installations (2017 Edition), which references the IET Wiring Regulations (BS 7671) with UAE amendments. At federal/emirate level, the UAE Electricity Wiring Regulations 2020 (issued by the Department of Energy) also apply, especially in Abu Dhabi; Dubai installations follow DEWA.

Workflow: enrolled contractor submits design/drawings, obtains Building NOC (electricity), executes work, then submits an Inspection Certificate in DEWA's prescribed form. All installations are subject to DEWA inspection, testing and final approval before energising. In special-jurisdiction free zones, Trakhees (Ports, Customs & Free Zone Corporation) or DDA (Dubai Development Authority) handle approvals instead of DEWA's standard route. Company must also hold a valid Dubai Economy / DET electrical contracting trade licence.

Core standard: DEWA Regulations for Electrical Installations (2017 Edition), aligned to BS 7671 (IET Wiring Regulations, 18th Edition) with UAE amendments; UAE Electricity Wiring Regulations 2020 at federal level. Control/instrument cables comply with BS 6231. Earthing per DEWA: copper/steel earth rod (typically 20mm/26mm dia) driven to minimum 3m depth in a 300x300x300mm inspection pit; earth and bonding conductors sized by the adiabatic equation in BS 7671.

Key materials/equipment: copper conductors (not aluminium for final circuits), PVC/XLPE insulated cables, conduit/trunking, distribution boards from Schneider, ABB, Legrand, Hager; MCBs, RCBOs and 30mA RCDs for socket/wet-area protection; breaking capacity rated in kA (6kA/10kA). IP-rated fittings for wet areas.

Vocabulary: connected load (kW), DB (distribution board), MCB, RCBO, RCD, isolator, points/circuits, ring/radial final circuit, earth bonding, kA breaking capacity, inspection & testing certificate. Mandatory tests: insulation resistance, continuity, earth electrode resistance, polarity, recorded on DEWA's Inspection & Testing Certificate prior to energising.

Indicative only (Dubai, verify per project). Price drivers: number of points/circuits, cable runs and sizes, single vs three-phase, DB capacity, copper price, whether DEWA inspection/NOC and material supply are included, occupied vs new build. Small fault repairs and single-point additions are typically a few hundred AED plus call-out; full apartment/villa rewires and fit-outs are quoted per point or lump-sum running into thousands of AED depending on size.

Red flags: lump-sum 'electrical works' with no point/circuit count or cable schedule; undersized cable (1.5mm2 on socket circuits, no 2.5mm2); missing 30mA RCD on socket/wet-area circuits; aluminium instead of copper conductors; off-brand/unbranded DB and breakers with no stated kA rating; no DEWA enrolment number; DEWA inspection, NOC and connection fees excluded or hidden; VAT (5%) not shown; no testing & inspection certificate offered; quote far below others usually means uncertified labour or no DEWA approval, leaving the installation unconnectable or unsafe.

DEWA Enrolment of Consultants & Contractors — https://www.dewa.gov.ae/en/about-us/service-guide/general-information/enrollment-of-consultants-contractors
DEWA Circulars & Regulations — https://www.dewa.gov.ae/en/builder/useful-tools/dewa-circulars
DEWA Regulations for Electrical Installations 2017 (PDF) — https://www.dewa.gov.ae/-/media/DEWA_Regulations_for_Electrical_Installations_2017_Edition.ashx
DEWA Consultants & Contractors Classification — https://crm.dewa.gov.ae/irj/portal/anonymous/cclass
DEWA Technical Publications & Resources — https://www.dewa.gov.ae/en/builder/useful-tools/tech-publications-resources
UAE Electricity Wiring Regulations 2020 (Dept of Energy PDF) — https://www.doe.gov.ae/-/media/Project/DOE/Department-Of-Energy/Media-Center-Publications/EWR-2020-EN-V8-B-Online.pdf
BS 7671 18th Edition (IET) — https://electrical.theiet.org/bs-7671-18th-edition-wiring-regulations/
DEWA Getting Electricity Fit-Out Connections — https://www.dewa.gov.ae/en/builder/electricity-network-services/getting-electricity-fit-out-connections
DEWA Building NOC Electricity — https://www.dewa.gov.ae/en/about-us/service-guide/builder-services/building-no-objection-certificate-Electricity
Trakhees (PCFC) — https://www.trakhees.ae/

topic: Field expertise — UAE codes, standards & specs
content:
# ELECTRICAL SUPPLIERS — UAE FIELD KNOWLEDGE BASE

## GOVERNING AUTHORITY & APPROVALS

Electrical work in the UAE is primarily regulated by **DEWA (Dubai Electricity and Water Authority)** for all grid-connected installations, metering, and connection approvals. Any project requiring mains connection must obtain DEWA's **Electrical Installation Approval Certificate** and **Connection Agreement**. For solar installations and net-metering, **Shams Dubai** (DEWA's solar programme) issues separate approvals and handles grid-tie compliance.

**Dubai Civil Defence (DCD)** and the **UAE Fire and Life Safety Code of Practice** govern fire-safety aspects of electrical systems, particularly emergency lighting, fire alarm integration, and cable routing in high-rise and commercial buildings. DCD issues **Fire Safety Certificates** and conducts inspections on completion.

**Dubai Municipality** oversees building permits and electrical plan approvals as part of the overall construction permit (via the **Building Department**). Electrical drawings must be stamped by a licensed consultant engineer registered with the **Dubai Municipality**.

**SIRA (Security Industry Regulatory Agency)** and **Dubai Police** regulate CCTV and security-related electrical installations; these require separate licensing and approval if integrated with alarm systems.

For free-zone and port installations, **Trakhees** (Jebel Ali Free Zone Authority) and relevant port authorities impose additional electrical compliance requirements.

**Emirates Conformity** and **ESMA (Emirates Standards and Metrology Authority)** enforce product certification and conformity for electrical equipment imported into the UAE; CE marking alone is insufficient—UAE-specific certification or ESMA approval is mandatory for many components.

## STANDARDS

Electrical design and installation must comply with **IEC 60364** (International Electrotechnical Commission wiring code), **NFPA 70 (National Electrical Code)** principles, and **BS 7909** for temporary installations. DEWA enforces its own **DEWA Technical Regulations for Electrical Installations** and **DEWA Grid Code**. Emergency systems follow **NFPA 110** and **NFPA 111** (backup power). Fire-safety systems adhere to **NFPA 72** (fire alarms) and **NFPA 101** (Life Safety Code). Solar installations must meet **IEC 61724** (PV system performance) and Shams Dubai's technical guidelines. Grounding and earthing follow **IEC 61936** and DEWA specifications. Cable sizing, voltage drop, and load calculations are governed by **IEC 60228** and DEWA load-demand tables.

## SCOPE & SPECS

Electrical suppliers in the UAE typically provide: **main distribution boards (MDBs)**, **sub-distribution boards (SDBs)**, **cable trays and conduits**, **power cables** (single-core and multi-core, rated for 0.6/1 kV, 3.6/6 kV, or higher), **control and automation equipment**, **switchgear and circuit breakers** (MCBs, RCBOs,

Best practice: quote against the approved submittal, not the BOQ wording; put brand, catalogue number and country of origin on every line; state a validity period and the copper-adjustment basis; deliver with mill and routine test certificates against drum numbers; keep fire-rated and LSZH stock segregated from standard PVC. Common mistakes: buying on rate per metre without checking conductor class and weight per metre; assuming a tier-1 catalogue number means a European factory; specifying 6kA where the fault level at the supply demands 10kA or more; ordering exact BOQ quantities with no 5-10% wastage allowance on wiring; forgetting drum deposits and cutting charges; skipping the consultant submittal and having material rejected on site; running a credit account past terms until deliveries stop mid-programme; omitting the 5% VAT line; and leaving no spare ways in the DB, which turns a later EV-charger or solar retrofit into a board replacement instead of a breaker addition.

LME copper dominates cable pricing, so quotes carry short validity - 3-7 days is normal, 24 hours in a volatile week - with a copper-adjustment clause tied to price on the day of delivery. The AED is pegged at 3.6725/USD so FX is not a driver; 5% VAT applies, plus 5% GCC customs duty on mainland import, suspended while goods sit in a free zone. Cost drivers: conductor cross-section and core count, copper vs aluminium (aluminium is cheaper per amp-metre but needs a size up plus bimetallic lugs), armouring, LSZH over PVC, fire-rated at a multiple of standard, drum length and cutting charges, brand and country of origin. Terms: 30-90 day credit against trade references, post-dated cheques still standard, cash or advance for new accounts, LC on imported MV gear. Levers: full drums instead of cut lengths, one consolidated delivery, and a committed call-off schedule.

UAE electrical supply is a three-tier trade: manufacturers (Ducab, Elsewedy Electric, alfanar), brand-franchised distributors and agents (Al Mashroom for Legrand, Majid Electromechanical for Schneider), and general stockists clustered in Deira/Naif, Al Quoz, Ras Al Khor, Sharjah Industrial Areas 4-13 and Mussafah. Buyers are MEP contractors, panel builders, FM companies, developer procurement teams and free-zone factories. Core vocabulary: DB, SMDB/MDB, MCB/MCCB/ACB, RCBO, RCD, XLPE, SWA, LSZH, fire-rated, busbar trunking, containment (tray/ladder/trunking/conduit), ELV. The buying cycle tracks construction: BOQ enquiry, technical submittal, consultant approval, then call-off releases against site progress over 6-18 months. Seasonality: Q1 and Q4 tender peaks; June-September drives villa DB and AC-circuit replacement; Ramadan and peak summer compress site access and delivery windows.

Ask in order, mandatory first. 1) Supply-only, or supply and install? If install, or if any meter, load or connection change is involved, it needs an authority-enrolled contractor - reclassify to Electrical Contractors. 2) Which emirate and delivery address, mainland or free zone? 3) What is being bought: cable, switchgear/DB, lighting, accessories, containment or ELV? 4) Quantities and sizes, or is a BOQ/cable schedule available - ask for the file. 5) Brand specified, or is approved-equal acceptable? 6) Is there an approved consultant submittal? 7) Required delivery date. 8) Cash or credit - if credit, trade licence and TRN. No quantities and no BOQ means not quotable: ask once, then park. Fire-rated cable, fire alarm and emergency lighting route only to DCD-listed suppliers. MV gear, transformers or generators escalate as long-lead. Never ask the buyer to pick a spec or a budget.

Cable: building wire 1.5-6mm2 (450/750V), LV power 600/1000V XLPE and PVC single and multicore, SWA armoured, LSZH, fire-resistant to BS 6387 CWZ, flexible and control, MV 6.35/11kV and 33kV, overhead conductor, welding and instrument cable. Protection: MCB, RCBO, RCD, MCCB, ACB, contactors, relays, VFDs, soft starters, ATS/AMF panels, capacitor banks. Assemblies: consumer units, DBs, SMDBs, MDBs, MCCs, feeder pillars and IEC 61439-2 type-tested panels. Also wiring accessories, lighting and LED drivers, emergency and exit fittings, earthing (rods, tape, exothermic welds), lightning protection, containment, glands and lugs, ELV, EV chargers, solar PV balance-of-system, UPS and generators. Wrapped services that win the order: cut-to-length off the drum, kitting per floor or per DB, submittal packs with datasheets, panel assembly and wiring, and site delivery with offloading.

To quote at all a supplier needs: line-by-line quantities with units, cable type, cores, size and voltage grade (450/750V, 600/1000V, 6.35/11kV), brand plus catalogue number plus country of origin, breaker rating in A with Icu in kA and trip curve, DB way count and IP rating, delivery emirate and exact site, required date, and payment basis. A complete quote states lead time per line, drum lengths and whether cut lengths carry a charge, validity and the copper-adjustment basis, delivery terms including offloading and floor access, 5% VAT shown separately, and warranty. Suppliers ignore or reject an enquiry when: no quantities are given, it says 'as per drawing' with no drawing attached, no brand or approved-equal position is stated, no delivery emirate, credit requested with no trade licence or TRN, or a 200-line BOQ arrives with a same-day deadline on non-stock items.

Dubai: DEWA (https://www.dewa.gov.ae/) enrols contractors, issues the Building NOC and energises; the binding document is the DEWA Regulations for Electrical Installations 2017 Edition, still current, aligned to BS 7671. Abu Dhabi and Al Ain: TAQA Distribution via ADDC (https://www.addc.ae/) and AADC (https://www.aadc.ae/), with the Department of Energy (https://www.doe.gov.ae/) publishing the UAE Electricity Wiring Regulations 2020. Sharjah: SEWA (https://www.sewa.gov.ae/). Ajman, UAQ, RAK, Fujairah: EtihadWE (https://www.etihadwe.ae/), which replaced FEWA under Federal Law 31 of 2020. Free zones: Trakhees/PCFC (https://www.trakhees.ae/); TECOM areas: DDA. Fire safety: Dubai Civil Defence (https://www.dcd.gov.ae/), UAE Fire and Life Safety Code of Practice 2018 as amended. Product conformity: MoIAT (https://moiat.gov.ae/) runs ECAS and EQM, absorbing the former ESMA role.

Regional manufacture: Ducab (six UAE plants including Jebel Ali; Ducab HV, Ducab Metals, AEI Cables UK, NCF Oman) is the default consultant-specified cable; also Oman Cables, Elsewedy Electric, alfanar and RR Kabel. Protection tier-1: Schneider Electric, ABB, Siemens, Eaton, Legrand, Hager, Terasaki; tier-2 accepted on warehouses and labour accommodation: LS Electric, Chint, Havells. Accessories: MK (Honeywell), Legrand, Schneider Unica/Clipsal, ABB, Hager, Panasonic. Lighting: Signify/Philips, Ledvance/Osram, Zumtobel, Thorn, NVC, Opple. UAE panel builders: Binghalib, Powertech Switchgear, Emirates Transformers & Switchgear. Commercially critical: the same tier-1 catalogue number built in India, China or Europe can differ 15-30% in price - pin the country of origin and demand the authorised-distributor letter, because parallel-import and relabelled stock is common in this market.

Three buyers with different objectives sit behind one enquiry. The contractor wants price, credit and delivery certainty; the consultant wants compliance with the specified brand list and an approved submittal; the owner or FM wants lifecycle cost and spares availability. Name the trade-offs: copper vs aluminium (capex against termination complexity and route space); PVC vs LSZH (cost against smoke toxicity in occupied, underground and atrium areas); 6kA vs 10kA (dictated by the fault level at the supply, not by preference); tier-1 European vs tier-2 Asian protection (price against 20-year spares availability); staged call-off vs buying the full cable schedule (copper price exposure against storage cost and site copper theft). Warn on substitution: a brand swap outside the approved submittal triggers a 2-4 week re-approval cycle that costs more than the saving.

At enquiry: BOQ or cable schedule, single-line diagram, load schedule and layout drawings. At approval: material submittal with datasheets, catalogue cut sheets and a clause-by-clause compliance statement against the specification. At manufacture and delivery: mill/works test certificate and routine test certificate referenced to drum numbers, IEC 61439-2 type-test or design-verification report for assemblies, MoIAT ECAS/EQM conformity certificate for regulated products, Dubai Central Laboratory approval and DCD listing for fire-rated cable, fire alarm and emergency lighting, certificate of origin and commercial invoice for customs, authorised-distributor letter, ISO 9001 and warranty. Commercially: LPO reference on every delivery note and a tax invoice showing TRN and 5% VAT. At handover the installing contractor files the DEWA Inspection & Testing Certificate before energisation.

Technical and counterfeit: copper-clad aluminium sold as copper, nominal 2.5mm2 delivered at 2.1mm2, and relabelled breakers carrying a kA rating they cannot clear. Defend with drum print checks, weight per metre against IEC 60228, and mill certificates. Commercial: copper moving between quote and delivery on a fixed-price subcontract; long-lead MV switchgear, transformers and generators at 16-40 weeks stranding a programme. Financial: 90-day cheques from a contractor with a stretched payment record - bounced-cheque recovery is slow, so take the trade licence, TRN and two trade references before extending credit. Legal: supplying non-ECAS or non-DCD-listed goods, or substituting a brand outside the approved submittal, turns delivered material into a non-payable write-off. Operational: copper theft from site stores, drums degrading in sun and sand, and delivery to the wrong emirate.

Archetypes: (1) manufacturer direct - best price on full drums, 4-10 week lead on non-stock sizes, minimum order quantities; (2) authorised distributor - genuine goods, principal warranty, traceable, 5-15% premium; (3) general stockist - fastest, mixed and sometimes grey stock, thin documentation; (4) panel builder/assembler; (5) online traders holding no stock who broker the same wholesalers. Verify before quoting a buyer: DET/DED or free-zone trade licence carrying an electrical trading activity, VAT TRN, authorised-distributor letter from the principal, ISO 9001, DCD/DCL listing for fire-rated cable and emergency lighting, and the ability to produce mill and routine test certificates against drum numbers. Delivery norms: Dubai and Sharjah same or next day from stock, Abu Dhabi and Al Ain 1-2 days, RAK and Fujairah 2-3 days; Jebel Ali and DAFZA need customs entry/exit paperwork.

Sizing is where quotes diverge. UAE ambient of 45-50C, grouping in trays, and buried duct or sand thermal resistivity force derating factors that routinely push a circuit one or two sizes above the European table value. Typical finals: 1.5mm2 lighting, 2.5mm2 sockets, 4-6mm2 AC and water heaters, dedicated circuits for ovens and EV chargers. Volt drop limits per BS 7671 - 3% lighting, 5% power - decide long runs, not current rating. Breaking capacity must match the prospective fault level at the supply point: 6kA typical on final DBs, 10-25kA on SMDBs, 36-50kA at MDB; check Icu against Ics and the discrimination/cascading tables. Earthing: copper-bonded rod driven to 3m in a 300mm inspection pit, conductors sized by the adiabatic equation. Standards: IEC 60364, 60228, 60502-1, 60947, 61439-1/2, 60332 flame, 60754/61034 LSZH, 62305 lightning, plus IP54/IP65 and IK enclosure ratings.

Recurring UAE failure modes: nuisance RCD tripping from cumulative standing earth leakage across many LED drivers and VFDs - split the circuits and use a 100mA time-delayed device upstream of 30mA finals; overheated terminations at aluminium-to-copper joints made without bimetallic lugs and at untorqued screws, found by thermographic scan at full load; conductors running hot with volt drop past 5% because derating for 45-50C ambient, tray grouping and buried duct was ignored at design; neutral overload on three-phase circuits from triplen harmonics; corrosion and terminal greening in coastal plantrooms where IP54/IP65 and galvanised enclosures were not specified; MCBs tripping on LED inrush where a B curve should have been a C curve. Diagnostic order: visual, insulation resistance, continuity and polarity, earth loop impedance, RCD trip time, then load and leakage logging.

topic: Field expertise — UAE codes, standards & specs
content:
# ELV & Security Systems Suppliers – UAE Field Knowledge Base

**GOVERNING AUTHORITY & APPROVALS**

ELV (Extra-Low Voltage) and security systems in the UAE operate under a multi-layered regulatory framework. Dubai Civil Defence (DCD) and the UAE Fire and Life Safety Code of Practice govern fire detection, alarm systems, and emergency lighting integration. The Security Industry Regulatory Agency (SIRA), operating under Dubai Police, mandates licensing and compliance for CCTV systems, access control, and alarm monitoring centres—suppliers must verify customer end-user credentials and system integrator certifications. DEWA (Dubai Electricity and Water Authority) approves electrical connections and earthing/grounding specifications for all ELV infrastructure. Dubai Municipality issues building permits that reference ELV compliance; Trakhees handles approvals for port and free-zone installations. For solar-integrated systems, Shams Dubai net-metering registration applies. Emirates Conformity Assurance (ECAS) certification is required for certain equipment imports. RTA (Roads and Transport Authority) oversees traffic management systems and vehicle access control in transport projects. All installations require NOC (No Objection Certificate) from relevant authorities before commissioning, and many systems demand third-party inspection and testing reports.

**STANDARDS & TECHNICAL REQUIREMENTS**

Systems must comply with IEC 60950 (electrical safety), IEC 62368 (audio/video equipment safety), EN 50130-4 (EMC for security systems), BS 5839 (fire detection and alarm systems), and ISO/IEC 27001 for data security in access control networks. NFPA standards guide emergency lighting and backup power. DEWA Technical Regulations specify voltage drop limits, cable sizing, and protection device ratings. UAE Fire and Life Safety Code mandates addressable fire alarm systems in commercial buildings above certain heights, with manual call points, smoke detectors, and heat detectors at prescribed intervals. SIRA requires CCTV systems to meet minimum resolution (typically 2MP for facial recognition compliance), 30-day minimum footage retention, and encrypted data transmission.

**SCOPE & SPECIFICATIONS**

Core deliverables include fire detection and alarm systems (addressable panels, detectors, sounders, manual call points), CCTV infrastructure (IP cameras, NVRs, cabling, PoE switches), access control (card readers, electric locks, biometric terminals, controllers), emergency lighting (LED exit signs, backup batteries, self-testing modules), structured cabling (Cat6A, fibre optic, conduit systems), UPS and backup power systems, and integration platforms. Specifications typically reference: camera resolution (2–8MP), frame rates (25–30fps), storage capacity (days of retention), cable gauge (AWG or mm²), voltage ratings (12V DC, 24V DC, 48V PoE), fire alarm response times (under 10 seconds), and system uptime SLAs (99.5–99.9%). Materials must be flame-retardant (as per BS 6891 for cables) and UV-resistant for outdoor installations.

**PRICE DRIVERS**

System scale (number of cameras

Best practice: survey before quoting - never price from a floor plan alone; write the retention calculation into the BOQ so the HDD size is auditable; get the SIRA Security Plan Certificate approved before ordering hardware, not after; use one authorised distributor per brand so warranty stays valid; label every cable both ends and hand over an as-built that matches reality; keep the security network independent; change default credentials and patch firmware at handover and every AMC visit; size PoE and UPS with 20-30% headroom; sell a four-visit AMC inside the contract, not as an afterthought. Common mistakes: awarding on the lowest total with no line-item comparison; omitting UPS, approvals or VideoGuard/Hassantuk connectivity to win price; indoor cameras on outdoor walls; wireless links without SIRA written approval; audio-enabled cameras without approval; proprietary controllers that lock the client in; and skipping training so the client cannot export footage when police ask.

Indicative UAE market ranges (2026, directional): 2MP dome from ~AED 180, 4MP IR bullet AED 450-850, wired labour AED 100-300/camera; 8-16 camera villa installed AED 4,000-10,000; 4-camera commercial IP system AED 3,500-7,000. Access control AED 300-800/door basic, AED 800-2,000 biometric/RFID, AED 2,000-10,000 networked, plus AED 200-1,000/door labour; ZKTeco SF100 ~AED 1,100, Suprema BioLite N2 ~AED 2,400, Honeywell NetAXS-123 ~AED 4,200. Fire alarm AED 400-15,000 for panel scope, install AED 500-5,000, AMC AED 1,000-3,000/yr. Boom barriers: NICE ~AED 3,000-5,000, CAME G4000 AED 4,000-8,500, FAAC B680H AED 5,000-10,000, BFT Maxima Ultra AED 6,500-12,000. Approvals: SIRA system-plan submission AED 120 plus consultant SPC, NOC and VideoGuard fees; DCD NOC AED 500-15,000 by area. Terms: 40-50% advance, 5-10% retention, 30-90 day payment, cloud storage AED 30-80/camera/month.

UAE ELV (extra-low voltage) work is the "low current" package of a building: CCTV/VSS, access control, fire alarm, PA/VA, structured cabling, BMS, barriers, intercom, AV. Route to market is layered: developer/consultant specifies, main contractor awards MEP, MEP sublets ELV, or the ELV firm is developer-nominated. Roughly three demand streams: new-build packages (12-36 month cash cycles, 5-10% retention held 12 months DLP), fit-out and retrofit (weeks, cash-positive), and compliance-driven replacement - SIRA audit failures, Hassantuk connection, end-of-life analogue-to-IP swaps. Volume clusters in Dubai and Abu Dhabi; Sharjah, Ajman and RAK are price-led. Q4 and pre-Ramadan drive retail and hospitality upgrades; villa handovers spike Q1. Margin sits in commissioning, approvals and AMC, not in boxes - hardware is a commodity with 8-15% gross.

Qualify in this order. 1. Emirate and zone - Dubai mainland (SIRA), PCFC/free zone (Trakhees), Abu Dhabi (ADMCC), other emirate; this decides who may legally quote. 2. Which subsystems - CCTV, access control, fire alarm, PA/VA, cabling, barriers, BMS - and is this new build, fit-out, retrofit or fixing a failed audit. MANDATORY. 3. Premises type and risk class - bank, jewellery, exchange house, ATM, data centre drive 90-day retention; standard commercial is 31 days. MANDATORY. 4. Quantities: cameras/coverage points, doors, detectors, network points, floors, exits. MANDATORY. 5. Existing SPC/DCD drawings or starting from scratch, and is a Hassantuk connection required. 6. Retention days, remote viewing, ANPR, facial recognition, NDAA requirement. 7. Reuse of existing cabling/NVR, ceiling access, UPS room. 8. AMC wanted and target handover date. Never ask budget or engineering choices.

Scope is normally quoted as separate ELV subsystems: video surveillance (IP cameras, NVR/VMS, ANPR, analytics); access control (readers, controllers, maglocks/strikes, turnstiles, REX, break-glass); intruder alarm (Grade 2/3 panels, PIRs, panic buttons); fire detection and alarm plus the Hassantuk/DCD monitoring link; EN 54-16/24 public address and voice alarm; structured cabling and passive (Cat6/6A, OM4/OS2 fibre, racks, patching); IP telephony; MATV/IPTV; audio-video and meeting rooms; nurse call; guard tour; master clock; car-park guidance and boom barriers; BMS and lighting control; data-centre containment and UPS. Services sold alongside: site survey, SIRA Security Plan Certificate drawings via an approved consultant, DCD design submission, supply-install-test-commission, as-built and O&M handover, training, AMC with minimum four preventive visits a year, and 24/7 SLA tiers.

A comparable ELV quote is itemised, not lump-sum. Require: device schedule by type, zone and quantity; per-camera resolution, lens/IR range, IP/IK rating and WDR; recorder channels, PoE ports, ONVIF version; HDD TB with the retention calculation shown and +20% spare; UPS runtime; cable stated as Cat6 pure copper with conduit and containment; per-door hardware split into reader, controller, lock, power supply, REX and break-glass; fire alarm by loop and device count with cable type; licences (VMS, analytics, per-door) named with term; approvals line covering consultant SPC, SIRA submission, NOC, VideoGuard/Hassantuk connectivity; testing and commissioning; as-built and O&M; AMC scope and visit count; warranty years and response SLA. Normalise rival bids to identical resolution, retention, FPS and approvals scope before comparing - unexplained 30-60% gaps are omissions, not savings.

Named authorities and sources. SIRA - Security Industry Regulatory Agency, Dubai Police; licenses security companies, technicians and equipment and approves designs: https://www.sira.gov.ae/en/services (spec v4.0 PDF at https://www.sira.gov.ae/assets/1554846d/Standard%20and%20Technical%20Specifications%20of%20the%20Security%20Systems.pdf.aspx). Dubai Civil Defence for fire and life safety NOCs: https://www.dcd.gov.ae. UAE Fire and Life Safety Code of Practice, issued by MOI/Civil Defence: https://moi.gov.ae. Hassantuk, the MOI national fire alarm monitoring service: https://hassantuk.moi.gov.ae. Trakhees CED for PCFC and free-zone areas: https://trakhees.ae. Abu Dhabi Monitoring and Control Centre, under the Supreme Council for National Security, governs Abu Dhabi CCTV. TDRA type approval for radio devices: https://tdra.gov.ae. MoIAT/ECAS conformity; Dubai Municipality Al Sa'fat for BMS.

SIRA and DCD approve to specification, not brand. Video: Hikvision and Dahua dominate volume; Axis, Bosch, Hanwha Vision and Avigilon are the premium/NDAA tier; VMS at scale is Milestone XProtect or Genetec Security Center. Access control: ZKTeco and Hikvision at entry, Suprema, HID and Paxton mid-tier, Honeywell (Pro-Watch/NetAXS), Gallagher, LenelS2 and Genetec Synergis on enterprise and critical sites. Fire: Notifier and Honeywell, Siemens Cerberus, Edwards/Kidde, Advanced and Zeta panels with Apollo or Hochiki devices; PA/VA from Bosch Praesensa, TOA or Honeywell. Passive: CommScope Systimax, Panduit, Nexans, R&M, Belden, Legrand. Barriers: CAME, BFT, FAAC, Nice, Automatic Systems, Magnetic. BMS: Siemens Desigo, Schneider EcoStruxure, Honeywell, Johnson Controls, Distech. Insist on authorised-distributor invoices - grey and refurbished stock carries no warranty or firmware support.

The trade-offs to surface before quoting. Economy (Hikvision/Dahua) versus premium/NDAA (Axis, Bosch, Hanwha): 2-3x price for longer MTBF, better WDR and firmware support - justified on banks, government, ports and multi-site estates, wasteful on a single retail unit. Local NVR versus cloud: cloud avoids a control room but costs AED 30-80/camera/month and can breach the independent-network rule. 31 versus 90 day retention triples storage. Wired versus wireless: wireless is prohibited under SIRA without written approval. Open ONVIF/BACnet versus proprietary: proprietary locks future expansion to one contractor. Lowest capex versus AMC: cutting the AMC below four visits a year fails compliance and shifts cost to callouts. Phased rollout protects cash but re-mobilisation and re-approval add 10-20%. Hotel and retail aesthetics push conduit into ceilings and lift labour cost.

Documents that gate an ELV job. Pre-award: supplier trade licence, SIRA company licence and technician cards, DCD contractor registration, ADMCC approval for Abu Dhabi, Trakhees CED registration in PCFC areas, manufacturer authorisation letters, TDRA type-approval certificates for any radio device, ECAS/EQM conformity marks via MoIAT, trade and workmen's compensation insurance. Design: site survey report, riser and layout drawings, Security Plan Certificate from a SIRA-approved consultant (CAD plus PDF), DCD design submission and initial NOC, material submittals with datasheets. Execution and handover: approved shop drawings, cable schedules and labelling register, test and commissioning reports, VideoGuard/Hassantuk connectivity report, SIRA audit NOC and stamped as-builts, O&M manuals, training sign-off, warranty certificates, AMC contract and the DCD completion certificate.

Rank risk on four axes. Compliance: an install by a non-SIRA firm, or without SPC/NOC/VideoGuard connectivity, is unlawful - Dubai Municipality withholds the completion certificate and licence renewal can be blocked; DCD non-compliance draws closure orders and fines from about AED 5,000. Technical: undersized HDD silently overwrites before day 31, an exceeded PoE switch budget drops cameras at night, and an unsegmented security VLAN exposes recorders to ransomware. Commercial: 40-50% advance against a supplier with no bank facility, 5-10% retention held through a 12-month DLP, and free-zone suppliers who cannot legally invoice mainland work. Project: developer-nominated ELV packages inherit main-contractor delay without compensation; gear without TDRA type approval or ECAS is held at customs. Data: audit logs and privacy exposure where cameras overlook public roads or neighbours.

A credible UAE ELV supplier is not one company type. Distinguish box-movers and distributors (no installation licence), SIRA-licensed security system contractors, DCD-registered fire alarm contractors, structured-cabling and IT integrators, and multi-discipline ELV integrators holding several approvals at once. In Dubai, security installation legally requires a SIRA company licence and every technician needs an individual SIRA registration card; fire alarm work requires separate DCD contractor registration; Jebel Ali, the Palm and other PCFC areas fall under Trakhees CED rather than DCD/DM; Abu Dhabi security systems require ADMCC-approved companies. Verify trade licence activity, valid SIRA/DCD/ADMCC registration numbers, manufacturer authorisation letters, in-house versus subcontracted labour, references at comparable size, and capacity to carry retention and a performance bond.

SIRA Standard and Technical Specifications v4.0 sets the Dubai baseline: colour cameras not below 1080p with SNR >=48 dB, outdoor >=IP66, IK10 where reachable under 2.5 m, WDR >=110 dB on backlit views, IR-cut auto day/night, remote zoom/focus above 4 m, no covert or audio cameras without approval. Recorders: ONVIF 2.0, RTSP, NTP, variable bit rate only, >=25 FPS live, >=10 FPS recorded on VMD covering >=70% of the day, retention not less than 31 days (90 for banks, jewellery, exchange houses, ATMs, data centres) sized with +20% spare HDD. Cabling twisted pair >=Cat6 pure copper - CCA/CCS banned - in PVC indoor or galvanised outdoor conduit, labelled both ends; the security network must be independent and private; UPS mandatory with >=30 minutes. VMS required at >=64 cameras or >=4 recorders. Pixel density: identification >=300 px/m, recognition >=125 px/m, ANPR >=400 px/m.

Recurring UAE failure modes and where to look first. Cameras dropping at dusk - IR engages, PoE draw jumps, switch budget exhausted; check total watts, not port count. Random offline devices on long runs - CCA/CCS cable sold as Cat6, voltage drop past 90 m; measure resistance. Washed-out night images on domes - IR bouncing off the bubble; reseat the gasket. Condensation and lens fog after summer - failed housing gasket or an indoor-rated unit fitted outdoors. Recorder full before day 31 - fixed bit rate, wrong VMD schedule or no +20% spare. Access control doors failing open in heat - undersized 12 V PSU and maglock heat rise; check standby battery age, 3-4 years. Fire panel earth faults - moisture in outdoor conduit or a nicked screen. Hassantuk/VideoGuard link loss - SIM, router or firewall change after an IT refresh. Sand and dust are the top AMC driver: clean housings quarterly.

Checklist: verify the consultancy's municipality registration and its category against your building height before appointing; confirm the jurisdiction of the plot and that the firm is registered there; get the affection plan, survey and soil report into the consultant's hands before design starts; agree the deliverable list, drawing scales, file formats and the number of included revision rounds in the appointment; separate design fee, supervision fee and reimbursables; put authority review cycles into the design programme as realistic ranges rather than fixed weeks; confirm professional indemnity cover and that it runs past handover; agree who pays authority fees; and make the stamped approval, the IFC set and as-built verification payment milestones. Buyer mistakes: asking several firms for free concepts and treating the prettiest render as the best consultant; appointing design-only and then having nobody on site; changing the brief after detailed design. Consultant mistakes: no soil report, MEP coordinated late, and egress never checked against the fire code before submission.

Fees are quoted either as a percentage of estimated construction cost or as a lump sum staged by deliverable, and either way design fee and supervision fee must be shown separately, because they behave differently and many clients need only one. Full design plus supervision commonly lands in the mid single digits as a percentage of construction cost, design-only well below that, and small projects are priced as a lump sum because percentages break down at low value. Cost drivers by impact: GFA and floor count; number of disciplines in scope; use complexity, since a hospital, laboratory or F&B kitchen carries far more design content per sqm than a warehouse; supervision intensity, full-time resident engineer against periodic visits; and the revision allowance, which is where scope creep lives. Payment is normally staged at signing, concept approval, detailed design, permit issue, then monthly through supervision. Cap the included revision rounds and price additional ones. Authority fees, printing and third-party specialists are usually reimbursable at cost.

Buyers split five ways: plot owners needing a design and a building permit for a villa or block; developers running full design, tender documentation and supervision on towers and communities; industrial and logistics clients needing sheds, racking-driven layouts and a fire strategy in DIP, ICAD, KIZAD and Sajaa; fit-out clients needing a stamped layout for a municipality and Civil Defence submission; and asset owners needing structural assessment, retrofit design, peer review or expert reports. Appointments are won on fee proposal, and occasionally by design competition on landmark work. Cycles: concept 2-4 weeks, detailed design 6-16 weeks, authority approval 4-12 weeks and largely outside the consultant's control, supervision running the full construction period. Firm tiers: international practices, established local consultancies holding municipality registration, and small design offices. Vocabulary: affection plan, FAR, GFA, BUA, setback, NOC, IFC drawings, RFI, shop drawing approval, snagging, PQP, supervision consultant.

Order: 1) project type and use class; 2) emirate, plot number or community, and jurisdiction - DM, DDA, Trakhees, DMT, Sharjah; 3) plot area and target GFA or BUA and floors; 4) whether an affection plan, survey and soil report exist; 5) scope stage wanted; 6) disciplines - architecture only, or plus structure and MEP; 7) authority submission and NOCs in or out; 8) supervision required or not; 9) target permit date and construction budget. Mandatory before fan-out: project type and use, emirate and jurisdiction, plot and area, scope stage, disciplines, timeline. Skippable, since consultancies propose them: BIM level, deliverable list, revision count, sustainability route. Enough when a consultancy can produce a staged fee proposal without a meeting. Scoping call instead when the use class is changing, the plot carries an existing structure, the project is phased or master-planned, a rating above the mandatory minimum is targeted, or the client expects design work before signing.

Design: architectural concept and schematic, detailed design and IFC drawings, structural analysis and design, MEP design covering HVAC, electrical, plumbing, drainage, firefighting, fire alarm and ELV, infrastructure and utility design, landscape and hardscape, interior design and FF&E specification, and specialist packages - facade engineering, acoustics, vertical transportation, traffic impact studies, fire and life safety strategy, energy modelling. Documentation: specifications, bills of quantities, tender documents, tender analysis and award recommendation. Authority work: affection plan interpretation, building permit submission, and DEWA, Civil Defence, RTA, telecom and drainage NOCs through to completion certificate closeout. Site services: full-time or periodic supervision, shop drawing and material submittal review, RFI response, site instructions, interim payment certification, testing witnessing, snagging and de-snagging, as-built verification. Also due diligence, condition surveys, structural assessment, peer review and expert witness.

Mandatory before quoting: project type and use class, emirate and plot number or community with the jurisdiction, plot area and target GFA or BUA with floor count, scope stage - concept only, full design, design plus tender documentation, or design plus supervision - whether structure and MEP are included or coordinated externally, whether authority submission and NOC follow-up is in scope, target permit and construction dates, and whether any existing design or survey exists. Useful but not blocking: construction budget, sustainability target, BIM level, deliverable format, expected number of design revisions. Fee drivers: GFA, use complexity, number of disciplines, supervision intensity, and the revision allowance. Delivery drivers: client decision speed and authority review cycles, which routinely add 4-12 weeks. Consultancies reject enquiries with no plot, no affection plan, no use class, an unrealistic permit date, or a client expecting free concept work before appointment.

Dubai Municipality (https://www.dm.gov.ae/) registers and classifies engineering consultancy offices, and the classification category caps the building height and type a firm may design and supervise; it also issues building permits and enforces the Dubai Building Code and Al Sa'fat. Dubai Development Authority (https://www.dda.gov.ae/) and Trakhees (https://trakhees.ae/) run their own consultant registration and permitting inside their jurisdictions, so registration with one does not carry across to another - always match the consultancy to the authority holding the plot. Abu Dhabi permitting and consultant classification run through the Department of Municipalities and Transport (https://www.dmt.gov.ae/), with Estidama Pearl requiring a Pearl Qualified Professional on the team. Dubai Civil Defence (https://www.dcd.gov.ae/) reviews fire and life safety design. Engineering practice is regulated federally, and registration with the UAE Society of Engineers (https://www.uaese.ae/) is normally expected of engineers signing submissions. Professional indemnity cover is a standard condition of consultancy licensing.

A consultancy sells people and process rather than products, so judge the toolset and the named team. Software in normal use: Autodesk Revit and AutoCAD, Navisworks for clash detection, ETABS, SAFE and STAAD.Pro for structural analysis, SAP2000, Tekla for detailing, Carrier HAP or Trane TRACE and IES VE or DesignBuilder for load and energy modelling, DIALux or Relux for lighting, Civil 3D for infrastructure, and Primavera P6 or MS Project for programme. Practices you will meet in the UAE range from international names such as Atkins, WSP, AECOM, Dar Al-Handasah and Khatib & Alami, through established local consultancies, to small design offices. What genuinely differs is the municipality registration category, whether the signing engineer is in-house, BIM maturity at LOD 300-400, and supervision staffing depth. Demand: municipality consultant registration certificate, professional indemnity cover with the sum insured stated, and CVs for the named design and supervision team.

They say they want good design; they want a permit issued on time, a building that earns its completion certificate, and no redesign after tender. Plot owners building one villa buy price and permit certainty; developers buy saleable area and programme; industrial clients buy operational fit - column grid, clear height, floor loading, truck access - and will trade aesthetics away entirely; institutional and government clients buy compliance and documentation depth. Trade-offs to name honestly: an international name adds design quality and credibility at 1.5-3 times the fee but usually still needs a locally registered firm to stamp; a design-only appointment saves the supervision fee but leaves the client alone against the contractor on site, which is where most money is lost; maximising GFA to the FAR limit raises construction cost per saleable sqm through deeper structure and more cores; and a concept that ignores setbacks or fire egress fails first submission and costs more in redesign than the fee it saved.

Ask the buyer for: title deed and affection plan showing plot number, permitted use, FAR and setbacks, topographic survey, geotechnical report if one exists, any previous drawings or permits for the plot, existing utility positions and available DEWA or ADDC load, the master community design guidelines where the plot sits inside one, and target permit and completion dates. Expect from the consultancy: trade licence with engineering consultancy activity, municipality consultant registration certificate showing the category, professional indemnity insurance certificate with the sum insured, company profile with comparable projects and permit references, CVs for the named design and supervision team, a staged fee proposal with a clear deliverable list and revision allowance, a design programme aligned to real authority review cycles, and at each stage the drawing set, specification, calculations, BOQ where in scope, and the stamped submission and approval correspondence.

Regulatory: a consultancy whose registration category does not cover your building height, or which is registered with a different authority than the one holding the plot - the sign is a firm that will not send its registration certificate. Professional: the engineer stamping the drawings is not employed by the firm, which voids accountability and can invalidate professional indemnity cover. Commercial: a fee 40-60 percent below market is a firm that has priced concept and permit only and will bill detailed design, coordination and supervision as extras - the sign is a proposal with no deliverable list and no revision cap. Schedule: a programme showing authority approval as a fixed two weeks. Technical: structural design started without a soil report; MEP added after the architecture is frozen so risers and plant do not fit; no clash detection before IFC. Insurance: professional indemnity lapsing at handover rather than running through the liability period. Client-side: an unresolved brief, then redesign blamed on the consultant.

Four archetypes. International practices bring design credibility and BIM discipline, price at 1.5-3 times local rates, and often partner with a locally registered firm to stamp submissions. Established local consultancies hold municipality registration in a category that permits the building height you need and carry in-house architecture, structure and MEP - they are the workhorses of UAE permitting. Boutique design studios do strong concept work but subcontract structure, MEP and the authority submission, which is where schedules slip. Contractor in-house design arms are fast and cheap but not independent of the builder. Before trusting any of them verify: trade licence with engineering consultancy activity in the right emirate, municipality consultant registration and its category limit against your building, whether the engineers signing the drawings are actually employed there and registered to practise, professional indemnity insurance with the sum insured stated, comparable completed projects with permit references, and who will physically supervise on site.

Codes in use: the Dubai Building Code, DMT regulations in Abu Dhabi, the UAE Fire and Life Safety Code for egress, compartmentation and smoke control, ASHRAE 90.1, 62.1 and 55 for MEP, BS EN 1992 or ACI 318 for concrete design, BS EN 1997 for geotechnics, and ASHRAE or CIBSE methods for load calculation. Sustainability: Al Sa'fat in Dubai, Estidama Pearl in Abu Dhabi requiring a Pearl Qualified Professional on the team, LEED where the client wants international recognition. Design inputs to demand before starting: affection plan with plot number, permitted use and FAR, geotechnical report, topographic survey, existing utility positions and available loads. Failure points: a layout that breaches setback or FAR and is rejected at first submission; egress width and travel distance failing Civil Defence review; structural design begun without a soil report; MEP risers and plant space never reserved in the architectural coordination; and no BIM clash detection before IFC issue.

Recurring: the submission was rejected and the permit date is gone. Sequence - obtain the authority's written comments, classify each as planning (setback, FAR, use), life safety (egress, compartmentation, access), structural, or documentary, fix planning and life safety first because they drive layout, and resubmit one consolidated package rather than piecemeal. Repeat rejections on the same point usually mean the reviewer's comment was never properly understood - request a pre-submission meeting. Design-versus-site conflicts: check whether the contractor is building to IFC or to superseded drawings, and whether an RFI was ever raised. Cost overrun at tender against the design estimate: reconcile BOQ quantities against the drawings before blaming the market. Supervision disputes over defective work: photograph it, issue a written site instruction, and withhold certification rather than arguing verbally. Escalate to the authority's technical affairs section after two failed resubmissions.

Checklist: confirm venue, date and headcount before pricing; pull the venue technical pack and exclusive-supplier list before quoting; file permits at brief plus one week, not build minus one week; issue an itemised BOQ with written exclusions; obtain stamped structural and electrical drawings by build minus fourteen days; carry public liability of AED 5-10 m naming the venue; book MOHRE work permits and venue passes two weeks out; rehearse a day early; sign every variation on site on a printed form; photograph venue condition at derig to protect the deposit. Customer mistakes to head off: no confirmed date, unapproved budget, free 3D renders expected, a VIP added after layouts are signed. Supplier mistakes: quoting labour without overtime and shift meals, ignoring build days in venue hire, assuming rigging points are free, uncertified fabric. Documentation: licence missing the activity, no TRN, verbal variations. Compliance: a Dubai permit does not cover Abu Dhabi.

Cost drivers ranked: venue and F&B minimums; technical production scale, above all LED square metres and truss tonnage; build complexity and one-use carpentry; manpower headcount and shift length; permits, insurance, medical and security standby; freight, customs and carnets; power and generators; and last, creative fees. Rough tiers per delegate for a full-day corporate conference: AED 350-650 economy, AED 700-1,400 mid, AED 1,800-4,000 plus premium. Value engineering that works: reuse modular stand systems, cut LED area and replace with fabric and lighting, shorten build days, fold rehearsal into a build day, drop the double-decker for a raised platform. Terms: 50% mobilisation, 40% pre-event, 10% within 30 days; government and large corporates pay 60-90 days against completion certificates. Rush inside 21 days adds 15-30%. Levers: multi-event frameworks, off-peak dates, early deposit.

Vocabulary: pax, covers, ROS (run of show), bump-in/bump-out, derig, shell scheme vs space-only vs raw space, double-decker, rigging points, SWL, tech rider, F&B minimum spend, DDR, PCO, DMC, AOR. Buyers: government entities tendering through Tejari and entity eSourcing portals; semi-government (ADNOC, DEWA, Emirates, Etihad Rail); banks (FAB, ENBD, ADCB); FMCG, auto and pharma brands buying through agencies of record; associations and PCOs. Government budgets run Jan-Dec, so tenders land Sep-Dec for the following year. Peak season is October to April; May to September is indoor or dead. Ramadan collapses daytime work into iftar and suhoor formats; Eid and National Day (2 December) are booked a year out. Tiers: full-service agency, technical production house, scenic and joinery fabricator, single-discipline rental house, and the one-man broker who subcontracts everything.

Ask in order. 1) Event type and objective. 2) Confirmed date plus build and derig window. 3) Venue - confirmed, shortlisted, or help us find one. 4) Headcount and format. 5) Budget band. 6) Scope - turnkey or technical only. 7) Emirate. All seven mandatory; theme, catering style and branding are skippable. Rules: if no date or no headcount, do not fan out - return one clarifying question. If the venue is unconfirmed, route to agencies only, never to fabricators. If outdoor, a tent or a stage over 1 m, flag Civil Defence and stamped structural drawings, add fourteen days. If ticketed, flag DET or DCT permits and approved ticketing. If Abu Dhabi, speaker details five working days ahead. If build window is under 48 hours or the date inside 21 days, mark rush, warn on 15-30%. If budget is under AED 50k against 500-plus pax, escalate to a scoping call. Fan out at confidence 0.7 or above.

Scope splits into: conference and congress (registration, plenary set, breakouts, interpretation booths to ISO 4043, delegate app); exhibitions (shell scheme, custom space-only, double-decker, hall dressing); galas; brand activations and roadshows (kiosks, mall atriums, sampling, hostesses); ground-breaking and inauguration ceremonies (sand ceremony, VIP protocol, tenting); weddings; hybrid streams. Wrapped services buyers forget to name: permits, temporary work permits, insurance, artist logistics and carnets, freight and customs clearance, security, medical standby, cleaning, waste, generator fuel, event Wi-Fi. Alternatives worth naming: modular reusable systems (Octanorm, Aluvision, beMatrix) instead of one-use carpentry; LED backdrop instead of printed scenic; hotel in-house AV where the venue charges patch fees. Lifecycle: brief, concept, budget, permits, build, live, derig.

Mandatory to quote: event type, confirmed or shortlisted venue, exact dates including build and derig days, headcount, format (seated, standing, exhibition), and budget band or approval limit. Then: indoor or outdoor, floor plan or hall number, ceiling height and rigging allowance, available power, whether F&B is venue-exclusive, branding and print scope, staffing numbers and hours, and who holds the permits. Price drivers: LED square metres and pitch, stage size and height, truss and hanging points, generator size, custom build area, number of build days, VIP protocol. Delivery drivers: permit lead time, venue access windows, freight and customs, and whether the date collides with GITEX, Arab Health, Big 5 or Gulfood, when crew and kit vanish. Suppliers reject an inquiry with no date, no venue, no budget, a build window under 48 hours, or a demand for free 3D renders before appointment.

Dubai: Department of Economy and Tourism (https://www.dubaidet.gov.ae) issues event, ticketed, activity and tent permits on ePermits (https://epermits.dtcm.gov.ae) - about AED 320, nominally one day but realistically two to four weeks if ticketed. Dubai Civil Defence (https://www.dcd.gov.ae/portal/en/) covers fire and life safety for tents, stages, pyro and occupancy under the UAE Fire and Life Safety Code. Dubai Municipality covers temporary structures and food, Dubai Police road closures, DCAS (https://www.ambulance.gov.ae) medical standby. Abu Dhabi: DCT Events Licensing System (https://dct.gov.ae/en/e.services/events.licensing.system.aspx) - AED 200 registration, AED 50 per speaker, five working days ahead - plus ADCDA (https://www.adcda.gov.ae/en). Sharjah: SCTDA (https://www.sharjahtourism.ae). Also UAE Media Council (https://uaemc.gov.ae) and MOHRE (https://www.mohre.gov.ae).

Audio: L-Acoustics (K2, Kara, A-series), d&b audiotechnik (regional distribution via Avientek), Meyer Sound, JBL VTX; RF from Shure Axient and Sennheiser 6000 for anything with a VIP. Lighting: Robe (BMFL, Forte), Ayrton, Martin by Harman, Claypaky; consoles MA Lighting grandMA3, Avolites, ETC. Video: Absen, ROE Visual, Unilumin, INFiLED LED; Barco UDX and Panasonic projection; Brompton Tessera and Novastar processing; disguise and Green Hippo servers. Structures: Layher, Prolyte, Milos, Litec; tents from Losberger De Boer, Roder and Al Laith. Modular stands: Octanorm, Aluvision, beMatrix. Power: Aggreko, Byrne Equipment Rental, Cummins. Demand from suppliers: manufacturer datasheets, SWL and load tables, current inspection certificates, fabric flame certificates showing test method and date, and serial-level asset lists - grey-market LED and copy truss fail inspection.

What they say: premium but cost-effective, wow factor, same as last year but better. What they mean: no visible cabling, guests seated on time, the chairman on stage with working audio, and photos marketing can post the same evening. Constraints they will not volunteer: an approval chain that eats three weeks, an unconfirmed VIP whose attendance rewrites the protocol layout, a sponsor contract dictating branding sizes, and a budget already committed to venue and F&B. They buy the visual; they live with the registration queue, the toilet ratio and the parking. Name the trade-offs out loud - bigger LED or better catering, longer build or higher overtime, imported artist or a schedule you can trust, custom joinery or reusable modular. A stand built to redeploy at two more shows pays back within three events. Establish risk tolerance early - outdoor in April is a wind and heat gamble.

At enquiry: brief, floor plan, venue technical specification, client trade licence. At quotation: itemised BOQ split by venue, technical, build, manpower and permits; equipment schedules; validity and exclusions. At contract: LPO or signed quotation, payment schedule, cancellation. For approvals: stamped structural calculations and drawings for stages, tents, double-deckers and rigging; electrical single-line diagram with earthing; fabric flame-retardancy and equipment inspection certificates; risk assessment and method statement (RAMS); crowd management and evacuation plan; insurance naming the venue; supplier trade licences; passport, visa and photo sets for speakers, performers and temporary staff. Post-event: completion certificate, delivery notes, variations signed on site, and a VAT-compliant tax invoice - UAE e-invoicing phases in from 2026, so capture the buyer TRN at contract.

Permit risk: filed inside two weeks, or scope changed after submission - the sign is a client still finalising the artist or layout. Technical: no stamped rigging or structural drawing by build minus ten. Schedule: a venue offering one overnight window for a two-day build - the warning is a contract with no exclusive-use clause. Supplier: a quote 30% under the field, no owned assets, or refusal to name the actual subcontractor. Financial: build starting on a verbal go-ahead with the LPO in process, or a late first tranche - late mobilisation predicts late final payment. Legal: trade licence missing the activity, no insurance naming the venue, unsigned variations, unlicensed music or brand IP. Operational: staff without MOHRE permits, crew without venue passes, no medical cover. Customer: several stakeholders with no decision maker, and a chairman who rewrites the run of show on show day.

Archetypes: (1) the full-service agency with creative, account and production staff but almost no owned kit - good on concept, adds 15-25% on every subcontract; (2) the technical production house owning stage, audio, lighting and LED - the Protec, Eclipse Staging, Gearhouse, Showtech, Blink, PRG and Delta Sound tier - fast, honest on kit, weak on creative; (3) the joinery and scenic fabricator in Al Quoz, Al Qusais or Mussafah with a real workshop, strong on build, slow on paperwork; (4) the broker with a licence, a laptop and zero assets. Verify: trade licence carrying the exact activity, owned-asset list with serials, a warehouse you can visit, DWTC or ADNEC approved-contractor status, public liability of AED 5-10 m, two recent references. Lead times: shell scheme two weeks, custom build four to eight weeks, imported LED or specialist rigging six to ten weeks in peak season.

Sizing logic: seating at 1.0-1.2 sqm per person theatre, 1.6-1.8 sqm on rounds of ten, plus 30-40% for stage, aisles and buffets. LED pitch by viewing distance - P2.6-P3.9 indoor near-field, P4.8-P10 beyond 15 m. Set the screen so the bottom edge sits 1.2 m above floor for sightlines. PA sized by room volume and target SPL, typically 95-100 dBA at mix position for corporate. Power: allow 1.2-1.5 kVA per 100 sqm of exhibit lighting plus real loads, size generators at 70-80% loading, spec N+1 on show-critical feeds. Rigging: every hanging point needs a venue-approved SWL and a stamped rigging plot with load schedule. Temporary structures need structural calculations against the authority wind criterion, fabrics certified to NFPA 701, BS 7837 or DIN 4102 B1. Failure points: undersized distro, single-path fibre, LED processing without redundancy, no phase balance check before doors.

Power trips in rehearsal: check phase balance and load against distro rating, isolate LED processors and motors, then look for a shared neutral or a generator past 80% loading. RF dropouts on wireless mics: scan the band on site rather than trusting last year's file, coordinate against the venue's own systems and any broadcast truck, raise antennas, shorten cable runs. LED showing dead lines or colour shift: swap receiving card and data cable first, then the processor, then the panel - never repatch a whole wall at doors minus one hour. Late permit: escalate through the venue's government liaison, not the portal, and prep a reduced-scope fallback. Structural rejection: get the comment in writing and reissue with the consultant stamp rather than arguing on site. Escalate to the client the moment a fix costs money or moves the run of show. Prevention: full technical rehearsal a day early.

topic: Field expertise — UAE codes, standards & specs
content:
Executive Assistant services in the UAE operate as a professional staffing and business-support trade rather than a licensed construction or technical trade, so the regulatory landscape centres on labour, commercial, and data-privacy frameworks rather than civil-defence or utility approvals.

**Governing Authority & Approvals.** The Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation (MOHRE) governs employment contracts, Wage Protection System (WPS) compliance, and end-of-service entitlements under UAE Labour Law (Federal Decree-Law No. 33 of 2021). For free-zone placements, the relevant free-zone authority — DIFC, ADGM, JAFZA, DMCC, Dubai Internet City, etc. — issues its own employment regulations and work permits. Staffing agencies and PRO service providers must hold a valid commercial licence from Dubai Economy and Tourism (DET) or the relevant free-zone authority, with the correct business activity code covering "manpower supply" or "business support services." Visa and residency processing runs through the General Directorate of Residency and Foreigners Affairs (GDRFA) Dubai. Where the EA role involves handling personal data, compliance with UAE Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021 on Personal Data Protection (PDPL) is mandatory. Notarisation or attestation of educational certificates through MOFA and the relevant embassy is standard for visa applications.

**Standards.** ISO 9001 quality management is referenced by premium staffing firms. DIFC and ADGM operate under their own employment regulations aligned with international best practice. No specific IEC, NFPA, or ASHRAE standards apply to this trade.

**Scope & Specs.** Core deliverables include calendar and diary management, travel and visa coordination, board-pack and minute preparation, CRM and document management (MS Office 365, SharePoint, Salesforce), expense reporting, stakeholder liaison, and C-suite gatekeeping. Buyers specify language proficiency (English mandatory; Arabic, French, Mandarin valued), typing speed (typically 60+ WPM), shorthand, confidentiality agreements (NDA), notice periods, and whether the role is full-time resident, part-time retainer, or virtual EA.

**Price Drivers.** Seniority level (C-suite vs. mid-management support), language stack, industry specialism (legal, finance, real estate), full-time vs. fractional engagement, visa sponsorship obligation, housing/transport allowance inclusion, and agency placement fee vs. direct hire. Monthly salaries range roughly AED 6,000–25,000+ depending on experience; agency placement fees typically run one to two months' salary.

**Compliance Pitfalls / Red Flags.** Misclassifying an EA as a freelancer to avoid WPS and gratuity obligations is a common violation. Agencies operating without a manpower-supply licence are illegal. Verify the supplier's MOHRE establishment card and trade licence activity. Confirm whether the candidate requires a NOC from a current UAE employer. Watch for CVs with unverified or unattested qualifications. Key qualifying questions:

Checklist, in order: confirm venue, hall, stand number, dimensions, open sides and tenancy dates; confirm the venue accreditation of the contractor for that specific venue, not just Dubai; lock design by week three; issue structural calculations to the engineer 6-8 weeks before build-up; submit initial floor plan 30 days out and final 2 weeks out; obtain the Permit to Build before any material leaves the workshop; order rigging and mains power before the organiser cut-off; collect fire certificates that name the exact installed material; register contractor badges and lodge the performance bond; walk a snag list before handover; sign off dilapidations at tear-down. Common mistakes: approving a render nobody costed; forgetting electrics, rigging and dismantling in the budget; declaring exhibit weights late; assuming DWTC accreditation covers Expo City; scheduling a summer build without allowing for the midday work ban; paying 100% upfront to a broker with no workshop.

Cost drivers ranked: build tier per sqm; deck area and structural engineering (AED 5,000-12,000 for sign-off); LED square metreage and AV hire; joinery complexity and curves; rigging points from about AED 2,200 each; graphics area; freight, carnet and site handling; peak-season labour in December and February. Benchmarks: shell upgrade AED 500-900/sqm; modular AED 1,200-1,800/sqm; mid custom AED 2,000-3,500/sqm; premium LED AED 3,500-6,000/sqm; double decker AED 3,500-8,000/sqm. Add raw space around AED 1,600/sqm, refundable performance bond from AED 2,500, mains from AED 1,800, 5% VAT. Value-engineering levers: reuse a stored frame, cut deck to storage-and-meeting only, swap LED wall for backlit fabric, drop bespoke furniture. Terms: 50% advance, 40% pre-dispatch, 10% post-show; anything under 40% upfront is a supplier taking risk. Rush inside six weeks adds 15-25%.

Vocabulary you use without explaining: shell scheme, space-only or raw space, PTB (Permit to Build), tenancy, build-up and tear-down, dilapidations, risers, catenary, top versus primary rigging, walk-on, dressing, BOQ. Buyers are marketing and events managers, country-pavilion commissioners (trade bodies, embassies), PCOs. Supplier tiers: shell-upgrade dressers; mid-market Al Quoz, Al Qusais and Ajman fabricators with 10-40 staff and their own workshop; top-tier turnkey houses running in-house CNC, spray booth, rigging crew and storage; and brokers with no workshop who subcontract everything. Season: September to December (GITEX, Big 5, Dubai Airshow) and January to May (WFES, Gulfood, Arab Health, ATM, INDEX). July and August are dead except tender season. Custom enquiry-to-build cycle is 8-14 weeks; shell upgrade 3-4 weeks. Corporates rebuild every two to three editions.

Ask in this order. 1) Venue and hall. 2) Stand number, dimensions and open sides. 3) Tenancy and build-up dates. 4) Shell scheme or space-only. 5) Budget band. 6) Design supplied or required. 7) Required zones, exhibit power and weight. 8) Deck, LED, rigging intent. 9) One-show or reused. Items 1-5 are mandatory; 6-9 are skippable at first pass. Rules: if space-only, then structural drawings and a Permit to Build are in scope and the timeline needs 8-14 weeks. If a deck is wanted, then require 36 sqm plus, a named structural engineer and 6-8 weeks of approval. If build-up is under three weeks away, then route to modular or shell upgrade only. If the venue is Expo City, then filter to DEC-accredited contractors. If budget is under AED 1,200/sqm on custom, then reset expectations before fanning out. Below 70% confidence or over AED 500,000, book a scoping call instead.

Taxonomy: shell-scheme upgrade (graphics, flooring, lighting on venue-supplied Octanorm); modular system builds (Octanorm MAXIMA 40/80, beMatrix b62, Aluvision) - reusable, fast, weaker on curves; custom joinery in MDF, plywood and aluminium extrusion - full design freedom, one-show life unless stored; hybrid, the practical default; double and triple decker for 36 sqm plus; country pavilions with 10-40 co-exhibitor pods. Rental of frame and re-skinning cuts 30-40% versus new-build but locks geometry. Wrapped services that must be priced in: 3D design and revisions, structural calculations, venue submissions and PTB, fabrication, transport, install and dismantle, graphics production, AV and LED with technician, furniture and floral hire, electrics, rigging, storage, daily cleaning and stand management. Select on venue accreditation, workshop ownership, then design.

Mandatory before any supplier can price: venue and hall, exact stand number and dimensions, open sides (island, peninsula, corner, inline), tenancy and build-up dates, shell versus space-only, target height and whether a deck is wanted, budget band, and whether design is supplied or required. Then: required zones (meeting rooms, storage, pantry, demo, kitchen), exhibit weights and power load in kW, LED or screen requirement, hanging banner or rigging intent, brand guideline pack, and who submits to the venue. Price and delivery move most on deck area, LED metreage, rigging points, joinery finish level and how many weeks remain to tenancy. Suppliers reject an enquiry that has no stand number or dimensions, no dates, no budget band, a build-up date under three weeks away for custom work, or an unnamed venue - they cannot check accreditation or the submission deadline.

Not separately licensed: you need a UAE trade licence with a fabrication or contracting activity plus per-venue accreditation. Dubai World Trade Centre runs approvals through the Organiser+ portal (https://organiserplus.dwtc.com/, https://www.dwtc.com/en/exhibit/): initial floor plan 30 days before tenancy, final 2 weeks for Dubai Civil Defence, Permit to Build mandatory before construction. Dubai Civil Defence (https://www.dcd.gov.ae) enforces the UAE Fire and Life Safety Code of Practice, sold via MOI (https://moi.gov.ae). Dubai Municipality owns Dubai Building Code 2022 (https://www.dm.gov.ae); DEWA (https://www.dewa.gov.ae); DET issues event ePermits (https://www.dubaidet.gov.ae). Abu Dhabi: DCT licensing (https://dct.gov.ae) and ADNEC (https://www.adnec.ae). Also MoHRE midday break 15 Jun-15 Sep, Dubai Chambers ATA Carnet, and FTA e-invoicing from July 2026.

Octanorm Emirates in Al Quoz Industrial 3, Dubai supplies MAXIMA 40/80/120, Octawall, Octalumina, Octamax deck and Octafloor - the reference for system builds locally. beMatrix b62 and Aluvision frames dominate LED-integrated and lightbox walls. Rigging: Eurotruss and ChainMaster hoists through Procom Middle East, Prolyte through Provision AVL, plus Litec and Milos; unbranded Global Truss copies circulate in Al Quoz - refuse anything without a load chart. LED: Absen, Unilumin and Leyard at the top, Samsung and LG for displays; budget cabinets fail on colour consistency and spare receiving cards. Panels and boards: Egger and Kronospan MDF, 3A Composites Dibond, Alucobond and Alubond. Finishes: Jotun and Caparol paint, 3M, Avery Dennison and Orafol vinyl. Demand: fire test report naming the exact material, standard and issue date; truss load charts; LOLER-marked eyebolts.

What they say: we want something premium and eye-catching. What they mean: more meeting rooms, more storage, and visibility from the main aisle. Real constraints they surface late: a fixed marketing budget already spent on space, headquarters brand guidelines with mandatory materials, a hospitality area they forgot to declare, and product exhibits with weight or power demands nobody measured. Functional needs are meeting seats, demo positions, storage, pantry; operational needs are power, network, cleaning and a stand manager for show days. Name the trade-offs aloud: an open stand pulls traffic but loses storage; a decker buys area but costs 6-8 weeks of approval and a fixed rigging position; a rental frame saves 30% but constrains geometry; hero LED eats a third of the budget. Ask whether the stand is a one-show asset or must be stored and reused for three editions.

Client side: floor plan with stand number, brand guidelines and logo artwork, exhibit list with weights and power. Supplier side: 3D visuals and elevations, dimensioned plan and section, BOQ split by carpentry, metal, graphics, electrics, AV, furniture and services, and a method statement plus risk assessment for build-up. Approval pack: technical drawings, structural calculations and drawings stamped by a qualified structural engineer for space-only, decks, stages and pavilions; 3D renders as PDF; stand location on the hall plan; electrical single-line and load schedule; fire test certificates for every fabric, drape and board; rigging plot with point loads and eyebolt certification. Commercial: trade licence, public liability insurance, performance bond or bank guarantee, contractor badge applications, and post-show handover with snag list and dilapidation sign-off.

Approval risk is the big one: early sign is a supplier who has not asked for your stand number or tenancy dates by week two - they are not planning a submission. Structural risk: a decker quoted without a named structural engineer or a stated deck live load. Schedule risk: fabrication starting under three weeks from build-up, or drawings still unsigned at the venue deadline. Financial risk: a quote 30% under the field usually excludes electrics, rigging, the performance bond or dismantling. Supplier risk: no workshop photos, no contractor badge history, a labour crew met on site for the first time. Legal risk: building without a Permit to Build, or fire certificates that name a different material than what is installed. Customer risk: late artwork and late exhibit weights. Operational risk: rigging points booked after the organiser's cut-off, which cannot be recovered.

Four archetypes. The turnkey house owns a 2,000+ sqm workshop, holds venue accreditation, employs a draughtsman and books its own rigging - expect 20-35% higher rates and near-zero approval risk. The mid-market fabricator owns a workshop but outsources structural calculations and AV; strong on joinery, weak on submissions and deckers. The design studio sells renders and subcontracts the build; the render you approved is not what the joiner priced. The broker has a trade licence, a laptop and no workshop; identify by no photos of their own production, no DWTC badge history, and a quote in two hours. Verify before trusting: valid UAE trade licence with a fabrication or contracting activity, venue accreditation for the specific venue, contractor badge and performance bond history, public liability cover, workshop visit or build photos, and two client references.

Design against Dubai Building Code 2022 and AISC for steel; decks and stairs to the venue handbook.
