No formal trade license segregation exists for gypsum suppliers alone; most operate under general contracting or fit-out licenses issued by Dubai Municipality.

## STANDARDS & TECHNICAL COMPLIANCE

Gypsum board products must comply with GSO (Gulf Standardization Organization) standards, particularly GSO 1217 for gypsum plasterboard specifications. Fire-rated suspended ceilings must meet the UAE Fire and Life Safety Code's fire-resistance classifications (typically 30-minute, 60-minute, or 120-minute ratings depending on occupancy). Installation methods follow BS 5234 (Code of Practice for Internal Non-Load-Bearing Partitions and Stud Work) and EN 13964 (Suspended Ceilings – Performance Requirements and Test Methods). Acoustic performance is governed by ISO 354 (Sound Absorption Testing). Structural load ratings and deflection limits align with BS 5950 (Structural Use of Steelwork) for metal framing systems. ASTM C840 (Installation and Finishing of Gypsum Board) is widely referenced for workmanship standards. Moisture-resistant and mold-resistant gypsum variants must meet ASTM C1396 specifications. All materials imported must carry CE or GSO certification marks and pass ECAB inspection upon entry.

## SCOPE & SPECIFICATIONS

Core deliverables include gypsum plasterboard (standard, fire-rated, moisture-resistant, and acoustic variants), metal stud framing (galvanized steel, typically 0.6–1.2 mm thickness), suspended ceiling grids (T-bar aluminum or steel), acoustic tiles, joint compounds, taping, and finishing materials. Suppliers specify board thickness (9.5 mm, 12.5 mm, 15 mm), fire ratings (Class A, B, or C per UAE Fire Code), and acoustic absorption coefficients (NRC ratings 0.5–0.9). Typical installations include drop ceilings for MEP concealment, demountable partitions, fire-rated enclosures, and acoustic treatment in offices

Get the Civil Defence-approved reflected ceiling plan and the fire compartmentation drawing before a single hanger goes up - retro-fitting fire-stopping after boarding costs more than the ceiling did. Specify the certified system, not the board: quote the tested assembly reference so the rating survives inspection. Match board to zone - H1/H2 moisture-resistant in bathrooms, kitchens, external soffits and coastal exposures; Type F in escape routes, stairwells, service cores and between tenancies. Fix the access-panel schedule at design stage off the MEP drawings and carry a count in the BoQ. Put control joints on runs beyond roughly 10-12m and stagger board joints away from opening corners. Recurring mistakes: comparing quotes on m2 rate alone; accepting "gypsum works" lump sums; leaving paint and access panels out of scope; omitting cavity insulation on acoustic partitions; stopping partitions at the ceiling where the spec said slab-to-slab; and no VAT or wastage line.

Indicative 2026 UAE rates, ex-VAT (5%). Board ex-stock per 1200x2400 sheet: standard 12.5mm AED 18-30; moisture-resistant 12.5mm AED 28-42; fire-rated 15mm AED 35-55; acoustic or perforated AED 45-70; 600x600 mineral-fibre tile AED 12-35 each. Supply-and-install per m2: plain flat ceiling AED 35-55 residential, 45-90 commercial with skim; moisture-resistant board in wet areas AED 50-75; exposed-grid tile ceiling AED 55-95; fire-rated double-layer corridor AED 80-130; stepped, coffered or curved feature ceilings AED 90-160. Gypsum partitions AED 90-180/m2 for single board each face with insulation; fire-rated double-layer sits above that. Cost drivers: board type and layer count, steel gauge (0.5 vs 0.8mm BMT) and stud centres, insulation density, working height and access, MEP cut-out density, finish level, and night-shift or occupied-premises working.

UAE gypsum and false-ceiling work sits inside the fit-out chain: developer or landlord, consultant, main contractor, then the gypsum subcontractor, usually 4th tier and paid on 60-90 day terms. Demand follows handover waves: Q4 and Q1 as developers close out before year-end, post-Ramadan commercial fit-outs, and 5-7 year office re-fit cycles in DIFC, Business Bay and TECOM. Summer (Jun-Aug) is the slack window - crews are free and rates soften. A typical firm runs 15-60 workers, owns its scaffold and screw guns, and buys board from distributors rather than direct from the mills. Margins are thin, so the trade competes on m2 rate and makes or loses money in the scope gaps. Abu Dhabi work skews government, healthcare and education; Dubai skews retail, F&B, hospitality and residential towers.

Mandatory before matching: work type - flat gypsum ceiling, grid and mineral-fibre tile, decorative bulkhead or cove, or partition; area in m2 for ceilings plus linear metres and height for partitions; space type - villa, apartment, office, retail, F&B, clinic, warehouse; new build, fit-out of an existing shell, or replacement; fire rating required and how many minutes (60/90/120); wet or humid areas needing moisture-resistant board; acoustic target Rw; supply-only or supply-and-install; emirate and jurisdiction (DM, DDA, Trakhees, Abu Dhabi DMT); whether permits and the Civil Defence NOC are in the supplier's scope; timeline plus any after-hours or occupied-premises restriction; and drawings or site photos. Escalate to supplier acquisition when zero verified suppliers match - typically cleanroom, hospital and acoustic-critical scopes. Never ask the buyer's budget directly.

Scope splits into: plain flat gypsum ceiling on GI furring; stepped, coffered and curved bulkheads with cove lighting; exposed-grid suspended ceilings with 600x600 or 600x1200 mineral-fibre tiles (mains at 1200mm centres, cross-tees at 600mm); concealed-spline, metal pan and linear ceilings; and metal-stud gypsum partitions, single or double board per face, to ceiling height or full height to slab. Ancillaries that must be priced as separate lines, not assumed: hinged and lay-in access panels, shadow-gap and reveal trims, cut-outs for grilles, sprinklers and downlights, fire-stopping at MEP penetrations, cavity mineral wool, tape-and-joint, two-coat skim and paint. Offerings run from supply-only board and profiles, through supply-and-install, to strip-out and making good on re-fits.

A usable gypsum quote states, per system: board brand and type (Gyproc, Knauf, Gypsemna, USG), thickness in mm, layers per face, framing size, steel gauge and stud or furring centres, hanger spacing, insulation type, density and thickness, fire rating in minutes with the certified tested system reference, acoustic Rw, finish level, and whether painting is included. It must also state supply-only versus supply-and-install, whether area is measured net or gross of openings, the access-panel count and type, wastage allowance, VAT shown separately, validity (7-30 days), payment terms and programme in working days. Send back anything reading "gypsum works - lump sum". Normalise spec before comparing rate: a 30% price gap almost always resolves into thinner board, single layer where double was needed, wider stud centres, or excluded skim, paint and panels.

Jurisdiction follows location. Dubai mainland: Dubai Municipality via the Building Permit System (BPS), dm.gov.ae - fit-out fees around AED 1.00 per sq ft of BUA, minimum AED 200, permits typically 5-15 working days. TECOM and other DDA districts: Dubai Development Authority, dda.gov.ae - fit-out permit AED 0.90 per sq ft (min AED 200, max AED 10,000), valid 6 months, feedback in 2 working days, and a Civil Defence completion certificate is required before the fit-out completion certificate. Palm Jumeirah, Jumeirah Islands and JAFZA: Trakhees, trakhees.ae. Anything fire-rated answers to Dubai Civil Defence, dcd.gov.ae, under the UAE Fire and Life Safety Code of Practice (2018 edition, with Abu Dhabi amendments). Abu Dhabi: DMT, dmt.gov.ae, with Abu Dhabi Civil Defence. Product conformity (ECAS/EQM) sits with MoIAT, moiat.gov.ae, which absorbed ESMA in 2020.

Made in country: Saint-Gobain Gyproc Middle East runs a seven-hectare Abu Dhabi plasterboard plant open since April 2010, supplying GypWall partitions, Gyproc MF ceilings and Gyptone/Rigitone perforated acoustic boards, with a newer Saint-Gobain plant in Ras Al Khaimah. Gypsemna manufactures at Mussafah, Abu Dhabi - regular, lightweight, fire-rated, H1/H2 moisture-resistant, mould-resistant, glass-mat and DuraCem boards plus steel profiles - and publishes EPD and HPD declarations. Knauf supplies through Knauf Gypsum; having acquired USG in 2019 and Armstrong's ceilings business outside the Americas, USG Boral and Armstrong-branded ceiling product now sits under Knauf (the UK/Ireland ceilings arm was divested as Zentia). Tile and grid: Armstrong, Knauf AMF, Rockfon, OWA. Metal and specialist ceilings: Hunter Douglas, SAS International, Durlum.

Buyers arrive with an m2 figure and no spec, so put the trade-offs in front of them. Exposed-grid tile is the cheapest option and gives full service access, but it reads as office ceiling; flush gypsum looks better and then every valve, VAV box and damper needs an access panel - budget one panel per serviceable item, not one per room. Standard 12.5mm board saves 15-20% over 15mm Type F but is not permissible the moment the space is an escape route or a tenancy separation. Level 5 skim costs more and is the only finish that survives grazing LED cove lighting; Level 4 under wall-washers shows every joint. Partitions run to slab cost 25-40% more than ceiling-height but are the only ones that deliver the Rw a boardroom or clinic needs. A compressed programme means more crews, not fewer hours - it raises the rate.

Ask for and expect: trade licence showing a gypsum or false-ceiling activity; DM, DDA or Trakhees contractor registration; Ejari plus landlord or master-developer NOC; consultant-stamped layout, reflected ceiling plan and partition setting-out; MEP-coordinated RCP; fire compartmentation drawing; board datasheet with the EN 520 or ASTM C1396 declaration; the fire test report (BS 476 Part 22 or ASTM E119) for the exact assembly rather than a generic board certificate; insulation datasheet; MoIAT/ECAS conformity where applicable; material submittal and approved sample board; method statement and risk assessment. At close-out: Civil Defence inspection sign-off, as-built RCP, workmanship warranty (typically 12 months) and the fit-out completion certificate. Interim payment applications need measured sheets agreed against the approved RCP.

The most frequent commercial risk is unpermitted work: Dubai Municipality fines run about AED 5,000 for a first residential offence and AED 10,000-50,000 for commercial premises depending on BUA, plus AED 500-2,000 per day while unauthorised works continue, and the landlord can stop the job outright. Technical risk concentrates in rated assemblies - an unapproved penetration through fire compartmentation is the single most common Civil Defence inspection failure and can force a ceiling strip-out weeks before handover. Commercial risk: an unnamed board brand licenses substitution, and excluded access panels or painting return as variations at two to three times the original rate. Programme risk: gypsum sits behind MEP first-fix, so any MEP slippage compresses the ceiling window. Payment risk: 4th-tier subcontractors on 60-90 day terms fail first when a project stalls.

Three supplier types answer these RFQs. Distributors and traders - Fepy, QCON International, Al Khashab Building Materials, Dani Trading, Woodmark, Gemini Building Materials, Lumber World - sell supply-only board, profiles and insulation ex-stock from Dubai Investment Park, Al Quoz or Mussafah. Licensed fit-out and gypsum subcontractors hold DM, DDA or Trakhees contractor registration, do supply-and-install, and can carry drawings and permits. Small maintenance crews do villa and apartment ceilings cheaply but are rarely permit-capable. Verify before matching: trade licence carrying a gypsum or false-ceiling activity, contractor registration with the relevant authority, Civil Defence familiarity for rated systems, workmen's compensation and third-party liability, whether they own scaffold, and three named UAE projects with contactable references.

Boards classify to EN 520 (Type A regular, H1/H2 moisture-resistant, F fire-rated, D high-density, I impact) or ASTM C1396. Thickness: 9.5mm for curves only, 12.5mm standard, 15mm for fire and acoustic, 18mm in multi-layer assemblies; sheets 1200x2400 and 1200x3000. Framing follows ASTM C754/C840/C1002 - perimeter channel, CD furring, studs and tracks 48-100mm at 600mm centres, hangers about 1200mm along mains. Exposed grid follows ASTM C635/C636. Fire resistance is tested to BS 476 Part 22 or ASTM E119 and the rating belongs to the certified system - board type, stud gauge, insulation, fixing centres - never to the board alone. A single 15mm Type F each face typically gives 60 minutes; 120 minutes needs double layer. Acoustics use Rw (ISO 717) or STC (ASTM E413); Rw 45-55 needs cavity wool and sealed perimeters.

Sagging between hangers: hangers beyond 1200mm centres, 9.5mm board where 12.5mm was required, or board run parallel to the furring instead of across it. Straight-line cracking along joints: no control joints on long runs, thermal movement where external swings pass 45C, or skim applied over compound that had not set. Cracks radiating from opening corners: board joints aligned with the corner rather than staggered. Screw popping: over-driven screws or 0.5mm gauge steel used where 0.8mm was specified, letting the frame flex. Softening, staining and mould in bathrooms, kitchens and external soffits: standard board where H1/H2 moisture-resistant was needed, with coastal RH above 80%. Rust bleed at fixings near the coast: under-specified galvanising - move to a heavier GI coating or aluminium. Drumming and poor Rw: missing cavity wool or unsealed perimeters and service cut-outs.

Ask: What tasks (list)? [MANDATORY]; Quantity / scale? [MANDATORY]; One-off or ongoing?; Materials supplied by you or the contractor?; Preferred date? Note: very small jobs may fall below the platform minimum. Never ask budget.

Ask: (1) Is this a one-off job/repair or an ongoing Annual Maintenance Contract (AMC)? (2) Property type and size - apartment (how many beds), villa, townhouse, office, retail - and total area or number of rooms? (3) For a one-off: exactly what needs doing (list tasks), with photos and quantities (e.g. number of taps, switches, sqm to paint)? (4) Which systems are involved - AC/HVAC, electrical, plumbing, carpentry, painting, appliances, civil? (5) For AMC: which systems do you want covered and how many preventive visits per year (monthly/quarterly)? (6) Do you want parts/materials included up to a cap, or labour-only with parts billed? (7) What emergency response time (SLA) do you need - 24/7, 4-hour, next-day? (8) Are materials supplied by you or the contractor, and any brand preferences? (9) Is the building managed (owners association) - is an NOC or approved-contractor list required for work? (10) For electrical work, do you require a DEWA-registered contractor? (11) Access/timing constraints (working hours, tenant occupied, security/gate pass)? (12) How many AC units, and when were they last serviced (gas top-up likely)? (13) Budget range and is this owner or tenant (who approves)? (14) Preferred start date and whether you need a site survey first?

Two quote types: per-job/per-visit handyman work and Annual Maintenance Contracts (AMC). A complete one-off quote itemises: scope per task (e.g. 'replace 3x mixer taps', 'repaint 2 bedrooms 40 sqm'), labour (hours x rate or fixed), materials/parts supplied (brand, qty) vs client-supplied, call-out/minimum charge, number of technicians, any specialist (DEWA-registered electrician, certified AC tech, plumber), waste removal, warranty on workmanship, and 5% VAT. A complete AMC quote specifies: number of preventive visits/year and frequency (e.g. 4 quarterly or 12 monthly), systems covered (AC servicing, electrical, plumbing, general handyman, water heater, civil), what each visit includes (AC coil/filter clean, gas top-up?), response/SLA times for emergencies (e.g. 4-hour, 24/7), number of free callouts, parts policy (parts included up to a cap vs labour-only with parts charged), consumables included (filters, sealant), exclusions, and contract value/payment terms. Differentiators WITH units: visits/year, SLA response time (hours), parts cap (AED), emergency cover (24/7 or business hours), and whether AC gas/refrigerant is included. Strong quote: clear visit count + SLA, parts policy stated, DEWA-registered electrician named, written workmanship warranty. Corner-cutting: 'comprehensive AMC' with vague visit count, labour-only hidden as full cover (every part billed extra), no SLA, no DEWA registration for electrical, single all-in price with no scope list, low headline AMC price that excludes AC gas/major parts. Highlight to customer: visits/year, what's truly included vs chargeable, SLA, and parts cap.

topic: Field expertise — UAE codes, standards & specs
content:
Handyman & Maintenance in the UAE operates under a fragmented but specific regulatory landscape. The primary licensing authority is the **Department of Economic Development (DED)** in Dubai (or equivalent emirate-level DED), which requires any commercial maintenance company to hold a valid trade licence with the correct activity code covering general maintenance, fit-out, or technical services. For work inside free zones (JAFZA, DAFZA, Dubai South, etc.), **Trakhees** or the relevant free-zone authority issues its own contractor approval, and mainland DED licences are not automatically accepted. **Dubai Municipality** sets baseline standards for building maintenance, minor civil works, and material quality through its building regulations and the **UAE Fire and Life Safety Code of Practice** (administered with **Dubai Civil Defence**) — any maintenance task touching fire-rated walls, fire doors, suppression pipework, or emergency lighting requires DCD awareness and must not compromise existing fire compartmentation. **DEWA** approval is mandatory before any work on electrical DB panels, meter rooms, or infrastructure connected to the grid; minor internal electrical repairs still require a DEWA-registered contractor. For maintenance in residential towers or commercial buildings, the **Real Estate Regulatory Agency (RERA)** and **Owners Association** management companies often mandate pre-approved contractor lists and NOC letters before works commence in common areas.

Technical standards governing materials and workmanship include **BS** and **EN** standards for fixings, fasteners, and plasterboard systems; **IEC** standards for electrical components; **ASTM** standards for sealants and adhesives; and **Dubai Municipality's approved materials list** for paints and coatings. Waterproofing membranes should reference **ASTM** test methods for elongation and adhesion.

Core scope items buyers and suppliers discuss: carpentry repairs (door adjustments, cabinet hinges, furniture assembly), gypsum/drywall patching and skim-coat finishing, tile grouting and re-grouting, silicone sealant replacement (sanitary and structural grades), minor plumbing (tap washers, flexi-hose replacement, cistern internals — not main riser work), basic electrical (lamp replacement, socket face-plates, switch gear — DEWA-registered operative required for DB work), painting (interior emulsion, exterior weathershield, epoxy floor coatings), AC filter cleaning (split-unit, cassette), door-closer and lock replacement, pressure washing, and minor waterproofing patch repairs. Key materials discussed: Hilti/Fischer anchor systems, Knauf or Saint-Gobain gypsum board, Sika or Mapei sealants and grouts, Dulux or Jotun paint systems, UPVC and copper fittings for plumbing, and MCB/RCBO components from Schneider or Legrand.

**Price drivers**: labour nationality and skill grade (skilled Filipino/Indian tradesmen vs. semi-skilled); mobilisation distance and parking costs in Dubai; material supply vs. labour-only split; building access restrictions (SZR high-rises, gated communities); working-hours restrictions (Dubai Municipality noise bylaws prohibit

A Dubai maintenance/handyman company needs a Dubai Department of Economy and Tourism (DET) trade licence for the relevant activity - typically 'Building Cleaning & Maintenance' / 'Technical Services' or trade-specific activities (electromechanical, AC maintenance, plumbing, electrical works) - plus a registered office and Ejari tenancy. Companies offering HVAC, electrical or plumbing usually need additional approvals from Dubai Municipality, and electrical work must be carried out by a DEWA-registered/approved contractor (DEWA controls connection to its network and registers electrical contractors by grade). Technicians should be on the company's MOHRE-sponsored visas with Emirates IDs. In managed buildings and communities, work commonly requires an owners-association/master-developer NOC and use of an approved-contractor list, and larger fit-out or structural works require Dubai Municipality (or free-zone authority e.g. Trakhees, DDA) building permits and DEWA approvals. AC refrigerant handling and disposal is regulated; reputable firms follow environmental rules. Verify the contractor's DET licence covers the exact activity, that electrical staff are DEWA-registered, and that for community properties the firm is on the approved list or can obtain the NOC. Avoid unlicensed individual 'freelance' handymen for electrical or gas work - it can void insurance and breach building rules.

Core scope vocabulary: AMC (Annual Maintenance Contract), PPM (planned preventive maintenance), SLA (service level agreement / response time), reactive/breakdown calls, snag/snagging, callout/minimum charge. AC servicing: filter and coil cleaning, drainage/condensate line flush, gas/refrigerant top-up (R410A/R32), thermostat check, fan-coil unit (FCU) and air-handling unit (AHU) service; ducted split, window/wall split, and central chilled-water systems differ in scope. Electrical: DEWA-registered contractor required for fixed wiring; works should follow the DEWA wiring/electrical installation regulations and UAE codes; RCD/MCB, distribution board (DB), earthing. Plumbing: PPR/PEX pipework, water heater (geyser) descaling and anode, pressure-reducing valve, water-tank cleaning (often a Dubai Municipality-regulated activity for tanks). Painting: surface prep, primer, two-coat finish, paint brand/sheen. Fire and life safety upkeep falls under the UAE Fire and Life Safety Code where applicable. Quality markers: named part brands, manufacturer-recommended service intervals, calibrated tools, and certified technicians. A good AMC schedule states visit frequency, a task checklist per visit, consumables included (filters/sealant), parts policy with a cap, and measurable SLA response times for emergencies (e.g. 4 hours, 24/7 hotline).

Indicative Dubai pricing (verify; varies by scope and property): per-visit handyman call-outs commonly carry a minimum charge of roughly AED 100-250 before materials; hourly skilled labour often ~AED 80-200/hr. AC split-unit service indicatively ~AED 100-250 per unit (gas top-up extra). Residential AMC packages are commonly tiered by apartment size/villa - indicative apartment AMC ~AED 1,000-3,500/year and villa AMC higher (verify), priced by number of visits, systems covered, and whether parts are included. Drivers: number of preventive visits, systems and units covered (AC unit count especially), parts-included cap vs labour-only, emergency SLA (24/7 commands a premium), and property size. Red flags: an unusually cheap AMC headline that turns out labour-only with every part and AC gas billed extra; vague 'unlimited visits' with no defined SLA or task checklist; no DET activity match or no DEWA registration for electrical work; freelance/unsponsored technicians; no written workmanship warranty; large upfront full-year payment with no service schedule; and refusal to itemise labour vs materials. For one-offs, watch undisclosed minimum/callout charges and missing 5% VAT.

Dubai Department of Economy and Tourism (trade licensing) - https://www.dubaided.gov.ae/en
Dubai Municipality (building maintenance / environmental approvals) - https://www.dm.gov.ae/
DEWA - registered electrical contractors and regulations - https://www.dewa.gov.ae/en/consumer/building-services/registered-contractors
DEWA - Green Building / energy and AC guidance - https://www.dewa.gov.ae/en
UAE Fire and Life Safety Code of Practice (Dubai Civil Defence) - https://www.dcd.gov.ae/portal/en/preventive-safety/rules-regulations/uae-fire-and-life-safety-code-of-practice.jsp
MOHRE (labour/visa compliance for technicians) - https://www.mohre.gov.ae/en/home.aspx
Dubai REST / Dubai Land Department (Ejari, owners associations) - https://dubailand.gov.ae/en/
Starting a building maintenance company in Dubai (licence guidance) - https://paramountzone.ae/blog/start-a-building-maintenance-company-dubai/
AMC contract scope reference (residential AMC) - https://www.wewillfixit.com/annual-contract/residential/
AC AMC scope and value guidance - https://geem.com/blog/ac-annual-maintenance-contract-dubai

topic: Field expertise — UAE codes, standards & specs
content:
# Hospitality Supplies Companies – UAE Field Knowledge Base

**GOVERNING AUTHORITY & APPROVALS**

Hospitality Supplies Companies in the UAE operate under a layered regulatory framework. Dubai Municipality is the primary licensing authority for hospitality-related businesses and suppliers; companies must hold a valid trade license specifying their activity code (typically under "Wholesale of Food & Beverage Supplies," "Hotel Equipment & Supplies," or similar classifications). For food-contact supplies and catering equipment, the Dubai Municipality's Food Safety Department enforces compliance with UAE food safety standards and hygiene protocols. Dubai Civil Defence (DCD) and the UAE Fire and Life Safety Code of Practice govern fire-safety equipment, emergency supplies, and evacuation aids supplied to hotels and F&B establishments. If supplies include electrical equipment (kitchen appliances, heating, refrigeration), DEWA (Dubai Electricity and Water Authority) certification and compliance with DEWA technical regulations are mandatory. For security-related supplies (safes, access control, CCTV integration), SIRA (Security Industry Regulatory Agency) and Dubai Police may require approval. Suppliers importing goods must obtain Emirates Conformity certification where applicable (particularly for electrical and mechanical equipment). Free-zone suppliers operating from Jebel Ali Free Zone or other zones must register with Trakhees and comply with free-zone-specific regulations. General import/export documentation and customs clearance fall under Dubai Customs.

**STANDARDS & TECHNICAL REQUIREMENTS**

Hospitality supplies must comply with IEC standards for electrical safety (IEC 60950 for IT equipment, IEC 61010 for laboratory/analytical instruments if applicable). Food-contact materials and kitchenware follow ISO 8649 (stainless steel flatware) and relevant food-contact polymer standards. Fire-safety equipment (extinguishers, alarms, emergency lighting) must meet BS 5306 and ISO 3864 for safety signage. ASHRAE standards apply to HVAC and refrigeration supplies. Pressure equipment (steam generators, hot-water systems) must comply with PED (Pressure Equipment Directive) equivalents recognized in UAE. All electrical appliances require CE marking or equivalent UAE/GCC certification. Textiles (linens, uniforms) must meet ISO 6330 for durability and ISO 3175 for care labeling. Furniture and fixtures follow general safety standards (stability, non-toxicity of finishes). Hygiene and sanitation supplies must be certified for food-safe use per UAE food safety guidelines.

**SCOPE & SPECIFICATIONS**

Core supplies include: kitchen equipment (commercial ovens, fryers, steamers, dishwashers, prep tables—rated by capacity in covers/hour and energy consumption in kW); refrigeration (walk-in coolers, reach-in fridges, blast chillers—specified by temperature range, capacity in cubic meters, and compressor type); tableware and glassware (porcelain, glass, stainless steel—rated by durability grade and breakage resistance); linens (bed sheets, towels, table cloths—specified by thread count, weight in GSM, and fiber composition); cleaning and sanitation supplies (detergents, disinfect

Checklist before releasing an RFQ: confirm project type and emirate; obtain the brand standard; fix quantities and par levels; state AISI grade and gauge in writing; state voltage, phase, gas type and water hardness; confirm goods lift access; set the Incoterm and delivery point; require the authorised distributor letter; require FCM conformity for food contact and Civil Defence approval for hoods; specify warranty, spares availability and year-one AMC price; fix payment terms and retention; phase deliveries. Customer mistakes: buying on unit price and paying in breakage; ordering all OS&E at once with nowhere to store it; finding the brand standard after the PO. Supplier mistakes: quoting an equivalent without declaring it, omitting commissioning, quoting stock they do not hold. Documentation: no TRN tax invoice, no certificate of origin, missing Arabic labels. Compliance mistake: still selling banned single-use plastics in 2026. Order 5-10% attrition crockery from the original batch.

Cost drivers ranked: brand tier and origin first (a European combi is 2.5-3x a Turkish or Chinese equivalent), then stainless grade and gauge, then freight and Incoterm, then certification, then customisation (logo print, embroidery, bespoke sizes), then installation and commissioning, then warranty and AMC scope, then payment terms. Landed cost adds 5% GCC customs duty on CIF plus clearance, then 5% VAT; free-zone stock re-entering mainland pays duty again on the Bill of Entry. On a 200-key hotel OS&E package: economy AED 900-1,400 per key, mid AED 1,500-2,800, luxury AED 3,500-6,000 and up. Value engineering: RAK Porcelain instead of European bone china, 430 on dry cladding, standard sizes over bespoke, phased delivery. Terms: hotels pay 45-90 days from invoice, LPO mandatory, 30-50% advance on fabrication, 10% retention on turnkey. Compressing 8 weeks to 3 adds 20-40% in air freight.

The trade splits into OS&E (crockery, cutlery, glassware, buffetware, linen, uniforms, amenities), FF&E and CKE (commercial kitchen equipment). Buyers are hotel purchasing managers, cluster procurement heads, F&B directors, executive chefs, pre-opening task forces, contract caterers serving ADNOC and construction camps, and cloud kitchens. Tiers: brand principals, sole UAE agents, turnkey fabricators like Al Halabi, stockist dealers, Deira traders reselling grey stock. Pre-openings buy off an OS&E schedule built from the operator brand standard; running hotels replenish par stock on a 2 or 3 par rule. October to April is peak occupancy with no closures allowed; June to August is the refurbishment window; Ramadan (2026 roughly 18 Feb to 19 Mar) spikes chafers, buffetware and iftar disposables; The Hotel Show at Expo City, 28-30 September, and February's Gulfood reset the calendar.

Order: 1) project type - pre-opening, refurbishment, replacement or running supply; 2) emirate and site; 3) scale in keys, covers or monthly volume; 4) operator brand standard; 5) item list with quantities; 6) delivery date; 7) installation and commissioning in scope; 8) budget or a reference item. Mandatory: 1, 2, 3, 5, 6. Skippable: 8 when the list is precise. If pre-opening, get the OS&E schedule and brand standard and route only to project-capable suppliers. For kitchen equipment, utilities and layout are mandatory; without them do not fan out. For food contact items, demand FCM conformity and drop suppliers lacking it. If disposables, confirm the item is not on the 2026 banned list and offer bagasse or paper. Custom fabrication needs a site survey. Fan out at 80% confidence on stock OS&E; below that, above AED 500,000, or on any Civil Defence scope, route to a scoping call.

Taxonomy: tabletop (porcelain, bone china, vitrified hotelware, tempered glass, 18/10 cutlery, stemware); buffet (chafers, induction warmers, risers); production (combi ovens, blast chillers, ranges, fryers, planetary mixers); refrigeration (upright, undercounter, blast, walk-in cold rooms); warewash (undercounter, hood-type, rack conveyor, flight); ice machines; extract canopies; stainless fabrication (tables, sinks, shelving); housekeeping (trolleys, vacuums, scrubbers); linen and terry; uniforms; amenities; disposables. Alternatives matter: bone china versus vitrified for chip resistance, hood-type versus undercounter dishwasher above 60 racks per hour, induction where no gas riser exists. Lifecycle: linen 150-250 wash cycles, crockery 2-3 years at 30% annual attrition, combi ovens 8-10 years. Wrapped services: layout drawings, installation, commissioning, training, AMC, spares.

Mandatory to collect: project type (pre-opening, refurbishment, replacement, running supply), emirate and exact site, keys or covers or seats, the operator brand standard if any, item list with quantities and par levels, delivery date, and whether installation and commissioning are in scope. For equipment add utilities (voltage, phase, gas type and availability, water hardness, drainage), the kitchen layout drawing or at minimum dimensions, and the access route with lift size. For OS&E add pattern, size, colour, logo artwork and branding method. For linen add GSM, size, blend and laundry method. State Incoterm, delivery point, warranty period and payment terms. Suppliers bin an inquiry with no quantities, no site and no date, an anonymous buyer requesting a full hotel OS&E list for benchmarking, a request to price from a photo, or a proprietary model with no equivalents allowed.

MOIAT (https://moiat.gov.ae) absorbed ESMA in 2020 and runs national standards, the Emirates Conformity Assessment Scheme (ECAS) and the Emirates Quality Mark (EQM). It administers the mandatory food contact materials scheme under Cabinet Resolution No. 21 of 2015, keyed to UAE.S GSO 2231 plus standards for melamine, ceramic, glass and plastics. MOCCAE (https://www.moccae.gov.ae) owns single-use plastics: under Cabinet Decision No. 23 of 2024 the final phase from 1 January 2026 bans import, manufacture and sale of plastic cups and lids, cutlery, plates, straws, stirrers, EPS containers and bags under 50 microns; fines start near AED 2,000. Dubai Municipality (https://www.dm.gov.ae) enforces the Food Code and Foodwatch (https://foodwatch.dm.gov.ae). Abu Dhabi is ADAFSA (https://www.adafsa.gov.ae). Civil Defence (https://www.dcd.gov.ae) approves kitchen extract and suppression systems.

Cooking: Rational and Convotherm (Welbilt, Ali Group) combis, Unox, Electrolux Professional, Angelo Po, Berto's, Lincat, Middleby including Blodgett and TurboChef. Warewash: Winterhalter, MEIKO, Hobart. Refrigeration and ice: Hoshizaki, Scotsman, Manitowoc, Foster, Williams. Prep: Robot Coupe, Hallde, Vitamix. Hoods: Halton, Jeven; suppression Ansul R-102 or Amerex. Tabletop: RAK Porcelain, made in Ras Al Khaimah and the default UAE hotel spec on price and lead time, then Steelite, Churchill, Bauscher, Schonwald, Villeroy and Boch, Arc (Arcoroc), Libbey, Pasabahce, Riedel; cutlery WMF, Sola, Amefa, Robert Welch. Amenities: ADA Cosmetics, Groupe GM. Care: Diversey, Ecolab, Tork, Karcher, Rubbermaid. Laundry: Girbau, Alliance (Primus, IPSO), Miele Professional. Disposables: Hotpack, Falcon Pack. Demand the CE declaration, NSF certificate, UAE agent authorisation letter and FCM conformity.

A chef says he wants a Rational; he actually wants covers out on time with the labour he has. A purchasing manager says lowest price; he is measured on cost per cover and on not being the reason the opening slipped. Ask what operator brand standard applies, because Marriott, Accor, Hilton and Rotana OS&E standards override taste and quietly disqualify three of your four bidders. Real constraints: kitchen footprint fixed by the shell, electrical load already allocated by the MEP consultant, no gas riser in most towers, goods lift dimensions, and a hotel that cannot close. Trade-offs to name aloud: cheap crockery costs more per year once 30-40% breakage is counted; a bigger dishwasher saves two staff; one brand across the kitchen simplifies AMC but loses 8-12% on price. Always ask about phase two, because matching a discontinued pattern in year three is impossible.

At inquiry: item BOQ with quantities and units, kitchen layout drawing with equipment schedule, and the brand standard extract. At tender: datasheets, dimensional and utility drawings, CE or UKCA declaration of conformity, NSF certificate where hygiene is claimed, warranty statement, and the authorised distributor letter. For anything touching food: UAE.S GSO 2231 food contact conformity, the MOIAT ECAS certificate where the product is regulated, and migration test reports from an accredited lab for melamine, plastics and coated ware. For kitchens: Civil Defence approved shop drawings for canopy and suppression, MEP coordination drawings and method statement. At delivery: commercial invoice, packing list, certificate of origin, Bill of Entry, signed delivery note, warranty certificates, O and M manuals and commissioning report. Keep the TRN-bearing tax invoice.

Technical: 60Hz or 110V equipment on a 50Hz 415V board; early sign is a datasheet quoting only US voltages. Compliance: no FCM conformity for crockery or melamine; early sign is a supplier sending a photo instead of a test report. Legal: quoting single-use plastic items off an old catalogue after the 1 January 2026 ban; early sign is stock offered well below market. Commercial: a price 30% under the field almost always means AISI 430, thinner gauge or grey stock; early sign is refusal to state material grade in writing. Supplier: no authorised distributor letter means no principal warranty; early sign is a warranty offered by the trader, not the factory. Schedule: a European indent quoted at 6 weeks when the factory quotes 12; early sign is no order acknowledgement. Financial: a buyer pushing 120 days on a first order with no LPO. Operational: no service engineer in the emirate.

Four archetypes. Sole agents and brand offices (Rational Middle East, Electrolux Professional, Winterhalter) hold real spares and factory-trained engineers, and rarely discount past 15%. Turnkey CKE contractors (Al Halabi, Alpha Kitchen, Silverline) fabricate stainless in house, accept main-contractor terms with 5-10% retention, and suit a full kitchen. Stockist dealers (Restofair RAK, Al Diwan, Excel Kitchen, Kitchen Warehouse) hold OS&E on the shelf and ship next day but rarely engineer. Deira traders move parallel imports cheap, with no warranty the principal honours. Verify before trusting anyone: trade licence with the correct activity, a current authorised distributor letter, a service department with engineer and vehicle counts, a warehouse you can visit, VAT TRN, and two recent hotel references. Lead times: stock 2-5 days, European indent 8-14 weeks, fabrication 4-8 weeks.

Specify AISI 304 stainless for all food contact and wet areas, 1.2mm minimum on worktops, 1.5mm where a chef stands on it; AISI 430 belongs on dry cladding only and pits within a year under chloride-heavy UAE water. Power is 220-240V single phase and 415V three phase at 50Hz; US 60Hz units run motors wrong and fail submittal. Water is the silent killer: TDS commonly 150-400 ppm, so every dishwasher, combi steamer and espresso boiler needs a softener or RO with hardness stated in the quote, or it scales in months. Size warewash by racks per hour against covers, not price; a 400-cover buffet needs a rack conveyor, not two undercounters. Hood extract airflow follows canopy type and appliance duty per the UAE Fire and Life Safety Code, with UL300 wet chemical suppression, baffle filters and a grease trap sized to the Municipality rule. Cold rooms need condensing units rated for 50C ambient.

Dishwasher leaving film and scale: check incoming TDS and hardness first, then softener regeneration, then rinse-aid dosing, then final rinse temperature at 82-85C, then the booster element; nine times in ten it is untreated UAE water, not the machine. Combi oven tripping: check phase balance and cable size against the nameplate, then the RCD rating, then the boiler probe. Crockery chipping fast: measure rim thickness and inspect racking and handling before blaming the brand, since most losses happen at the dishwash landing table. Cold room not holding in August: verify the condensing unit ambient rating, then condenser fouling from dust, then door seals and strip curtains. Linen greying or shrinking: check wash temperature, chlorine dosing and GSM against the spec. Escalate to the principal when a warranty claim is refused, a fault repeats three times, or an inspection is at risk.

Checklist before fanning an inquiry out. One, signed terms of business with fee, guarantee and a 6-12 month introduction period. Two, a written scorecard with 5-7 must-haves and an AED salary band. Three, confirmed jurisdiction and free visa quota. Four, Emiratisation status checked on the MOHRE portal. Five, attestation started the day the offer is verbal. Six, a single point of contact and a decided exclusivity position. Customer mistakes: briefing four agencies at 15 percent each and receiving the same five CVs, refusing to state a budget, interviewing over six weeks and losing every shortlisted candidate, and treating a recruiter as a visa sponsor. Provider mistakes: CV-spamming without qualification, quoting a percentage with no floor fee, promising an overseas start in four weeks. Documentation mistakes: no DPA under the PDPL, verbal fee agreements, missing PI cover. Compliance mistakes: charging candidates, and nationality-based screening.

Fee models. Contingency: 12-15 percent of annual gross for junior, 15-20 percent mid-market, 20-25 percent plus for senior, floor fee AED 15,000-25,000. Retained and exec search: 25-33 percent in thirds at engagement, shortlist and start, minimum AED 60,000-150,000. RPO: retainer AED 25,000-80,000 per dedicated recruiter, or AED 8,000-25,000 per hire. EOR: AED 900-2,500 per employee per month plus visa cost at cost. Manpower supply: worker wage plus 25-45 percent margin. PRO and new-visa processing: AED 5,000-9,000 per employee all-in. Advisory: AED 1,200-3,000 an hour, handbook AED 15,000-45,000, benchmarking AED 25,000-90,000. Drivers ranked: seniority, scarcity, exclusivity, volume, guarantee length, overseas versus local. Terms: 30 days from start date, 60-90 day replacement guarantee. Levers: exclusivity, multi-role commitment, staged retainer, longer guarantee not a discount.

Vocabulary: contingency, retained, exec search, RPO, MSP, EOR/PEO, secondment, manpower or labour supply, PRO, Tas-heel, WPS, SIF, NOC, EOSB/gratuity, MOHRE skill levels 1-9, quota, Nafis, Tadbeer, ICV. Buyers are HR managers and heads of talent in firms above 100 staff, founders and GMs below that, and procurement in government-linked groups where three quotes are mandatory. Cycles: budgets approve Dec-Feb, requisitions land Jan-Mar and Sep-Nov, and July-August plus Ramadan are dead for interviews though visa admin continues. Tiers: global branded agencies, regional mid-market houses of 10-40 consultants, one-desk boutiques, blue-collar supply companies with their own accommodation and MOHRE supply permit, and PRO/typing shops that call themselves recruiters. Volume blue-collar demand tracks construction and hospitality; white-collar tracks banking, logistics and tech funding.

Ask in order. 1, permanent placement, outsourced or EOR headcount, manpower supply, or advisory? Mandatory, everything forks here. 2, legal entity and jurisdiction: mainland, free zone, DIFC or ADGM? Mandatory. 3, job titles, quantity and AED monthly salary band? Mandatory; no band, no quote. 4, start date and notice constraints? Mandatory. 5, who sponsors the visa and is quota free? Mandatory for outsourced and supply. 6, Emiratisation status? Mandatory above 20 staff. 7, exclusive or multi-agency? Skippable, but it moves the fee. Rules: if outsourced or EOR, route only to providers with their own quota. Domestic staff route to Tadbeer only. Above AED 45,000 a month, route to retained search, not contingency. Above 20 blue-collar heads, route to supply firms with accommodation. If jurisdiction is unknown or headcount above 50 with unclear quota, book a scoping call, not a fan-out.

Split the category five ways. Permanent placement: contingency for volume and mid-market, retained or exec search above AED 45,000 a month. Outsourced headcount: EOR/PEO where the provider sponsors the visa and invoices monthly, contract staffing, and manpower supply for blue-collar labour by head or hour. Process: RPO, payroll and WPS running, PRO and visa processing, onboarding admin. Advisory: HR audit, handbook and policy drafting, grading and job architecture, salary benchmarking, HRIS selection, Emiratisation strategy, outplacement. Domestic: Tadbeer centres for maids, nannies and drivers, a separate licensing route. Scope boundary that causes disputes: an agency that places is not a sponsor, and only an EOR or supply firm carries the visa, WPS liability and gratuity. Lifecycle: brief, scorecard, shortlist, interviews, offer, attestation, permit, medical, Emirates ID, guarantee.

Mandatory before any provider quotes: legal entity name and jurisdiction (mainland, free zone, DIFC or ADGM), trade licence, current headcount, exact job titles with an AED monthly salary band, permanent versus contract versus outsourced, number of positions, emirate of work, who sponsors the visa, target start date, and whether the Emiratisation quota is currently met. For blue-collar supply add trade, shift pattern, duration, and who provides accommodation and transport. Price and turnaround move on seniority, scarcity, exclusivity, volume, guarantee length and hire origin. Providers reject an inquiry when there is no salary band, when the fee is pure success deferred past probation, when the offer is 8 percent, when the brief is a nationality filter, when no trade licence exists, when the client wants a shortlist in 48 hours, or when three agencies already hold the same role.

MOHRE, https://www.mohre.gov.ae, licenses recruitment and labour supply offices, issues work permits, approves contracts, runs WPS and Emiratisation, and settles labour complaints amicably within two weeks. ICP, https://icp.gov.ae, issues entry permits, residence and Emirates ID; GDRFA covers Dubai. Core law: Federal Decree-Law 33 of 2021, amended by 20 of 2023. Domestic work: Federal Decree-Law 9 of 2022, amended by 21 of 2023, covering 19 professions, banning commission charged to the worker and requiring a medical within 30 days before entry, via MOHRE Tadbeer centres. Emiratisation: Nafis, https://www.nafis.gov.ae: 2 percent skilled growth a year to 10 percent by 2026 for 50-plus firms, AED 6,000 a month per unfilled post, AED 108,000 from January 2026 for 20-49 staff firms in 14 sectors. Free zones: DIFC Employment Law No. 2 of 2019 as amended, ADGM Employment Regulations 2019.

Agencies active here: Michael Page, Hays, Robert Half, Robert Walters, Nadia Global, Charterhouse, BAC Middle East, Mackenzie Jones, Cooper Fitch, Manpower Middle East, Adecco, Randstad. Executive search: Korn Ferry, Heidrick and Struggles, Egon Zehnder, Spencer Stuart, Russell Reynolds, Stanton Chase. Outsourcing and manpower: Transguard Group, TASC Outsourcing, Airswift, plus EOR platforms Deel, Remote, Papaya Global and Safeguard Global. Sourcing: LinkedIn Recruiter, Bayt.com, GulfTalent, Naukrigulf, Indeed. Systems: Bullhorn and JobDiva for agencies, Greenhouse and Workable for clients, Bayzat and Palm HR for SME payroll, Oracle Fusion, SAP SuccessFactors and Workday for enterprise. Screening: HireRight, Sterling, First Advantage. Credentials to check: CIPD, SHRM-CP or SCP, REC membership. The real difference is database depth and whether the firm sponsors visas itself.

What they say is best candidate on the market. What they mean is fill it in three weeks, inside a budget set two years ago, with someone already on a cancellable UAE visa. Real constraints they rarely volunteer: salary band 15-25 percent below market, an unwritten nationality or gender preference that is legally exposed and a serious agency will refuse in writing, Arabic requirement, UAE driving licence, 30-90 day notice periods, and no free visa quota. Functional need is a filled seat; operational need is a permit that clears MOHRE and ICP without a rejection. Trade-offs to name out loud: speed versus fit, since insisting on both produces a fall-off inside 90 days; exclusivity versus three agencies sending the same CVs and killing your leverage; a cheaper overseas hire that costs 6-10 weeks and AED 7,000 of processing; and paying market versus reopening the role in five months.

Terms of business signed before any CV moves: fee percentage, payment trigger, introduction and ownership period of 6-12 months, replacement guarantee and refund scale. Retained work adds an engagement letter with milestones and an off-limits clause. NDA where the search is confidential, and a data processing addendum plus documented candidate consent under Federal Decree-Law 45 of 2021. Provider side: trade licence with the correct activity, MOHRE establishment card, professional indemnity cover of AED 1-5 million, and Tadbeer approval for domestic work. Candidate side: MOHRE job offer signed before the entry permit, MOHRE standard employment contract, degree attested by the UAE embassy and MOFA, police clearance where required, medical fitness certificate, Emirates ID, and medical insurance. Outsourcing adds an EOR service agreement, assignment schedule and WPS SIF setup.

Legal: an unlicensed intermediary or a nationality-filtered brief. Warning sign is a provider invoicing from a different entity than the one on the terms. Compliance: a breached Emiratisation quota freezes new permits; the early sign is MOHRE portal errors on a routine renewal. Financial: charging candidates a fee, which is prohibited for domestic recruitment and reputationally fatal elsewhere; the sign is a candidate asking about a deposit refund. Commercial: fee disputes over who introduced the candidate first, signalled by duplicate CVs arriving from two agencies inside 48 hours. Operational: attestation failure, spotted when the candidate cannot produce an embassy-stamped degree. Schedule: an overseas start promised in four weeks. Provider: a supply firm with WPS defaults. Customer: a client that will not confirm the salary band, which usually means there is no approved budget.

Archetypes: the global branded agency with process and a high fee; the regional mid-market house that actually fills mid-level roles fastest; the one-desk boutique that owns a niche and nothing else; the manpower supply company with labour accommodation, buses and a MOHRE supply permit; the EOR with its own free-zone licence and visa quota; the ex-Big-Four HR consultancy; and the PRO typing shop reselling CVs. Tell them apart by the trade licence activity code, not the website. Verify: licence activity actually covers recruitment or labour supply, MOHRE establishment card and classification, an unused visa quota if they will sponsor, professional indemnity cover, WPS compliance history, and whether consultants are employed or on someone else's visa. Turnaround: shortlist 5-10 working days mid-market, 3-6 weeks retained, 24-72 hours for blue-collar supply from an existing pool.

Method: a written scorecard with 5-7 must-have competencies, competency-based STAR interviewing, structured scoring, and psychometrics only where the role justifies it. Key variables that decide the quote: MOHRE skill level 1-9, which sets permit fee and Emiratisation weighting; mainland versus free zone versus DIFC or ADGM, which decides the contract template; hire origin, since a local candidate on cancellation moves in 2-4 weeks and an overseas candidate needs 6-10. Metrics that matter: time-to-fill, offer-acceptance rate, and fall-off inside the guarantee. Technical failure points seen weekly: job title on the work permit not matching the offer letter, which rejects the application; degree not attested by the UAE embassy in the issuing country then MOFA; skill level set too low for the salary; medical fitness fail; a DIFC contract issued to a mainland-sponsored employee.

Recurring problems and the sequence a veteran runs. Work permit rejected: check job title against the offer letter, then skill level against salary, then attestation, then the establishment quota, in that order. Candidate accepts then ghosts: almost always a counter-offer, so diagnose at offer stage by asking about their current employer's retention behaviour. Fall-off inside 90 days: check whether the brief had a written scorecard; unwritten briefs fall off two to three times more often. Start date slipping: pull the entry permit status from ICP before blaming the agency. Payroll flagged: reconcile the WPS SIF against the MOHRE contract salary, since a mismatch of even AED 100 rejects the file. Escalate to MOHRE only after a written demand and 14 days. Prevention: written terms before the first CV, salary band agreed in the brief, attestation started before the offer is issued.

topic: Field expertise — UAE codes, standards & specs
content:
# HVAC Suppliers — UAE Field Knowledge Base

## Governing Authority & Approvals

HVAC installation and supply in the UAE falls under multiple regulatory bodies. Dubai Municipality issues building permits and conducts inspections on all mechanical systems within buildings. Dubai Civil Defence (DCD) enforces the UAE Fire and Life Safety Code of Practice, particularly for smoke management systems, fire-rated ductwork, and emergency ventilation in high-rise and commercial properties. DEWA (Dubai Electricity and Water Authority) approves electrical connections for all HVAC equipment, including VFD (variable frequency drive) installations and power consumption compliance. For chilled water systems and district cooling connections, Emaar or the relevant district cooling operator must approve interface specifications. In free zones (JAFZA, Dubai Silicon Oasis), Trakhees or the zone authority issues additional mechanical permits. Emirates Conformity Marks (ECM) or CE certification may be required for imported equipment. All ductwork, insulation, and refrigerant handling must comply with Dubai Municipality's mechanical code and DCD fire safety standards.

## Standards & Technical Requirements

HVAC design and installation must meet ASHRAE standards (particularly ASHRAE 62.1 for indoor air quality and ventilation rates), ISO 9001 for quality management, and BS 1192 for CAD coordination. Refrigerant handling follows EPA and local environmental guidelines; R410A and R32 are standard, with phase-out restrictions on older refrigerants. Ductwork design complies with SMACNA standards for construction and sealing. Electrical components must meet IEC 60038 for voltage standards (400V/230V in UAE). Chilled water systems follow ASHRAE 90.1 for energy efficiency. All equipment must be rated for UAE ambient conditions (50°C+ outdoor design temperature).

## Scope & Specifications

Core offerings include split AC units (residential/commercial), packaged rooftop units (RTU), variable refrigerant flow (VRF) systems, chilled water plants, air handling units (AHU), ductwork (galvanised steel, fibreglass-lined), insulation (foam, mineral wool), thermostats, controls, and BMS (Building Management System) integration. Capacities range from 1 TR (ton of refrigeration) residential splits to 500+ TR central plants. Tonnage, EER (energy efficiency ratio), sound levels (dB), and static pressure ratings are critical specifications. Refrigerant charge, compressor type (scroll, screw, centrifugal), and expansion device (TXV, capillary) define performance.

## Price Drivers

Equipment cost varies by capacity, brand (Daikin, Carrier, Trane, Midea, Gree), and technology (inverter vs. fixed-speed, VRF vs. traditional split). Installation labour is driven by building height, ductwork complexity, and site accessibility. Chilled water systems command premium pricing. Refrigerant type and charge volume affect material costs. Energy efficiency ratings (SEER, HSPF) influence long-term value perception. Warranty terms (1–5

Checklist: fix the load in TR from a stamped calculation before pricing; demand a selection printout at 46-50C showing kW/TR and IPLV; confirm the ECAS CoC and EESL label before shipment; confirm UL 555/555S dampers for Civil Defence; get scope inclusions and exclusions in writing - offloading, craneage, starters, VFDs, AV mounts, first refrigerant fill, testing, commissioning, training; tie warranty to the commissioning date; state the Incoterm, 5% VAT and delivery point; put submittal-approval dates in the programme; make O&M manuals, as-builts, TAB report and authority sign-off conditions of final payment; hold 5-10% retention 12 months. Buyer mistakes: "urgent chiller quote" with no load; comparing supply-only against supply-install. Supplier mistakes: catalogue ratings, no ESP allowance, no craneage. Documentation: expired dealership letter, nameplate not matching the certificate. Compliance: ignoring MOCCAE refrigerant controls and Al Sa'fat efficiency minimums.

Cost drivers by impact: capacity in TR; efficiency tier (MEPS-baseline to best-in-class kW/TR adds 15-30% capex); supply-only versus supply-install-commission (install adds 25-50% on plant, 40-80% on unitary); machine type (oil-free centrifugal runs 2-3x screw per TR); coil coating; VFDs and BMS integration. Value engineering that holds: locally built Eurovent-class AHUs instead of European imports, factory-standard controls rather than bespoke BMS graphics. Value engineering that bites back: dropping coil coating on coastal sites, thinner GI than SMACNA, unlisted dampers, deleting VFDs. Terms: 30-50% advance, balance against delivery or LC at sight, 5-10% retention for 12 months on install scope. Levers: order outside the May-September peak, split the PO, trade discount for a 3-5 year AMC or extended compressor warranty, and force FOB/CIF/DDP and 5% VAT to be shown separately.

Buyers fall into four groups: MEP contractors pricing tender BOQs for DM, Trakhees, DDA, ADM and Sharjah Municipality projects; FM and O&M firms buying replacement plant, compressors and spares; developers doing chiller and VRF retrofits; and industrial, data centre and cold-chain users in JAFZA, DIC, KIZAD and Sharjah industrial areas. Cycles follow the tender calendar - BOQ pricing runs 2-4 weeks, submittal approval another 2-6. Retrofits cluster October-March so plant is down outside peak; May-September spikes emergency compressor, chiller and FAHU demand and stretches lead times. Supplier tiers: OEM regional offices (Daikin, Carrier, Trane, JCI/York, LG, Midea, Zamil, SKM, Petra), authorised dealers, local duct/AHU/FCU fabricators in Al Quoz, Sharjah and Ajman, and trading houses. Vocabulary: TR, CHW/CDW, delta-T, ESP, TDH, DX, VRF, FAHU, IPLV, ASHRAE 90.1, submittal, T&C, TAB.

Order: 1) application and building type; 2) emirate, location or free zone; 3) cooling load in TR, or BOQ/drawings - if neither, floor area in sqft and occupancy; 4) new build, retrofit or like-for-like replacement; 5) system type wanted (chiller, VRF, split, package, AHU) or open; 6) supply-only or supply, install and commission; 7) quantity and required on-site date; 8) brand or approved vendor list, or open; 9) budget range. Mandatory before fan-out: application, emirate, load/drawings/area, scope, quantity, timeline. Skippable, since suppliers propose them: refrigerant, efficiency tier, warranty, finish. Enough when a supplier can produce a selection and firm price without a callback. Scoping call instead when there is no load, drawings or area; multi-building or phased scope; a district cooling ETS tie-in; Civil Defence smoke-control design; or a budget far below equipment cost.

Chillers: air-cooled scroll and screw, water-cooled screw and centrifugal, magnetic-bearing oil-free, modular, absorption and process chillers. Unitary: window, wall/floor/ceiling split, ducted split, cassette, package and rooftop units, VRF/VRV heat pump and heat recovery. Air side: AHU, FAHU with DX, chilled water, heat wheel or desiccant dehumidification, FCU, ECU, ERV/HRV, kitchen and car-park exhaust and jet-fan systems. Distribution: GI duct, pre-insulated phenolic/PIR panel duct, flexible duct, fibreglass and Class O rubber insulation, VCD/FD/FSD and motorised dampers, grilles, diffusers, VAV boxes, attenuators. Hydronics: CHW and condenser pumps, cooling towers, district-cooling ETS skids, PICVs, BTU meters, pre-insulated pipe. Controls: BMS/DDC, VFDs, thermostats. Services: supply-only, supply and install, T&C, TAB, AMC/PPM, duct cleaning, IAQ testing, energy audits, retrofit.

Mandatory before quoting: application and building type, emirate and exact site, cooling load in TR or the mechanical BOQ and drawings, system type (or open), supply-only versus supply-install-commission, quantity, required on-site date, and the approving authority. Useful but not blocking: design ambient, indoor conditions, fresh-air rate, refrigerant preference, 400V/3ph/50Hz confirmation, panel scope, warranty term, approved vendor list. Price drivers: capacity, efficiency tier, refrigerant, coil coating and casing material, BMS integration, VFDs, and whether Civil Defence rated dampers are in scope. Delivery drivers: stock versus factory build - imported chillers and AHUs run 8-20 weeks, local duct and FCUs 1-4 weeks - plus summer peak and submittal approval time. Suppliers reject inquiries with no load, no drawings, no emirate, no timeline, or a budget below equipment cost.

MOIAT (https://www.moiat.gov.ae/, ex-ESMA) runs ECAS conformity and the EESL energy label; UAE.S 5010-1 (household) and 5010-5 (commercial/central) set MEPS, and a valid Certificate of Conformity is needed before customs release. Dubai Municipality (https://www.dm.gov.ae/) issues building permits and enforces the Dubai Building Code and Al Sa'fat; Al Sa'fat Silver mandatory for new DM permits in 2026. Dubai Civil Defence (https://www.dcd.gov.ae/) enforces the UAE Fire and Life Safety Code: fire and smoke dampers, smoke-control and pressurisation fans. DEWA (https://www.dewa.gov.ae/) approves load. Dubai's RSB (https://rsbdubai.gov.ae/) permits district cooling per Executive Council Resolution 6 of 2021; Abu Dhabi's DoE (https://www.doe.gov.ae/) licenses it under Law 11 of 2018. MOCCAE (https://www.moccae.gov.ae/) controls HFC quotas. Free zones: Trakhees (https://trakhees.ae/).

Premium: Daikin (Daikin Middle East FZE, Jebel Ali; McQuay chillers), Carrier, Trane, Johnson Controls-York, Mitsubishi Electric Climaveneta, Smardt and Danfoss Turbocor oil-free. Mid: LG, Samsung, Midea, Hitachi, Fujitsu General via Taqeef. Regional factories worth quoting: SKM (Fujairah), Petra Engineering (Jordan), Zamil Cooline, Trosten (Sharjah). Components: Ruskin Titus Gulf builds dampers, grilles and VAV in the UAE; TROX and Systemair air side; Grundfos and Armstrong pumps; BAC and Evapco towers; Kingspan KoolDuct and PalDuct duct; Kimmco and Rockwool insulation via Leminar. What genuinely differs: compressor and heat-exchanger source, fin thickness and coil coating, casing thermal-bridge class, spares held in-country. Demand AHRI 550/590 or 210/240 certificates, Eurovent casing class, UL 555/555S damper listing, ECAS CoC, a current dealership letter, factory run-test report.

They say lowest price; they want no callback in August, first-time consultant approval, clean authority inspection. MEP contractors need BOQ-compliant submittals and pay-when-paid-proof terms; FM firms buy spares availability and response time; developers buy capex while the operator pays the DEWA bill - name that split incentive aloud. Ask about phase two, fit-out load and added floors: 20% headroom beats a second chiller later, but blanket oversizing wrecks part-load efficiency - stage modules. Risk tolerance differs: a hospital or data centre pays for N+1 and dual feeds, a warehouse tolerates two days. Trade-offs to name: capex versus 15-year energy - 0.55 against 0.75 kW/TR pays back in 2-4 years; a local AHU in 4-6 weeks versus a certified European unit in 14-20; VRF's lower capex, proprietary spares and leak risk against chilled water's longer life and open spares market.

Ask the buyer for: mechanical BOQ, tender specification, HVAC layouts and schematics (duct, chilled water, refrigerant piping), equipment schedules, the heat load calculation (HAP, Carrier or Elite output), single-line electrical and available power, site photographs for replacements, and the approving authority. Expect from the supplier: technical submittal with selection printout, dimensional and wiring drawings, MOIAT/ECAS Certificate of Conformity and UAE.S 5010 energy label for regulated units, AHRI or Eurovent certificate, BS 476 or ASTM E84 Class O fire test report for insulation, UL 555/555S damper certificates, ISO 9001, trade licence and VAT certificate, warranty statement, O&M manuals, and TAB plus commissioning reports at handover. For imports: commercial invoice, packing list, certificate of origin and refrigerant import clearance where the gas is quota-controlled.

Technical: selection at 35C, not the 46-50C design ambient - sign is a quote citing nominal TR with no selection printout naming ambient. Compliance: no ECAS CoC or EESL label, container sits at Jebel Ali - sign is a supplier who cannot give the CoC number, or gives one in another importer's name. Fire: "equivalent to UL" wording in a damper submittal means DCD rejection. Commercial: a bid 25-40% under the pack is a parallel import, a carved-out scope, or both - sign is a one-page quote with no exclusions list. Financial: heavy advance to a thin trade licence, or payment to a third-country account. Schedule: no submittal-approval milestone in the programme; summer peak inflates craneage. Operational: exotic brand, no local service department. Customer: unsigned load calc, then variations. Warranty: a clause running from shipment, not commissioning, on plant that idles for months.

Four archetypes. OEM regional offices quote genuine selections with AHRI or Eurovent certificates but hold order minimums and push small jobs to dealers. Authorised distributors and dealers should produce a dealership authorisation letter - verify it, because parallel imports void warranty and often carry no ECAS registration. Local fabricators in Al Quoz, Sharjah and Ajman build GI duct, AHUs, FCUs and panels fast and cheap; ask for SMACNA or DW/144 compliance, their leakage test method. Trading houses and general MEP suppliers carry a broad catalogue but thin engineering and subcontract selection. Before trusting any of them verify: valid UAE trade licence with the correct activity, VAT TRN, ISO 9001, dealership letter, references at the same TR class, and whether they self-perform installation. A free-zone-only licence cannot invoice onshore install work without a mainland partner.

Design ambient is 46-50 degC dry bulb; always confirm the selection ambient, since catalogue ratings at 35 degC overstate capacity by 15-25%. Standards in use: ASHRAE 90.1, 55 and 62.1 for fresh air, AHRI 550/590 and 210/240 for rated capacity, Eurovent for AHU casing class, SMACNA and DW/144 for duct construction and leakage class, BS 476 and ASTM E84 Class O for insulation, UL 555 and 555S for fire and smoke dampers. Sizing: cooling load in TR, then airflow CFM at design delta-T, then external static pressure from duct run and filter loading, then fan power; water side needs flow, delta-T (5.5-8 degC) and total dynamic head. Failure points: ESP underestimated, condensate trap depth wrong on draw-through units, no epoxy or Blygold coil coating so coastal coils fail in 3-5 years, duct leakage worse than Class B, VRF pipe length and lift beyond limits, fouling factors omitted.

Recurring: plant not holding setpoint in July. Sequence - confirm actual load against the design calc, read supply air and CHW temperatures, check condenser approach and coil fouling, charge and superheat, check VFD limiting on high head, then TAB against design airflow. Usual roots: dirty condenser, low airflow, or a 35C selection. High-pressure trips: clearance below manufacturer minimum, discharge recirculation, ambient above selection. Coil leaks at 2-4 years: uncoated coils on coastal sites. Low delta-T syndrome: open three-way valves, bypass, oversized coils - prove delta-T at load before adding a chiller. VRF faults: duplicate addresses, pipe length or lift over limit, charge not corrected for the run. Escalate to the OEM on in-warranty compressor failure or repeat trips after two visits, with BMS trend logs. Prevent: quarterly coil wash, water treatment log, filter DP switches.

Checklist: freeze and sign the IO list before pricing; include 20% IO spare and panel space; specify 50 degC ambient and size cooling for it; confirm hazardous-area classification in writing; require source code and licences to transfer in the client's name at handover; witness FAT before shipment and never let SAT substitute for it; write the cause and effect matrix before code; check the ICV certificate and licence activity before shortlisting; keep version-controlled backups from day one; budget DLP and AMC in the same approval as the capex. Common mistakes: customers requesting a budget price with no P and IDs; providers pricing off a walkdown, not an IO list; skipping the FDS so FAT becomes a design workshop; wireless gateways installed without TDRA type approval; fire alarm interfaces built without Civil Defence sign-off; documentation left as a punch item so retention is never released; and a shutdown window agreed by procurement without the production manager present.

Models: lump-sum turnkey for panel plus integration, unit rate per IO point, engineer day rate (AED 1,200-2,500 for a control engineer, AED 2,500-4,000 for a DCS or SIS specialist, plus per diem and mobilisation to Ruwais, Habshan or Fujairah), AMC retainer at 10-18% of installed value per year, and time-and-material for legacy fault-finding. Cost drivers ranked: hardware brand and licences; IO count and redundancy; hazardous-area Ex requirement; shutdown window plus night working; documentation and SIL verification depth; site remoteness; retrofit versus greenfield. Budget bands: OEM machine retrofit AED 25k-80k; plant PLC/SCADA upgrade AED 150k-600k; DCS migration or SIS package AED 1m-10m and up. Terms: 20-30% advance against a guarantee, milestones at FAT and delivery, 10% at SAT, 5-10% retention through the DLP. Levers: free-issue hardware, phased IO, drop redundancy.

Vocabulary runs on ISA-95 levels: L0 field instruments, L1 PLC/DCS controllers, L2 SCADA/HMI, L3 MES/historian, L4 ERP. Expect DCS, RTU, SIS, ESD, F and G, VFD/VSD, MCC, P and ID, SLD, FAT/SAT, DLP, OEE, SIL, Ex d/Ex i, IO count. Four buyer types: end users (ADNOC, ENOC, EtihadWE, DEWA, Emirates Global Aluminium, Dubai Municipality wastewater, Agthia); EPC and main contractors buying on the end user's spec; OEMs and machine builders in JAFZA, DIC, KIZAD and SAIF Zone; and facilities/BMS buyers who think automation is a subset of MEP. Supplier tiers: vendor's own local arm, certified multi-brand system integrator, panel shop with a programmer, freelance programmer. Cycles follow budgets set Q4, tenders Q1, awards Q2, execution pinned to shutdowns. Turnarounds cluster October to March; Ramadan and the July-August heat gut site productivity.

Ask in order. 1) Greenfield, retrofit or migration? 2) Which emirate, site, process? 3) IO counts by type, or an IO list. 4) Existing controller make, model, firmware, and who holds the source code? 5) Hazardous area, which zone? 6) SIL or fire and gas requirement? 7) Shutdown window. 8) Who supplies panels and installation? 9) Dates and budget. 10) ICV or approved-vendor need. Mandatory: 1-5 and 7. Skippable: 9 and 10 on small OEM jobs. Rules: if retrofit and no source code, add a reverse-engineering allowance and route to survey. If hazardous area, fan out only to integrators with IECEx or ATEX competence. If SIL is claimed, demand the cause and effect matrix or route to a scoping call. If IO count is unknown on a live site, book a walkdown. Fan out at 70% confidence to 3-5 matched suppliers; below that, scoping call. Escalate anything touching fire and gas, ESD or utility networks.

Taxonomy: control and MCC panel design and build to IEC 61439-1/2; PLC and HMI programming; DCS configuration, expansion and migration; SCADA on Ignition, WinCC, AVEVA, Geo SCADA or iFIX; safety systems, ESD and fire and gas to IEC 61511; VFD packages; instrumentation supply, calibration and loop checking; networking on Profinet, EtherNet/IP, Modbus TCP, HART, Foundation Fieldbus and OPC UA; historian, MES and energy monitoring; OT cybersecurity to IEC 62443; AMC and 24/7 support. Boundaries: the integrator owns controls, not civils, mechanical installation, cable tray or HV switchgear. Alternatives are an OEM package unit with its own embedded PLC, or a vendor-direct migration. Lifecycle: URS, FDS, DDS, panel build, FAT, shipment, installation, loop check, SAT, commissioning, 12-month DLP, then AMC. Select on a reference plant in the same process, not a brochure.

Mandatory before fan-out: scope type (greenfield, retrofit, migration); process and industry; emirate, site, and whether gate passes apply; IO list or IO counts by type; P and IDs and single line diagrams; existing controller make, model and firmware, and whether source code and licences are in the client's hands; hazardous-area classification; client standards; integration points (ERP, historian, package units, fire alarm); redundancy and SIL requirement; shutdown window and target dates; division of supply for panels and installation; FAT and SAT witness expectations and documentation set; ICV or approved-vendor prerequisites; budget band. Price and turnaround are driven by IO count, Ex scope, redundancy and shutdown constraints. Integrators reject inquiries with no IO list, no drawings, inaccessible legacy code, a 24-hour cut-over fantasy, or an obvious free-engineering exercise.

The trade is not licence-restricted; the approval chain is. MOIAT (https://moiat.gov.ae) runs the Industrial Registry under Federal Decree-Law 25 of 2022, ECAS and Emirates Quality Mark for regulated electrical goods, ENAS accreditation with its conformity assessment body directory, and the National ICV programme, whose score gates tenders at ADNOC and utilities. EIAC (https://eiac.gov.ae), under Dubai Government, accredits the labs and inspection bodies behind your certificates. TDRA (https://www.tdra.gov.ae) type-approves wireless gateways. Abu Dhabi Department of Energy (https://www.doe.gov.ae) licenses generation, desalination and district cooling. DEWA (https://www.dewa.gov.ae) needs contractor enrolment; Dubai Municipality (https://www.dm.gov.ae) runs the contractor register under Dubai Law 7 of 2025. Federal Decree-Law 25 of 2025 replaces the 1985 Civil Transactions Law.

Control platforms active in the UAE: Siemens (S7-1500, TIA Portal, PCS 7), Rockwell Automation (ControlLogix, Studio 5000, FactoryTalk), Schneider Electric (Modicon, EcoStruxure, AVEVA, Geo SCADA), ABB (AC 800M), Honeywell (Experion PKS), Emerson (DeltaV, Ovation), Yokogawa (Centum VP), Mitsubishi, Omron and Inductive Automation Ignition. Instrumentation: Endress+Hauser, Rosemount, KROHNE, VEGA, Pepperl+Fuchs, Turck, Phoenix Contact. Enclosures: Rittal, Eldon, Schneider Spacial, plus local builders in Al Quoz, Mussafah and Sharjah. Honeywell, Emerson, Yokogawa, ABB, Siemens and Schneider all run Abu Dhabi or Dubai offices, which is why end users specify them by name. What genuinely differs: vendor Solution Partner or Certified System Integrator status, IECEx/ATEX competence, ISO 9001 from a body accredited by ENAS or EIAC, MOIAT ICV score, and whether the firm owns a test bench for FAT.

They ask for a SCADA upgrade. What they want is a line that stops tripping, an alarm history that survives an audit, and one contractor to blame. The functional need is IO, loops and screens; the operational need is uptime, spares on the shelf and an engineer who answers at 2am. Constraints: production cannot stop, so it is a hot cut-over or a 48-72 hour window; the incumbent holds the source code; capex is approved but AMC opex is not. Risk tolerance is near zero on safety and fire and gas, generous on reporting. Trade-offs to say out loud: an open platform such as Ignition with OPC UA is cheaper to own but gives no single throat to choke; single-vendor costs more and locks spares pricing for a decade; redundancy roughly doubles controller cost and only pays back above about AED 50k per hour of downtime; a like-for-like migration is quick but carries every bad tag name forward.

Pre-award: NDA before P and IDs move, trade licence with the right activity, vendor partner certificate, MOIAT ICV certificate, ISO 9001 and 45001, professional indemnity and public liability cover, named engineer CVs. Contract: PO or contract with scope, exclusions, liquidated damages and warranty, technical and payment schedules, advance payment guarantee and a performance bond around 10%. Engineering: URS, FDS, DDS, IO list, loop and hook-up drawings, panel GA and wiring, cause and effect matrix, SIL verification report, IEC 62443 zone diagram. Execution: FAT and SAT protocols with signed punch lists, loop check sheets, permits to work, gate passes. Handover: as-built drawings, commented source code with licences transferred in the client's name, O and M manuals, training records, spares list, calibration certificates from an accredited laboratory, DLP certificate and AMC agreement.

Technical: legacy source code missing or password-locked; the early sign is a vendor quoting migration without asking to open the project file. Commercial: scope creep through IO growth, signalled by an IO list still marked draft at FDS review. Legal: liquidated damages tied to a shutdown the client cannot actually schedule, plus decennial exposure under the 2026 Civil Transactions Law; the sign is dates with no confirmed turnaround slot. Financial: retention and 90-120 day payment against 30-day hardware terms; the sign is an integrator asking 40% advance. Operational: gate passes and permits eating a third of site time; the sign is a plan with no permit allowance. Schedule: 8-16 week hardware leads; the sign is a delivery date with no stated PO-to-hardware lead. Provider: one engineer holds all knowledge. Customer: no nominated technical decision-maker, so drawing reviews stall.

Five archetypes. The vendor's own local arm: unbeatable on its own platform, 8-16 week hardware lead, premium rate, will not adopt a competitor's code. The certified multi-brand integrator, 20-120 staff in Dubai Investment Park or Mussafah: writes an FDS, runs FAT and SAT, builds panels, holds partner status. The panel fabricator with one programmer: strong on MCC and simple PLC, weak on SIS, historian and cyber. The freelance programmer: fast, cheap, no PI insurance, no panel shop. The MEP/BMS contractor claiming process automation: check the references.
