Security AI in the UAE encompasses AI-powered surveillance, threat detection, access control analytics, and behavioural intelligence systems deployed across commercial, residential, hospitality, and critical infrastructure sites. The field sits at the intersection of physical security hardware and intelligent software, making regulatory compliance multi-layered.

**Governing Authority & Approvals**

The primary regulator for security systems in Dubai is SIRA (Security Industry Regulatory Agency), which operates under Dubai Police. Any entity supplying, installing, or operating AI-driven CCTV, video analytics, or access control systems in Dubai must hold a valid SIRA licence — both the company and individual technicians. Dubai Police's Command and Control Centre sets integration requirements for systems connected to city-wide surveillance networks. For Abu Dhabi, the equivalent authority is the Abu Dhabi Police / Critical Infrastructure and Coastal Protection Authority (CICPA) for sensitive sites. Free-zone installations (Jebel Ali, DIFC, Dubai Airport Free Zone) fall under Trakhees or the relevant free-zone authority, which may require parallel NOC submissions alongside SIRA. Dubai Municipality approval is required where structural modifications accompany installations. For AI systems processing personal biometric data (facial recognition, gait analysis), compliance with the UAE Federal Personal Data Protection Law (Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021) is mandatory, with the UAE Data Office as the oversight body. Government and critical national infrastructure deployments may require additional clearance from the Signals Intelligence Agency (SIGINT/NSA-equivalent) or the National Electronic Security Authority (NESA), now operating under UAE Cybersecurity Council frameworks.

**Technical Standards**

Relevant standards include IEC 62676 series (video surveillance systems for use in security applications — covers IP cameras, recording, and transmission), ONVIF conformance profiles (Profile S, T, G) for interoperability, ISO/IEC 27001 for information security management of AI platforms, NDAA Section 889 compliance (prohibiting certain Chinese-manufactured components on US-aligned government contracts, increasingly referenced in UAE federal tenders), and EN 50132 series for CCTV. For access control integration, Wiegand, OSDP, and RS-485 protocol standards are commonly specified. SIRA's own Code of Practice for Electronic Security Systems is the binding local technical reference and supersedes generic international standards where they conflict. Cabling infrastructure must comply with TIA/EIA structured cabling standards and, where power is involved, DEWA's Wiring Regulations (based on IEC 60364).

**Scope & Specifications**

Core components include AI-enabled IP cameras (fixed, PTZ, fisheye) with edge-processing SoCs (Ambarella, Hisilicon, NVIDIA Jetson at the edge), Video Management Software (VMS) platforms (Milestone, Genetec, Avigilon, Dahua DSS, Hikvision HikCentral), AI analytics engines for facial recognition, crowd density estimation, perimeter intrusion detection, licence plate recognition (LPR/ANPR), object classification, and behavioural anomaly detection. topic: Field expertise — UAE codes, standards & specs
content:
# Security Companies (Guarding & Systems) — UAE Field Knowledge Base

**Governing Authority & Approvals:** SIRA (Security Industry Regulatory Agency, under Dubai Police) is the primary regulator in Dubai — it licenses security companies, manned guarding personnel, CCTV/systems installers, cash-in-transit operators, and event security providers. Any manned guarding contract or CCTV/alarm installation in Dubai requires the contractor to hold a valid SIRA license category matching the service (guarding, systems installation, monitoring/response). Guards must individually hold SIRA ID cards after training/certification. Outside Dubai, equivalent Police-affiliated security regulators apply per emirate (e.g., Abu Dhabi's SSD/Critical National Infrastructure Authority framework for CNI sites). For fire alarm/life-safety integration (fire alarm panels tied into detection), Dubai Civil Defence (DCD) approval and DCD-registered contractors are required — security integrators doing combined fire/security packages need DCD-approved subcontractors for that scope. Free zones (JAFZA, DAFZA, Trakhees-governed areas, ports) may require additional facility-specific security clearances and Trakhees NOC for installation works. Telecom/wireless alarm transmission equipment must be TRA-type-approved. For monitoring centers and armored transport, additional Dubai Police approvals apply. Always confirm the installer's SIRA license category matches the exact scope quoted.

**Standards:** CCTV, access control, and intrusion systems commonly reference IEC and EN standards for equipment (e.g., EN 50131 family for intrusion, IEC standards for CCTV camera performance); cabling follows structured cabling standards; fire-integrated systems follow the UAE Fire and Life Safety Code of Practice (DCD) and NFPA references embedded within it. ISO 9001 is common for company QA; ISO 18788 (security operations management) appears in tender-grade RFPs.

**Scope & Specs:** Manned guarding (unar

Checklist: split guarding and systems into two RFQs; verify the SIRA company licence and its category on sira.gov.ae before shortlisting; demand a site survey and marked-up drawing before any price; fix retention days, pixel density at named identification points and storage TB in the BOQ; confirm the SIRA design approval reference before mobilisation; hold 10% to final inspection; take as-builts, IP schedule, admin passwords and VMS licence keys at handover; sign the AMC before warranty ends. Best practice is design-then-price, with one integrator owning cabling through commissioning. Customer mistakes: comparing bids on camera count, letting the fit-out contractor pull security cable, buying cameras online and expecting approval, skipping UPS. Supplier mistakes: no as-builts, no NTP, default passwords live, guards on visit visas. Documentation: a missing approval reference or material submittal is the top cause of failed inspection. Compliance: PDPL signage in Arabic and English.

Guarding is ~80% manpower: WPS salary, visa, accommodation, transport, SIRA licence and training. Drivers ranked: post-hours (a 24/7 post is two 12h shifts plus relief - about 3.1 guards, not 2), armed/female/bilingual premium, site risk grade, contract term. Expect AED 4,500-6,500/guard-month for a 12h unarmed SIRA-licensed post, AED 9,000-13,000 for 24/7. Under AED 4,000 someone is underpaid; you inherit the turnover. Systems: retention storage dominates - SIRA's 31-day minimum at 4MP H.265 is 0.6-1 TB per camera. Installed per camera AED 700-1,200 budget, 1,500-2,500 mid, 3,500-7,000 Axis/Avigilon; VMS AED 400-900/channel Milestone, 900-1,800 Genetec; access AED 2,500-6,000 per door. Value-engineer camera count and resolution class, never retention, cabling or UPS. Terms: guarding 30-45 days; systems 20-30% advance, 10% to SIRA final inspection. Levers: 3-year term and one fixed BOQ.

Two distinct businesses under one label. Manned guarding is a high-headcount, low-margin, SIRA-licensed service sold per guard per month, dominated by large operators with visa and accommodation infrastructure. Electronic security (CCTV, access control, intrusion, ANPR) is a project-and-integration business sold per system. Buyers: FM companies, developers, owners associations, retail chains, schools, logistics operators, and event organisers. Demand is steady with event-driven spikes (exhibitions, Ramadan, DSF) and is highly regulated in Dubai. Fluent terms: SIRA licence, guard force multiplier, post order, control room, retention period, ANPR, PSIM.

First split the inquiry: guarding, systems, or both — and if both, treat as two RFQs. Then: 1) emirate and free-zone status. 2) Premises type and size. 3) For guarding — post count, hours, armed/unarmed, gender requirement, contract term, start date. 4) For systems — camera and door counts, required retention days, new or upgrade, existing cabling condition, and whether SIRA submission is in scope. 5) Budget indication and decision timeline. Mandatory before matching: emirate, guarding-vs-systems split, and either post count or camera count. Skippable: brand preference. Enough information once the scope split and the primary count are established. Low confidence if the buyer cannot state retention requirements for a Dubai CCTV job, because that is the single largest cost driver and implies the specification has not been set.

Guarding: static guards, mobile patrol, CCTV control-room operators, event and crowd security, executive protection, receptionist-concierge security, and guard-force management with supervision and reporting. Systems: IP CCTV (fixed, PTZ, multi-sensor, thermal), NVR/VMS and storage, access control (card, PIN, biometric, mobile credential), intrusion detection, ANPR and barrier/boom gate integration, intercom, guard-tour systems, and integration into a PSIM or BMS. Services: risk assessment and security design, SIRA drawing submission and approval, installation and commissioning, monitoring, and AMC/service contracts.

For guarding, mandatory: number of posts, hours per post, armed/unarmed, male/female, site type and risk level, contract duration, and whether vehicles, uniforms, supervision and control-room monitoring are included. For systems, mandatory: premises type, number of cameras and doors, required retention days, whether SIRA approval and drawing submission are in scope, existing infrastructure and cabling condition, and network availability. Affects price heavily: retention period and storage, thermal/ANPR cameras, civils and containment, and working in a live premises. Suppliers reject inquiries that mix guarding and systems into a single lump sum, omit retention requirements, or ask for a price without stating the emirate. Attach: floor plans, camera position marks, existing system details.

SIRA (Security Industry Regulatory Agency, Dubai) — https://www.sira.gov.ae/ — licenses security companies, security managers, individual guards and CCTV installers, approves CCTV designs before installation, and sets minimum camera resolution and video retention requirements. In Abu Dhabi the equivalent regime sits with the Private Security Business Department (PSBD) / Abu Dhabi Police. Northern emirates follow their respective police authorities. Data handling is subject to UAE Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021 on Personal Data Protection (PDPL). Trakhees applies in Ports and Free Zone Corporation areas. Confirm emirate first: a Dubai SIRA approval does not transfer to Abu Dhabi.

CCTV premium: Axis, Avigilon (Motorola), Bosch, Hanwha Vision - non-China supply chain, so these pass NDAA-889 clauses on ADNOC, aviation and defence sites. Mid: Uniview, Vivotek. Budget: Hikvision, Dahua - most Dubai installs, fine for retail. What actually differs: sensor size, real WDR (120dB+), low-lux performance and firmware support life - Axis 7-10 years against 2-3 on budget OEM - not the megapixel on the box. VMS: Genetec and Milestone XProtect at the top, native Hik/Dahua NVR at the bottom. Access: Gallagher, C-CURE 9000, LenelS2 premium; Suprema, HID, Paxton mid; ZKTeco budget. Distribution: Norden Communication ME, Aptec-Ingram Micro, Redington Gulf, ASBIS ME; Axis, Hanwha, Genetec and Milestone keep Dubai offices. Demand a SIRA product approval reference, a distributor authorisation letter naming this project, and serial-verified warranty - grey Sharjah stock is common.

Clients say "I need cameras". They mean an insurance claim, a landlord or SIRA notice, a theft they cannot prove, or court-usable identification. Ask which - deterrence is wide-angle and cheap, evidence is pixel density at named points and expensive. FM wants one contact and a fixed monthly number, HSE wants response times, finance wants capex turned into opex. Real constraints: fit-out dates slip while SIRA design approval does not, landlords restrict cable routes and facade drilling, coring needs shutdown windows. Size for expansion first - NVR channels, switch PoE budget, spare containment and VMS licences at 30% headroom cost little now and triple later. Name the trade-off aloud: faster means shelf-list cameras and no analytics tuning; cheaper means shorter retention and thinner supervision; better means Axis or Hanwha on Genetec with redundant storage and 6-8 weeks more programme.

Request: site layout and floor plans with camera and door positions, existing system asset list, SIRA design drawings and approval reference, BOQ, technical specification, method statement, material submittal with SIRA-approved product references, commissioning and handover reports, storage/retention calculation, and AMC scope. For guarding: post orders, roster/shift schedule, site risk assessment, guard licence copies, and the service level agreement with escalation and reporting requirements. Tenders from owners associations and government bodies will also require trade licence, establishment card, SIRA licences and insurance certificates.

Regulatory: installing before SIRA design approval - the tell is a supplier quoting in a day with no survey or drawing reference. Licensing: company or guard licences expiring mid-contract; the tell is refusal to share expiry dates. Technical: undersized storage or PoE budget - the tell is a BOQ with camera counts but no TB figure or switch schedule. Commercial: a bid 30% below the field; the gap is retention days, guard wages or unlicensed labour. Financial: guarding firms missing WPS - the tell is guards asking your staff about late pay. Operational: churn, spotted when a supervisor cannot recite the post orders. Schedule: SIRA approval and inspection sit outside supplier control - the tell is a programme with zero float. Legal: PDPL exposure where cameras cover neighbours or rest areas. Customer-side: scope creep once cabling is in, and variations ordered verbally, no signed VO.

Archetypes: (1) large SIRA-licensed guarding companies with 500+ staff competing on price and coverage; (2) boutique guarding firms for premium residential and events; (3) SIRA-approved systems integrators who design, submit and commission CCTV and access control; (4) IT/ELV contractors extending into security, often strong on network and weak on SIRA approval; (5) equipment distributors (Hikvision, Dahua, Axis, Avigilon, Bosch, Genetec, Milestone, HID, Suprema). Almost no supplier is genuinely excellent at both guarding and systems — matching both scopes to one supplier is a common source of poor outcomes. Verify SIRA company licence and category, individual guard licences, and for systems the SIRA installer approval.

CCTV design is driven by identification requirement, not camera count: SIRA specifies minimum resolution and pixel density for identification at defined points (entrances, cash points, lifts, perimeters) and minimum retention, commonly 30-90 days depending on premises type — retention is the dominant storage cost driver. Lens/field-of-view calculation, low-light performance and WDR matter more than headline megapixels. Network design (PoE budget, switch capacity, VLAN separation) is routinely underestimated. Access control: door hardware type (maglock vs strike vs motorised), fail-safe vs fail-secure and its fire-alarm interface, and anti-passback. For guarding, the technical variable is the roster mathematics: covering one 24/7 post needs roughly 4.2 guards once leave, rest days and relief are accounted for.

Cameras dropping at night: PoE budget exhausted when IR engages - measure switch load, do not swap cameras. Gaps in the archive: RAID degraded, disk read-only, or overwrite set under 31 days; read the VMS retention report before blaming the recorder. Blurred plates at the gate: lens and angle, not resolution - ANPR needs a dedicated camera, approach under 30 degrees, shutter near 1/1000. Doors failing open: PSU or battery at end of life, or a maglock with no suppression diode. Intermittent readers: runs over 100m or shared containment with mains inducing noise. Sequence: reproduce, read logs and timestamps, verify power and PoE, verify link and IP, verify NTP sync (drift ruins every investigation), swap hardware last. Escalate to the manufacturer only with firmware version, serial and a packet capture. Prevention: the quarterly PPM the SIRA Preventive Systems Manual requires.

Ask: Sign type (3D letters / lightbox / pylon / vehicle wrap / interior / billboard)? [MANDATORY]; Quantity + approx sizes? [MANDATORY]; Illuminated?; Indoor or outdoor?; Install location (mall / facade / roadside)? — outdoor advertising needs a Municipality permit; Artwork ready? (photo). Never ask budget.

1) Sign type: shopfront fascia, 3D built-up letters, lightbox, pylon/totem, wall logo, directional, vehicle, or building/facade sign? 2) Dimensions — overall size and letter height (and is it visible from a public road)? 3) Location and jurisdiction: Dubai Municipality area, a DDA/TECOM free zone, Trakhees, or adjacent to an RTA road (which sets the approval path)? 4) Illuminated or non-illuminated — and if lit, front-lit, halo/back-lit, or edge-lit? 5) Material preference: acrylic, ACP, stainless steel, brushed/mirror finish — and any fire-rated ACP requirement for a facade? 6) Brand artwork, exact colours (Pantone/RAL) and a vector logo file? 7) Mounting surface and height (glass, ACP cladding, masonry) and access for installation (cherry picker, scaffolding)? 8) Does the trade licence name/activity match the signage text (required for approval)? 9) Will the supplier handle DM / DEWA / RTA / free-zone approvals and pay the fees, or client-arranged? 10) Power supply availability near the sign location? 11) Landlord/building NOC and any community sign guidelines? 12) Timeline (note approvals can take days to weeks). 13) Budget range. 14) Warranty on LEDs/structure and any maintenance contract?

A complete signage quote should itemise: design/artwork & approval drawings; the sign type and substrate (acrylic, ACP/aluminium composite panel, stainless steel, foam/PVC, flex/vinyl); fabrication method (CNC-cut, laser, routing); illumination (front-lit, back-lit/halo, edge-lit, LED module type, transformer/driver, dimming); structure/mounting (frame, raceway, fixings, wind-load engineering for large/high signs); electrical connection; transportation; installation (with access equipment); and crucially the authority approval fees and permits. Differentiators with units: material and thickness (e.g. 3-5mm acrylic, 3-4mm ACP, mm of steel face); letter height and depth; illuminated vs non-illuminated; LED brand/quality and IP rating; fire-rated ACP (A2/B grade) for facades. Strong quote: names material + thickness, illumination type and LED spec, mounting/structure detail, wind-load certification for large signs, and lists DM/DEWA/RTA approval fees separately. Corner-cutting: thin acrylic/ACP that warps in heat; low-grade non-IP-rated LEDs that fail; non-fire-rated ACP; weak fixings/no wind-load calc; cheaper face material swapped after the mock-up. Tricks to flag: approval/permit fees (Dubai Municipality, DEWA, and RTA for road-visible signs), structural engineering certification, and installation labour 'rarely included in the initial fabrication quote' — confirm they are in scope; supply-only vs supply-and-install; VAT excluded; vague 'LED sign' with no IP/brand.

topic: Field expertise — UAE codes, standards & specs
content:
Signage & 3D Letters in the UAE operates under a layered approval framework before any sign is fabricated or installed. In Dubai, the primary regulator is **Dubai Municipality (DM)** — specifically its Signage & Advertising Section — which governs outdoor advertising permits, hoarding licenses, and building-fascia sign approvals. Signage on Sheikh Zayed Road and key arterials additionally requires **Roads and Transport Authority (RTA)** clearance for anything that may affect driver sightlines or road furniture. Signs within free zones and port areas (Jebel Ali, Dubai South, DAFZA) fall under **Trakhees** jurisdiction rather than DM. The **Dubai Development Authority (DDA)** governs signage in its designated development zones (DIFC, Dubai Design District, etc.). For illuminated or electrically powered signs, **DEWA** connection approval and compliance with DEWA's wiring regulations are mandatory; any electrical installation must be carried out by a DEWA-approved contractor. Where signs incorporate high-voltage neon or large LED drivers, **Dubai Civil Defence (DCD)** may require fire-safety compliance under the UAE Fire and Life Safety Code of Practice, particularly for signs installed inside malls or on escape-route facades. Abu Dhabi signage falls under **Abu Dhabi City Municipality** and **ADDED** jurisdiction.

Applicable technical standards include **IEC 60598** (luminaires/LED fittings), **IEC 61347** (lamp control gear/drivers), **EN 50107** (neon sign safety), **ESMA** conformity marking for electrical components sold in the UAE, and **BS 559** (specification for the erection and installation of signs). Structural fixings must satisfy **Dubai Municipality structural loading guidelines**; wind-load calculations referencing local design wind speeds are required for projecting or pylon signs above a threshold size.

Core scope items buyers and suppliers discuss: **channel letters** (front-lit, back-lit/halo, side-lit); **built-up 3D letters** in aluminium, stainless steel (brushed, mirror-polished), acrylic, or brass; **pylon/totem signs**; **monument signs**; **LED module selection** (SMD vs. COB, IP65/IP67 rating for outdoor); **flex-face and tension-fabric lightboxes**; **neon/flex-neon**; **CNC-routed substrates** (aluminium composite material — ACM/Alucobond, dibond); **vinyl wrapping and digital print overlays**; **powder-coat vs. wet-paint finish**; **transformer/driver wattage and IP rating**; **anchor bolt and bracket engineering** for facade or ground mounting; **UL-listed or CE-marked** LED drivers.

Key price drivers: letter height and complexity of font; material choice (stainless steel commands 3–5× premium over acrylic); illumination type (halo-lit stainless is costlier than front-lit acrylic); quantity; access/rigging requirements (scissor lift, rope access on high

Signage approval depends on the sign's location and visibility. Dubai Municipality approves most building/shopfront signs on private facades, including those visible from public roads, and requires a permit application with: trade licence copy, site plan, facade photo, a scaled sign drawing with dimensions, a mock-up/perspective, and a landlord NOC — undated NOCs or non-scaled drawings cause rejection and restart (commonly 5-10 working days). Illuminated signs need DEWA electrical approval, and large or elevated signs require a qualified engineer's structural plans, material specs, electrical details and wind-load calculations. Signs adjacent to or visible from RTA-managed roads (billboards, hoardings, road-visible advertising) require an RTA signage NOC/permit (which can take up to ~20 working days). Free-zone locations use their own authority — Dubai Development Authority (DDA/TECOM) advertising permit for Media/Internet City etc., or Trakhees for Jebel Ali/Palm/Nakheel areas; DIFC for its district. The signage text/name must match the licensed trade name/activity. Temporary outdoor advertising and digital/LED screens have separate RTA/DM permit routes. Permits, DEWA fees and structural certification are real, often-overlooked costs that should be in the quote.

Core materials: acrylic (cast/extruded, 3-5mm, for faces and built-up letters), ACP/aluminium composite panel (3-4mm, for backing/cladding — facade use should be fire-rated, e.g. A2/FR grade given UAE facade-fire regulations), stainless steel (brushed/mirror, for premium letters), galvanised/aluminium frames and raceways, foam/PVC and flex/vinyl for budget or temporary signs. Illumination: LED modules (front-lit through acrylic face, halo/back-lit for a glow behind letters, or edge-lit), with appropriate transformers/drivers — outdoor LEDs and power supplies should be IP-rated (e.g. IP65) for weather and heat resistance. Fabrication: CNC routing, laser cutting, and channel-letter bending. Structural and wind-load: large or high-mounted signs require engineered fixings and wind-load calculations per the structural certification Dubai Municipality demands; electrical works follow DEWA regulations. Approval drawings must be to scale with dimensions and a mock-up. Vocabulary to capture in specs: material + thickness, letter height/return depth, illumination type, LED brand and IP rating, fixing/mounting method, and fire-rating of ACP. Specify exact colours by Pantone/RAL to match brand artwork.

Indicative only — signage is generally priced per square metre of sign area or per piece, and scales with size, material, illumination and finish. Rough market references: non-illuminated acrylic small panels around AED 300-800; backlit acrylic for shopfronts roughly AED 800-2,500; illuminated 3D letters around AED 1,500-8,000 for standard shopfront runs, rising to AED 15,000-40,000+ for large tower/hotel installations; lightboxes roughly AED 800-4,500 for standard sizes; large custom/outdoor signage from a few thousand to AED 100,000+. Larger signs are more cost-efficient per m2 because approval and install labour do not scale proportionally. Crucially, Dubai Municipality approval, DEWA electrical permits, structural engineering certification and installation labour can add roughly AED 1,000-5,000 and are 'rarely included in the initial fabrication quote' — confirm whether they are in scope. Add 5% VAT. Red flags: a quote well below peers often means thin acrylic/ACP that warps, non-IP-rated/low-grade LEDs that fail in heat, non-fire-rated ACP on a facade, or weak fixings with no wind-load calc; permit/DEWA/RTA fees and installation excluded; supply-only vs supply-and-install; face material downgraded after the mock-up; no LED warranty.

Dubai Municipality (signage permits) — https://www.dm.gov.ae/
RTA, outdoor advertising permits — https://www.rta.ae/wps/portal/rta/ae/home/rta-services/service-details?serviceId=3704564
Dubai Development Authority, Advertising Permit — https://dda.gov.ae/en/planning-development/advertising-and-events/advertising-services/advertising-permit
Trakhees (free-zone approvals) — https://www.trakhees.ae/
DIFC, External Works NOC — https://www.difc.com/business/submittals-requests-and-external-works-noc
DEWA (electrical connection) — https://www.dewa.gov.ae/
Department of Economy and Tourism (trade licence/name) — https://www.dubaided.gov.ae/
Dubai signage approval process guide — https://www.signagedubai.com/blog/how-to-get-signboard-approval-in-dubai-ded-rta-and-municipality-process.html
Signage cost guide Dubai 2026 — https://www.idesignads.ae/signage-cost-guide-dubai-2026-what-does-business-signage-actually-cost/
Signtrade (ACP material reference) — https://signtrade.com/product/aluminum-composite-panel-acp-sheet/

Ask: Which systems (lighting / AC / curtains / security / audio / access)? [MANDATORY]; New build or retrofit? [MANDATORY]; Property size / number of rooms? [MANDATORY]; Wired or wireless preference or advise?; Brand preference?; Drawings? (photo). Note: TDRA type-approved devices. Never ask budget.

1. Property type and stage: new-build/off-plan or retrofit of an occupied home? Wired is only easy pre-plaster. 2. Developer and community (Emaar/Nakheel/DAMAC/freehold)? Drives the NOC/fit-out approval path. 3. Built-up area and layout: floors, bedrooms, full room list (drives AP count, zones, cable drops). 4. Which subsystems: lighting, shading/curtains, HVAC, AV/multiroom audio, CCTV/access, intercom, irrigation, pool, gate, ranked must-have vs nice-to-have? 5. Lighting scope: how many circuits, which need dimming, and how many scenes per room? 6. AV expectations: audio zones, dedicated cinema, video distribution? 7. HVAC type: central/VRF, splits or FCUs, and how many independently controlled zones? 8. Security in scope? If CCTV/access control is included, SIRA applies, flag early. 9. Control preferences: wall keypads, touch panels, phone app, voice (Alexa/Google/Siri)? 10. Internet and networking: current ISP/router, willingness to install structured cabling and a rack, device count? 11. Budget band and whether they value vendor flexibility (KNX) or turnkey UX (Control4)? 12. Resilience: must it keep working offline during an internet outage? 13. Energy/solar/EV: any DEWA Shams Dubai PV, EV charger or energy-monitoring intent? 14. Aftercare: AMC wanted, remote support, and acceptable warranty term?

A defensible smart-home quote separates hardware (~55%), labour/programming (~40%) and infrastructure rather than lumping a 'smart home package'. Line items to demand: controller/processor with named model (Control4 EA/CORE, Crestron, KNX line/IP coupler + ETS programming, Lutron HomeWorks, Loxone Miniserver) - 'smart controller' with no model is a red flag; gateways/bridges per protocol (Zigbee/Z-Wave hub, KNX IP gateway, Matter controller); lighting load/dimmer modules quoted PER CIRCUIT with dimmable distinguished from switched and dimming type stated (leading/trailing edge, 0-10V, DALI); number of lighting scenes per room; keypads/touch panels by count and size (7in/10in, in-wall vs tabletop); AV zones and HVAC zones (one interface per FCU/AC); motorized curtains/blinds by track count with motor brand (Somfy/Lutron) and whether tracks are included; access/intercom (flag SIRA scope if CCTV/access added); network rack, managed PoE switch (port count), Wi-Fi 6 APs (count), UPS; structured cabling Cat6/Cat6A drop count, fibre backbone, conduit, patch panel, certified/tested drops; app/remote-access licensing (flag recurring); explicit programming hours; warranty years and AMC. Compare by normalising to the same room list and same count of circuits/zones/panels/drops; check protocol parity (a wired-KNX and wireless-Zigbee quote at the same price are not equivalent), and check what is 'by others' (cabling, conduit, DB modification). The cheapest corner cut, most-often-first: structured cabling (a 'wireless throughout' new-build saved on wiring and shifted risk to battery/mesh endpoints), then cable downgrade (Cat5e/unbranded), under-provisioned APs (one router for a multi-floor villa), token programming hours, omitted commissioning/testing, no surge/UPS, warranty/AMC excluded, and cloud-only control with no local fallback.

topic: Field expertise — UAE codes, standards & specs
content:
Smart Home Automation in the UAE operates within a layered regulatory and technical environment that installers and integrators must navigate carefully.

**Governing Authority & Approvals.** Electrical backbone work — consumer unit modifications, dedicated circuits for automation panels, low-voltage distribution — requires DEWA approval for any works touching the main supply in Dubai; a DEWA-registered contractor must sign off on electrical drawings. For villa or apartment fit-outs in free zones or port areas, Trakhees replaces Dubai Municipality as the permitting authority. Dubai Municipality Building Permits cover structural cable containment (conduit chases, trunking) in mainland projects. Where smart home systems incorporate CCTV or video doorbells with external-facing cameras, SIRA registration of the installer and system notification to Dubai Police may be required depending on scope. If the automation integrates fire detection or suppression control — smart smoke detectors networked to a central panel, for instance — Dubai Civil Defence approval is mandatory and the system must comply with the UAE Fire and Life Safety Code of Practice. For projects embedding solar or battery-storage control within the automation layer, DEWA's Shams Dubai net-metering approval process applies.

**Standards.** Wiring and electrical installations follow IEC 60364 as adopted by DEWA regulations. Structured cabling for data/control backbones references TIA-568 and ISO/IEC 11801. KNX installations should comply with EN 50090. Wireless protocols (Zigbee, Z-Wave, Matter/Thread) carry their own interoperability certifications; ESMA/ECAS conformity marking is required for any consumer electrical device placed on the UAE market. Audio-visual rack builds often reference AVIXA (InfoComm) standards.

**Scope & Specs.** Core components include: central automation controller/hub (KNX, Control4, Crestron, Lutron, Savant, Home Assistant); DIN-rail mounted actuators and relay modules; smart lighting (DALI-2 drivers, 0–10 V dimming, scene keypads); motorised window treatments (tubular motors, dry-contact or RS-485 integration); HVAC control via BACnet, Modbus or proprietary thermostat gateways; multiroom AV distribution (HDMI matrix, IP video, Dante audio); structured cabling (Cat 6A, fibre backbone, coax); IP intercom and video doorbell; smart locks (Wiegand, OSDP); energy monitoring sub-meters; UPS/battery backup for controllers; and touchscreen or tablet wall panels. Network infrastructure quality — managed PoE switches, VLAN segmentation, Wi-Fi 6 access points — is critical and frequently underspecified.

**Price Drivers.** Protocol choice (KNX/Crestron at premium vs. cloud-based consumer-grade); number of control points and zones; degree of HVAC integration complexity; quality of structured cabling infrastructure already in place; custom joinery for in-wall panels; programming and commissioning labour (often 20–35% of project cost); ongoing support/maintenance contracts;

A smart-home/ELV company needs a valid DED (Dubai Economy and Tourism) trade licence under an electrical/electromechanical/low-current or IT-systems activity. Any work touching the mains installation or distribution board must be done under a DEWA-enrolled electrical contractor; DEWA enrolment requires a valid DED licence and a sponsored graduate electrical engineer (>=1 year experience) supervising works per DEWA Regulations. Pure ELV automation that does not modify the DB may not itself trigger DEWA enrolment - confirm for the specific scope. TDRA equipment type approval is mandatory (verified, official TDRA) for any device with an RF feature (Wi-Fi, Zigbee, Z-Wave, Thread/Matter, Bluetooth, NFC/RFID): equipment must be registered/type-approved before sale, distribution or use; importers need TDRA Dealer Registration; three risk levels carry SLAs (Level 1 ~1 day, Level 2 ~5 days, Level 3 ~10 days) with ISO/IEC 17025 ILAC-accredited test reports. Grey-market wireless gear is a red flag; verify models against the TDRA Approved Equipment list. SIRA applies the moment CCTV or access control is added - the installer must be SIRA-approved with consultant design and a SIRA NOC; a pure-automation firm without SIRA cannot legally deliver that part. For fire-event automation, Dubai Civil Defence governs the certified fire system (NFPA 72-aligned, DCD-approved contractor, annual AMC); the smart system interfaces via a single dedicated interface panel (typically Modbus RTU over RS-485) and must not replace or compromise the fire system; villas may fall under the MOI Hassantuk scheme. DEWA Shams Dubai (Council Resolution 46 of 2014) governs grid-connected rooftop PV (DRRG-enrolled contractor, 1 MW cap). There is no confirmed public consumer DEWA meter API - do not promise live DEWA-meter integration. Apartment/villa fit-out changes require a DM fit-out permit or developer NOC (e.g. Emaar Community Portal) by a registered contractor.

Protocols and tradeoffs. KNX: wired twisted-pair bus (also RF/IP), open standard, decentralised (no single point of failure, each device intelligent), highly reliable/scalable and vendor-interoperable, best for new-build villas on a 10-15 year horizon, but higher cost/time and needs cabling pre-plaster plus ETS programming. Zigbee: wireless 2.4 GHz mesh, low-power, large ecosystem, but 2.4 GHz congestion and battery maintenance. Z-Wave: sub-GHz mesh, better range/penetration, lower bandwidth. Wi-Fi: high bandwidth for cameras/streaming but network load and cloud dependency. Thread/Matter: Thread mesh plus the Matter interoperability layer, still maturing. Design rule: a hybrid wins - a wired backbone (KNX or Control4 with structured cabling) plus wireless endpoints where cabling is infeasible. Ecosystem positioning: KNX (vendor independence/longevity), Control4 (turnkey owner-friendly AV UX), Crestron (high-end/custom), Lutron (premium lighting and shading), Loxone (value all-in-one). Cabling/infrastructure: Cat6/Cat6A home runs to a central rack (no daisy-chaining), Cat6A recommended for AP/camera/PoE backbone and future 10G; fibre backbone for large villas; dedicated KNX bus cable pulled pre-plaster; deliverables include patch panel, labelling and certified/tested drops; network rack with managed PoE switch, UPS and surge protection. Fire interface via a dedicated interface panel/Modbus RS-485 to the DCD panel. Codes/standards to reference: DEWA Regulations for Electrical Installations (mains/DB work), NFPA 72 / UAE Fire and Life Safety Code (fire interface), SIRA technical standards (CCTV/access), TDRA type approval (all wireless), ISO/IEC 17025-accredited test reports for type approval.

Indicative AED benchmarks (UAE integrator/secondary sources, 2025-2026, directional only): budget guideline roughly 4-7% of total fit-out cost for a properly engineered automation layer; 3-4BR villa mid-range KNX (lighting, climate, basic security) ~AED 80,000-150,000; 4BR (lighting, shading, climate, security) ~AED 80,000-160,000; mid-range with multi-zone audio plus security integration ~AED 200,000-500,000; 6BR premium full Control4 (whole-home AV, cinema, pool, irrigation) ~AED 220,000-450,000; palace-grade Crestron with custom UI ~AED 800,000-3,000,000+. Labour benchmarks (international, convert with judgement): integration/programming ~USD 80-150/hr, low-voltage cabling/camera tech ~USD 60-90/hr. Red flags: a price far below the 4-7%-of-fit-out band (scope or cabling missing); no named brands/models for controller, panels or dimmers; 'wireless throughout' on a new-build (corner cut = infrastructure/future-proofing); Cat5e/unbranded cable or no certification; one router and no PoE APs for a multi-floor home; programming hours absent or token (change-order trap); no surge/UPS on the rack and controllers; no warranty/AMC or warranty under 1 year/parts-only; cloud-only control with no local fallback; imported wireless gear with no TDRA approval; CCTV/access included but installer not SIRA-approved (illegal); fire-event automation promised without a DCD-approved contractor and interface panel; 'live DEWA meter integration' promised without a verifiable data path (likely overstated).

DEWA Shams Dubai solar program (official) — https://www.dewa.gov.ae/en/consumer/solar-community/shams-dubai
DEWA enrol as DRRG Solar PV consultant/contractor (official) — https://www.dewa.gov.ae/en/builder/shams-dubai-guides-tools/enroll-as-drrg-solar-pv-consultant-and-contractor
DEWA Enrolment of Consultants and Contractors (electrical contractor licensing) — https://www.dewa.gov.ae/en/about-us/service-guide/general-information/enrollment-of-consultants-contractors
DEWA Smart Living (consumption/smart meter) — https://www.dewa.gov.ae/en/consumer/consumption-management/smart-living
DEWA Smart Grid and Meters Smart Applications (DLMS/COSEM) — https://www.dewa.gov.ae/en/about-us/dewa-digital-journey/smart-grid-and-meters-smart-applications
TDRA Type Approval overview (official) — https://tdra.gov.ae/en/about/tdra-sectors/telecommunication/the-technology-development-affairs/type-approval
TDRA Telecommunications Equipment Type Approval Regime v2.0 (official PDF) — https://tdra.gov.ae/-/media/About/regulations-and-ruling/EN/Regulation---Telecommunications-Equipment-Type-Approval-Regime-V2-0-pdf.ashx
TDRA Register and Approve Telecommunication Equipment (service) — https://tdra.gov.ae/en/Services/register-and-approve-telecommunication-equipment
TDRA Approved Equipment list — https://tdra.gov.ae/en/approved-equipments
Dubai Civil Defence Life Safety Alarm Monitoring Category-04 (official) — https://www.dcd.gov.ae/portal/en/our-department/sms-dubai/private-and-public-buildings/specification-category-04.jsp
UAE Government Portal fire safety / Hassantuk (MOI) — https://u.ae/en/information-and-services/justice-safety-and-the-law/fire-safety
Emaar Home Modifications Fact Sheet (developer NOC, primary PDF) — https://properties.emaar.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/04/Home-Modifications-Fact-Sheet-2021-04-12.pdf

Best practice: fix the room list, circuit count and zone count before pricing anything - that is the only basis on which two quotes are comparable. Pull conduit and Cat6A everywhere at first fix even when budget funds only half the devices; conduit is cheap pre-plaster and impossible afterwards. Home-run every drop to one rack, certify and label it, and site that rack somewhere ventilated with UPS and surge protection. Specify local control fallback so lighting and AC survive an ISP outage. Make handover of programming files, admin credentials and as-builts a payment milestone. Common mistakes: accepting a 'smart home package' with no model numbers; 'wireless throughout' on a new build, which is a cabling saving dressed as a design choice; one router and no PoE access points in a three-floor villa; Cat5e cable; token programming hours that return as change orders; adding CCTV without a SIRA-licensed installer; and promising live DEWA meter data, for which no public consumer API exists.

Budget 4-7% of total fit-out for a properly engineered layer. Indicative AED: 3-4BR villa mid-range KNX (lighting, climate, basic security) 80,000-150,000; add multi-zone audio and security 200,000-500,000; 6BR full Control4 with cinema, pool and irrigation 220,000-450,000; palace-grade Crestron 800,000-3,000,000+. Unit rates: KNX 8-fold switch actuator 1,800-3,500; 4-fold dimmer 2,500-4,500; glass keypad 900-3,500; 10in touch panel 3,500-9,000; Control4 controller 6,000-15,000; Crestron 4-Series 18,000-35,000; DALI gateway 3,000-6,000; FCU interface 600-1,800 per zone; Somfy motor 1,200-2,500 per track; Cat6A drop installed 250-450; Wi-Fi 6 AP 700-2,500. Programming bills at AED 350-800/hr and is 20-35% of project cost. AMC runs 8-15% of hardware value a year. Terms: 50/40/10, 5% VAT, European KNX lead times 6-12 weeks.

UAE smart-home demand splits three ways: developer-fitted packages (Emaar, DAMAC, Nakheel hand over app-level lighting and AC control), ELV subcontract packages under the MEP main contractor on new villas and towers, and owner-driven retrofit, the largest slice for independent integrators. Drivers are physical, not fashion: 45-50C summers put cooling at 60-70% of villa electricity, DEWA slab tariffs punish waste, and Dubai's Al Sa'fat green building regulations plus Abu Dhabi's Estidama Pearl push controls into base spec. Seasonality is sharp - enquiries peak Oct-Mar and collapse Jun-Aug and through Ramadan; occupied-villa access, not labour, is the bottleneck. Sharjah, Ajman and RAK price 20-35% under Dubai with thinner brand support. A villa retrofit runs 6-14 weeks; a new-build ELV package sits inside a 12-24 month main contract carrying 5-10% retention.

Mandatory before routing: which subsystems (lighting, HVAC, shading, AV, CCTV or access, intercom, irrigation, gate); new build or retrofit of an occupied home; property type, built-up area, floors and the full room list. Then: developer and community, since Emaar, Nakheel and DAMAC each run their own NOC path; lighting circuit count and how many need dimming; HVAC type - central, VRF, splits or FCUs - and zone count; AV zones or a dedicated cinema; control preference (keypads, panels, app, voice); existing structured cabling; timeline against handover date; AMC expectation. Re-route when CCTV or access is in scope and no SIRA-licensed supplier matches, or when fire-panel interfacing is requested without a DCD-approved contractor. Flag high intent: large GFA, developer or multi-unit work, pre-plaster timing, drawings attached. Never ask budget directly - ask scope and infer the band.

Core scope: lighting control (switched relay circuits, dimmed circuits, DALI-2 broadcast or addressable, scene keypads); motorised shading (tubular motors, roller, sheer, blackout, pergola, skylight); HVAC zone control (FCU valve and fan interfaces, VRF gateways, central-AC damper zoning); multiroom audio and video distribution (HDMI matrix, AV-over-IP, in-ceiling speakers, cinema); CCTV, access control, IP intercom and video doorbell; smart locks; gate, irrigation, pool plant and water-feature control; energy sub-metering and EV charger integration. Underneath sits the infrastructure buyers forget: Cat6A structured cabling to a central rack, managed PoE switches, VLANs, Wi-Fi 6/6E access points, UPS and surge protection. Services billed separately: design and load schedules, containment, programming, commissioning, handover training and an annual maintenance contract.

A defensible quote separates hardware (~55%), labour and programming (~40%) and infrastructure. Demand named models; a 'smart home package' with no part numbers is not a quote. Insist on: processor with model number; protocol gateways; lighting modules priced per circuit, dimmed distinguished from switched, dimming type stated; scene count per room; keypads and panels by count and size; one HVAC interface per FCU; curtain tracks with motor brand and whether track is included; access and intercom, which triggers SIRA scope; rack, PoE switch port count, AP count and UPS; Cat6A drop count with certification; explicit programming hours; warranty years and AMC. Compare only after normalising to the same room list, circuit, zone and drop counts. Check protocol parity - a wired KNX quote and a Zigbee quote at one price are not one product - and list everything marked 'by others'.

DEWA (Dubai Electricity & Water Authority): mains or distribution-board work needs a DEWA-enrolled contractor - categories include Contractor-Electrical and Contractor-Fit Out, enrolment is online in about 5 working days and needs a supervising engineer with 1 year minimum experience: https://www.dewa.gov.ae/en/about-us/service-guide/general-information/enrollment-of-consultants-contractors . TDRA (Telecommunications and Digital Government Regulatory Authority): type approval is mandatory for every Wi-Fi, Zigbee, Z-Wave, Thread/Matter or Bluetooth device; three risk levels, certificate valid 3 years, late renewal AED 100/month: https://tdra.gov.ae/en/approved-equipments . SIRA (Security Industry Regulatory Agency) licenses CCTV and access work, Dubai only: https://www.sira.gov.ae . Dubai Civil Defence governs the fire-panel interface; MOI Hassantuk covers homes.

Wired and KNX: ABB, Siemens, Schneider Electric, Gira, JUNG, Hager, Theben, MDT, Zennio, Basalte, Ekinex and HDL - HDL and Zennio dominate the value end of UAE villa work. Proprietary ecosystems: Control4 (Snap One, now under Resideo) for turnkey owner UX, Crestron for palace-grade custom, Savant, Lutron HomeWorks QSX and RA3 for premium lighting and shading, Loxone for all-in-one value. Shading motors: Somfy, which runs a Dubai regional office, plus Nice and Elero. LED drivers: Tridonic, Helvar, Signify. Intercom and locks: 2N, Comelit, Aiphone, DoorBird, Yale/ASSA ABLOY, Salto, dormakaba. CCTV: Hikvision, Dahua, Axis, Hanwha - confirm the exact model is SIRA-listed. Network: Ubiquiti UniFi, Ruckus, Aruba, Araknis. Wireless retrofit and Matter: Aqara, Shelly, Sonoff, Tuya. Channel runs via Jumbo Electronics, Jacky's, Sharaf DG, Eros Group and Al-Futtaim Engineering.

The decisive trade-off is wired versus wireless, and building stage settles it, not preference. Pre-plaster, wired KNX or a structured-cabling Control4 backbone costs 25-40% more upfront but lasts 10-15 years, survives internet outages and keeps vendor choice open. Post-handover in an occupied villa, chasing walls means a developer NOC, dust and 3-6 weeks of disruption, so Zigbee or Matter retrofit wins on cost and time while accepting battery changes every 12-24 months and 2.4GHz congestion. Second: open standard versus turnkey. KNX gives vendor independence and any-integrator serviceability; Control4 and Crestron give a better family-facing interface but tie the owner to one dealer. Third: cloud convenience versus local control - insist on local fallback so lights work when e& or du drops. Fourth: full scope now versus conduit now and program later. Always pull the conduit.

Supplier side: DET or ADDED trade licence showing an electrical, electromechanical, low-current or IT-systems activity; establishment card; VAT TRN on every invoice; DEWA contractor enrolment certificate wherever the distribution board or mains is touched; SIRA company licence plus SIRA ID cards for technicians on CCTV or access work; TDRA type-approval certificates and dealer registration for imported RF devices; MoIAT certificate of conformity for electrical goods; a Dubai Civil Defence approved-contractor certificate for anything interfacing the fire panel; workmen's compensation and third-party liability cover. Project deliverables to name in the contract: single-line and containment drawings, device and cable schedules, IP and VLAN plan, Fluke certification report, the ETS or Control4/Crestron project file, as-builts, O&M manual, commissioning checklist, warranty and snag list.

Highest-frequency losses, in order. Scope creep into SIRA territory: one video doorbell added mid-job and an unlicensed integrator is now delivering illegally. Non-type-approved RF gear refused at customs, stranding a half-programmed system. Developer NOC refused post-handover, so the promised wall chasing never happens and the design collapses to wireless. Programming files withheld - Control4 project file, Crestron source, ETS project - leaving the owner hostage to one dealer and unable to obtain a second quote; make handover a payment milestone. Payment risk on new-build: pay-when-paid from the main contractor plus 5-10% retention held twelve months. Grey imports voiding warranty. Cloud-only products discontinued or regional servers moved. Labour: the midday outdoor work ban from mid-June to mid-September and reduced Ramadan hours both belong in the programme, not in the excuses.

Five firm types quote this work. KNX-certified integrators - ask for the KNX Partner certificate number and a licensed ETS6 seat, not a cracked copy. Authorised Control4, Crestron and Lutron dealers, tiered and verifiable with the brand's regional office. ELV subcontractors under MEP main contractors: strong on containment, weak on programming. SIRA-licensed security firms, the only ones who may legally deliver CCTV or access control in Dubai. Retail and Tuya installers doing sub-AED 30,000 wireless retrofits. Vet on: DET or ADDED trade licence carrying an electrical, low-current or IT-systems activity; DEWA contractor enrolment where the distribution board is touched; SIRA licence; TDRA dealer registration for imported RF gear; an in-house programmer; three reference villas you can call; and AMC headcount. No demo rig and no ETS licence means they subcontract everything.

KNX is a wired twisted-pair bus at nominal 29-30V DC; below roughly 21V at the device you get missed telegrams. Limits: 64 devices per line, 1000m of bus cable per line, 350m between PSU and device. Configure in ETS6 and give every device a unique physical address - duplicates are the classic commissioning fault after a device swap. DALI-2 allows 64 short addresses and 16 groups per line, 300m maximum, 2A bus current; never mix DALI-1 and DALI-2 drivers on one line. Dimming must match the driver: trailing edge for most LED, leading edge for iron-core transformers, 0-10V or DALI for commercial fittings, and respect minimum load or you get flicker. Cabling: Cat6A home runs to one rack, no daisy chains, fibre backbone beyond 90m, Fluke-certified and labelled. Network: managed PoE+ switch, VLAN separation for AV, cameras, control and guest, one AP per 80-110 sqm.

Recurring UAE failure modes. Heat first: racks in unventilated store rooms and controllers in roof voids where summer ambient passes 55C, causing thermal shutdown, PSU failure and dead Zigbee repeaters - measure rack temperature before blaming firmware. KNX bus voltage sagging under 21V, a pinched bus cable shorting a line, or duplicate physical addresses after a device swap. DALI flicker at low dim levels from mixed driver types, wrong dimming edge or minimum load not met. 2.4GHz congestion in towers: move Zigbee to channel 15, 20 or 25, clear of Wi-Fi 1/6/11. Remote access dying after an e& or du technician swaps the router - DHCP reservations and port forwards lost, and CGNAT blocks inbound anyway, so use the vendor cloud relay or a static IP. Battery endpoints flat at 12-24 months. Curtain limits drifting and RS-485 polarity reversed. No surge protection on the rack after a storm.

Ask: Rooftop or ground-mount? [MANDATORY]; Property type (villa / warehouse / commercial)? [MANDATORY]; Approx roof area or desired system size (kW)? [MANDATORY]; Grid-tied (Shams Dubai net-metering) or off-grid? — grid-tie requires DEWA-enrolled contractor & consultant; Typical monthly bill/consumption?; Timeline? Never ask budget.

1. Property type (villa, warehouse, factory, commercial roof) and ownership (you must own or have NOC from owner)? 2. Is this grid-tied net-metering (Shams Dubai), off-grid, or hybrid with battery? 3. What is your average monthly DEWA bill / annual kWh consumption (to size the system)? 4. Available roof area and type (concrete, tile, metal sheet, shaded by structures)? 5. Desired system size in kWp, or should it be sized to offset your bill? 6. Single-phase or three-phase DEWA connection? 7. Any module/inverter brand or tier preference (Tier-1 modules; Huawei/Sungrow/SMA/Fronius inverters)? 8. Battery storage required and target backup kWh? 9. Do you need DEWA Solar NOC, design approval and net-metering connection handled (must use a DEWA-enrolled solar contractor)? 10. Roof structural condition / load capacity assessed? 11. Monitoring and O&M / cleaning contract required? 12. Budget and expected payback period? 13. Timeline and site access? 14. Is the building in a free zone (Trakhees/DDA) or DEWA jurisdiction?

A complete on-grid (Shams Dubai) solar quote itemizes: system size in kWp (DC), number and wattage of modules (Wp) and brand/tier (Tier-1 e.g. LONGi, Jinko, Trina), module efficiency and warranties (product yrs + ~25-30yr performance), inverter brand/model and AC kW rating (string/hybrid; Huawei, Sungrow, SMA, Fronius, Goodwe), inverter warranty (5-10 yrs), mounting/racking and ballast, DC/AC cabling, isolators, interface protection device, DEWA Solar NOC/design approval and net-metering connection, civil/structural work, monitoring, and expected annual yield (kWh/kWp ~1,600-1,800 in UAE).

Spec parameters (with units): kWp, module Wp, module tier/efficiency %, inverter AC kW and type, DEWA-eligible equipment (must be on DEWA's List of Eligible Equipment), warranties yrs, annual generation kWh.

Strong vs underpriced: corners cut on module tier (cheap non-Tier-1), undersized inverter vs array (high DC:AC ratio clipping), non-DEWA-eligible modules/inverters (won't get NOC), shorter warranties, no monitoring, excluded structural/DEWA fees. Highlight to customer: kWp vs price (AED/Wp), module and inverter brand/tier, whether equipment is on DEWA's eligible list, inverter sizing vs array, warranty years, and whether DEWA NOC, design approval and net-metering connection are included.

topic: Field expertise — UAE codes, standards & specs
content:
Solar Energy Systems in the UAE are governed primarily by the Dubai Electricity and Water Authority (DEWA) for grid-connected installations under the Shams Dubai programme, which mandates a formal NOC and net-metering agreement before any grid-tied system is energised. The process involves a preliminary application, technical review of single-line diagrams and equipment datasheets, DEWA-approved contractor registration, installation inspection, and meter upgrade to a bidirectional smart meter. For Abu Dhabi, the equivalent authority is ADDC/AADC under the Distributed Renewable Energy programme. Free-zone and port areas (Jebel Ali, DAFZA, DP World facilities) fall under Trakhees, which has its own NOC and inspection process mirroring but separate from DEWA. Dubai Municipality approval is required for structural mounting systems affecting building fabric, and Dubai Civil Defence must be satisfied where battery energy storage systems (BESS) are co-located, particularly regarding fire suppression, ventilation, and compliance with the UAE Fire and Life Safety Code of Practice. ESMA oversees product conformity; inverters and panels sold in the UAE should carry Emirates Conformity Assessment Scheme (ECAS) marking or equivalent IEC certification.

Core technical standards include IEC 61215 and IEC 61730 for photovoltaic module qualification and safety, IEC 62109 for inverter safety, IEC 62548 for PV array design, and IEC 60364 for low-voltage electrical installations. DEWA's own Distributed Renewable Energy technical requirements document specifies protection relay settings, anti-islanding, power factor, and export-limit parameters. Earthing must comply with BS 7671 or IEC standards as accepted by DEWA.

Scope and specifications buyers and suppliers discuss: monocrystalline PERC or TOPCon panels (typically 400–700 Wp per module), string inverters versus central inverters versus hybrid inverters with battery-ready capability, DC/AC ratio, specific yield (kWh/kWp), performance ratio (PR), tilt angle optimisation for UAE latitude (roughly 24–25°N), soiling loss factors (critical in desert climate — dust derating can reach 15–25% without regular cleaning), mounting structures (ballasted flat-roof, pitched-roof rail systems, ground-mount galvanised steel), DC isolators, surge protection devices (SPDs) on both DC and AC sides, generation meters, monitoring platforms (SCADA/portal), and cable sizing for high-temperature ambient conditions (70°C conduit temperatures are common, requiring XLPE or equivalent rated cabling).

System sizes range from 3–10 kWp residential to hundreds of kWp for commercial rooftops and multi-MW ground-mount. DEWA currently caps residential export and has specific limits per connection capacity. Commercial systems are sized against DEWA tariff blocks (Tier 1–4) to maximise self-consumption ROI. Payback periods in Dubai typically run 5–8 years depending on consumption profile and tariff tier.

Price drivers include panel wattage and tier (

Grid-connected rooftop solar in Dubai runs under DEWA's Shams Dubai initiative (Distributed Renewable Resources Generation, DRRG) with net metering. Only DEWA-enrolled solar PV consultants and contractors may submit connection applications. To enrol, a company must first be enrolled with DEWA as Consultant-Electrical or Contractor-Electrical, hold the relevant trade licence (Renewable Energy Consultancy activity 731004 for consultants; Solar Energy System Installation activity 4322011 for contractors), and have staff certified as DEWA Solar PV Experts via DEWA's Solar PV Expert Training.

Workflow: enrolled contractor applies through DEWA's system, uploading documents and technical drawings to obtain the Solar NOC, Solar Design approval and DEWA invoice, then installs and requests connection/inspection and net-metering bi-directional meter. Equipment (modules, inverters, interface protection) must appear on DEWA's List of Eligible Equipment (DRRG). For systems 10-100 kW, external protection and isolation devices are required at the interconnection point; above 100 kW, dedicated protection switchgear applies. Free-zone properties may route approvals via Trakhees or DDA. Equipment compliance certificates must come from ILAC-accredited labs per ISO/IEC 17025.

Governing document: DEWA Standards for Distributed Renewable Resources Generators (DRRG, Version 3.0, December 2023). PV module eligibility requires compliance with IEC 61215-1-x/2 (design/type approval), IEC 61730-1/2 (safety) and IEC 61701 (salt-mist corrosion); IEC 62716 (ammonia) only for special environments. Inverters require IEC 62109-1/2 or UL 1741, IEC 61000-3-2 or 61000-3-12, plus EMC sets IEC 61000-6-1/-2/-3/-4 per usage category, and DEWA DRRG Appendix D.3/D.4 compliance; harmonic spectrum data must be supplied. Interface protection requires IEC 61850 and DEWA DRRG Appendix D.1/D.2. LV voltage-quality per IEC 61000-2-2 and IEC/TR 61000-3-14.

Materials/equipment: Tier-1 monocrystalline PV modules (LONGi, Jinko, Trina), string/hybrid inverters (Huawei FusionSolar, Sungrow, SMA, Fronius, Goodwe), aluminium mounting/racking with ballast, DC isolators, AC isolators, interface protection relay, bi-directional (net) meter. Vocabulary: kWp, Wp, DC:AC ratio, string, MPPT, net metering, NOC, DRRG, eligible equipment list, performance ratio, yield kWh/kWp.

Indicative only (Dubai 2026, verify). Turnkey on-grid residential/small-commercial systems are commonly quoted around AED 1.8-3.0 per watt installed (panels, inverter, mounting, DEWA approval, labour), so a ~10 kWp villa system often lands roughly AED 35,000-55,000 turnkey depending on brand and structure. Price drivers: module tier/wattage, inverter brand and type (string vs hybrid), roof type and structural work, system size (economies of scale), battery inclusion, DEWA fees, monitoring and O&M.

Red flags: price quoted only as lump sum with no kWp, module Wp/brand or inverter model; equipment not on DEWA's eligible-equipment list (will fail NOC); non-Tier-1 modules; inverter undersized relative to array causing clipping, or oversized with no benefit; very short or vendor-only warranties; DEWA Solar NOC, design approval and net-metering connection excluded; no structural assessment; missing monitoring; AED/Wp far below market usually signals off-brand gear, no DEWA enrolment, or omitted approval/structural scope. Always compare AED per Wp and confirm DEWA enrolment number.

Shams Dubai (DEWA) — https://www.dewa.gov.ae/en/consumer/solar-community/shams-dubai
DEWA Apply for Solar PV Connections — https://www.dewa.gov.ae/en/builder/electricity-network-services/apply-for-solar-pv-connections
DEWA DRRG Solar PV Consultants & Contractors Enrolment — https://www.dewa.gov.ae/en/builder/shams-dubai-guides-tools/enroll-as-drrg-solar-pv-consultant-and-contractor
DEWA Solar PV Equipment Eligibility — https://www.dewa.gov.ae/en/builder/shams-dubai-guides-tools/pv-equipment-eligibility
DEWA Standards for Distributed Renewable Resources Generators (DRRG v3.0, PDF) — https://www.dewa.gov.ae/-/media/Files/Consultants-and-Contractors/DEWA_Standards_for_Distributed_Renewable_Resources_Generators/DEWAStandards-(1).ashx
DEWA List of Eligible Equipment (DRRG) — https://www.dewa.gov.ae/en/builder/shams-dubai-guides-tools/drrg/eligible-equipment-list
DEWA Solar PV Certification Training — https://www.dewa.gov.ae/en/builder/general-technical-services/solar-pv-certification-training
Shams Dubai FAQs — https://www.dewa.gov.ae/en/consumer/solar-community/shams-dubai/shams-dubai-faq
Shams Dubai Solar Calculator — https://www.dewa.gov.ae/SolarCalculator/index.html
DEWA Solar Connection Process — https://www.dewa.gov.ae/en/consumer/solar-community/connection-process

Checklist before fanning out an RFQ: legal employer confirmed; mainland or free zone and the exact site; licence activity of every quoting supplier read, not assumed; MOHRE establishment number and WPS checked; quota headroom confirmed; salary band written down; job description signed; headcount and duration fixed; sourcing origin decided; accommodation and transport in or out of the rate; sector licence identified; rebate SLA agreed; terms signed before the first CV; attribution 12 months. Best practice: two or three suppliers per role, never five; exclusivity for anything senior; a rate card with overtime multipliers; audit the camp before mobilising. Frequent mistakes - client: no salary band, stale benchmarks, hiring direct after introduction. Supplier: quoting off basic pay, no gratuity accrual, promising overseas starts in two weeks. Documentation: unsigned terms, missing attestation. Compliance: charging the candidate, a mis-stated permit title, free-zone staff onsite mainland.

Models: contingency permanent 12-20% of annual gross (15% typical, 8-12% at volume); retained search 25-33% or a fixed AED 120,000-350,000 in three tranches; white-collar contract at a 10-18% markup on employment cost; blue-collar supply as an all-in monthly rate per head, roughly AED 1,800-3,500 for general labour with accommodation and transport, AED 3,500-7,000 for skilled trades; EOR payrolling AED 900-2,500 per head monthly plus pass-through visa cost around AED 5,000-9,000 mainland. Drivers ranked: who sponsors the visa, salary band, volume and duration, source country and attestation, regulated licence, accommodation and transport, urgency, rebate length. Add 5% VAT. Terms: placement invoiced on join, 30 days net; supply monthly at 30-45 days, though the supplier funds payroll on the 1st - that gap is the real negotiation. Levers: exclusivity, volume, longer rebate, buyout.

Vocabulary: contingency versus retained search, RPO, MSP/VMS, EOR, PEO, secondment, manpower supply, temp-to-perm, TAT, offer-to-join ratio, EOSB (gratuity), WPS, MOHRE establishment card, quota, Tas'heel, Tadbeer, Nafis, ILOE, NOC, absconding. Tiers: global brands (Korn Ferry, Michael Page, Hays); UAE mid-market (Charterhouse, Cooper Fitch, MacKenzie Jones, Nadia Global); volume outsourcers (TASC Outsourcing, Innovations Group, Sundus, Trans Skills); and unlicensed CV brokers. Buyers are HR directors and talent acquisition leads for white collar, procurement and project managers for site labour, founders for first hires. Cycles: budgets approve in January and September; hiring stalls mid-June to end-August and slows in Ramadan (6-hour days); Q4 brings construction and retail surges; Emiratisation scrambles peak in the weeks before the 30 June and 31 December MOHRE checkpoints.

Ask in order, 1-6 mandatory. 1 Who is the legal employer and visa sponsor - client or supplier? 2 Permanent, fixed-term contract, manpower supply or payrolling? 3 Job titles, headcount per title, salary or rate band? 4 Start date and duration? 5 Emirate, site, mainland or free zone? 6 In-country only or from abroad? 7 Accommodation and transport included - mandatory for blue collar, skippable for white. 8 Sector licence? 9 Emiratisation credit required? 10 Rebate expectation? Rules: if the supplier sponsors, route only to labour supply licence holders with live quota. If the client sponsors one senior role, route to search, not supply. If a free-zone entity wants mainland deployment, flag secondment first. If Emiratisation credit is sought via an outsourcer, escalate - it does not count. Headcount over 20, multi-emirate, or DHA/DOH/SIRA licensed: book a scoping call, do not fan out.

Taxonomy: contingency permanent placement (paid on join); retained executive search (three tranches, exclusivity, 8-14 weeks); contract white-collar staffing on the agency's visa; blue-collar manpower supply priced per head per month all-in; EOR payrolling of a candidate the client already found; RPO and embedded recruiters; Emiratisation sourcing via Nafis; domestic staff through MOHRE Tadbeer centres; background screening. Scope boundary that matters: brokerage ends at the join date; supply is a continuing employment relationship, with gratuity, leave, ticket and medical liability on the supplier. Alternatives: direct hiring via Bayt, GulfTalent or LinkedIn Recruiter, a freelance-permit contractor, referrals. Lifecycle: brief, terms signed, mapping, shortlist in 5-15 working days, interviews, offer, MOHRE permit and visa, medical and Emirates ID, onboarding, rebate window.

Mandatory to quote: who is the legal employer and visa sponsor; permanent, contract or supply; job titles with a real job description; headcount per title; salary or rate band; duration and start date; work location and emirate; mainland or free zone; shift pattern and expected overtime; nationality or language preference and whether the source is in-country or overseas; accommodation and transport, provided or costed; any sector licence needed (DHA, DOH, MOHAP, SIRA, RTA); rebate or replacement expectation; whether Emiratisation credit is required. Price and turnaround move on salary band, volume, duration, source country, attestation, licensing and urgency. Suppliers walk away from: no salary band, "send CVs and we will discuss terms", unsigned terms of business, five agencies on one role, a role priced 30% below market, and any client expecting the candidate to pay visa cost.

MOHRE (https://www.mohre.gov.ae) licenses recruitment agencies and labour supply companies, issues every work permit type, runs WPS and the Tadbeer domestic-worker centres; agency licences go to UAE nationals only, and no fee may be charged to a worker - employers pay (https://u.ae/en/information-and-services/jobs/searching-for-a-job). Framework: Federal Decree-Law 33/2021 as amended by 9/2024, Cabinet Resolution 1/2022, Decree-Law 9/2022 on domestic workers. ICP (https://icp.gov.ae) and GDRFA handle entry and residence visas. Emiratisation sits with MOHRE and Nafis (https://www.nafis.gov.ae) - 2% skilled-role growth a year toward 10%, checked 30 June and 31 December, with a contribution per unfilled post and heavy fines for fictitious Emiratisation. Trade licences come from Dubai DET, ADDED via TAMM, or the free zone. Overlays: DHA, DOH, MOHAP; SIRA for guards; PDPL 45/2021 on CV data.

Executive search here: Korn Ferry, Heidrick & Struggles, Egon Zehnder, Spencer Stuart, Russell Reynolds. Mid-market professional: Michael Page, Hays, Robert Walters, Robert Half, Charterhouse, BAC Middle East, Cooper Fitch, MacKenzie Jones, Nadia Global. Volume staffing and outsourcing: ManpowerGroup, Adecco, Randstad, TASC Outsourcing, Innovations Group, Sundus, Trans Skills. Energy and technical contract staffing: Airswift, Brunel, NES Fircroft. Global EOR platforms selling into the UAE - Deel, Remote, Papaya Global, Multiplier, G-P - are convenient, but the visa still comes from a licensed UAE entity behind them. Sourcing and software: Bayt.com, GulfTalent, Naukrigulf, LinkedIn Talent Solutions; ATS Bullhorn, Vincere, Zoho Recruit; VMS SAP Fieldglass and Beeline; screening DataFlow, HireRight. No accreditation is mandatory - REC or APSCo membership and ISO 27001 are voluntary signals.

They say "we need the best candidate"; they mean a joiner inside 30 days on a budget benchmarked two years ago. They say "flexible headcount"; they mean releasing people without paying gratuity or notice. Real constraints: an approved salary band, visa quota, an unmovable project start, often an Emiratisation deadline. Functional need is the skill; operational need is who carries sponsorship, payroll funding, accommodation, replacement and end-of-service liability. Trade-offs a professional says out loud: exclusivity buys real research while a four-agency free-for-all buys the same CVs three times; a cheap supply rate means a supplier who has not accrued gratuity and will fail in month 14; in-country hiring is fast but shallow, from abroad is deeper but adds 4-8 weeks; a 90-day rebate costs more than 30 and is worth it; outsourced Emiratis do not count toward the client's MOHRE target.

Terms of business or an MSA before any CV is sent - it must fix the fee, the introduction and attribution period (12 months is standard), the rebate scale, and a temp-to-perm buyout formula. For supply: a manpower supply agreement with rate card, overtime multipliers, replacement SLA, indemnity, and who holds gratuity liability. Client side: trade licence, establishment card, VAT certificate, signed job description. Supplier side: licence with the correct activity, MOHRE establishment number, WPS evidence, professional indemnity and employer's liability cover. Candidate side: passport, MOFAIC-attested degree for skilled permits, DataFlow PSV and a DHA or DOH licence for clinicians, police clearance where required, medical fitness certificate, Emirates ID, MOHRE offer letter and standard contract e-signed, NOC or cancellation paper for transfers. NDA before any org chart or salary data.

Legal: a supplier licensed for consultancy but quoting mainland supply - early sign is a free-zone address and vague licence wording. Regulatory: the supplier's MOHRE file turns red over WPS or unpaid fines and visas freeze mid-project - early sign is salaries landing late in the month. Financial: a supply rate below the honest cost of salary plus gratuity plus ticket plus insurance - early sign is a quote 25% under the field. Commercial: the client hires direct - early sign is a shortlist met with silence, then a LinkedIn start announcement. Operational: no municipality-permitted accommodation, so workers refuse to mobilise - early sign is a supplier who will not name the camp. Schedule: hiring from abroad against a fixed start - early sign is missing attestation. Candidate: counteroffer or renege - early sign is one who will not resign until the visa is stamped.

Archetypes: (1) Emirati-owned mainland recruitment agency holding the MOHRE licence - can place, often supply; (2) mainland manpower supply company with hundreds of visas, camps and buses - the only option for site labour; (3) free-zone HR consultancy - can headhunt, cannot sponsor for mainland deployment; (4) global brand working through a local partner; (5) a solo CV broker with a WhatsApp group. Turnaround: white-collar shortlist 5-15 working days; executive longlist 3-4 weeks; in-country transfer 5-15 working days; hiring from abroad 3-8 weeks with attestation, medical and Emirates ID; bulk labour from India or Nepal 6-12 weeks. Verify before trusting: licence activity wording (recruitment versus manpower supply), MOHRE establishment number and colour class, live WPS status, real quota headroom, accommodation with a municipality permit, three referenceable clients at the same volume.

Scoping logic: fix the legal employer first, then role family, skill level (MOHRE skill 1-5 drives attestation and permit fee), salary band, headcount, duration, location and shift pattern. Methods: competency-based structured interviewing, psychometrics (SHL, Hogan, Thomas International, Talogy), trade tests for technicians, and primary source verification through DataFlow for regulated professions. Variables inside a supply rate: basic salary, housing and transport allowance, overtime factor, gratuity accrual (21 days a year for the first five years, 30 days after), leave and ticket, medical insurance, visa amortised over contract length, ILOE, margin. Failure points: quoting off basic pay only, so overtime and gratuity eat the margin; a permit job title that does not match the real role, which triggers refusal; assuming free-zone visa holders can work a mainland site.

Recurring problems and the sequence a veteran runs. Offer declined or reneged: check total package against market - benefits, school allowance, joining date - not just basic. Visa rejected or delayed: check quota headroom, establishment colour class, WPS status, then the permit job title against skill level and attested certificate, then any nationality restriction. Worker absconds in month two: check accommodation, transport, overtime pay, and whether the real job matched what was sold at interview. Supply invoice disputed: reconcile timesheets against the rate card and overtime multiplier first. Emiratisation target missed despite hires: check whether the Emirati sits on the client's own establishment card and WPS, not the vendor's. Escalate to a scoping call when headcount exceeds 20, when DHA, DOH or SIRA licensing applies, or when Emiratisation credit is sought via an outsourcer.

topic: Field expertise — UAE codes, standards & specs
content:
Steel & Reinforcement Suppliers in the UAE supply reinforcement (rebar), structural steel, mesh, and fabricated/cut-and-bend product for construction. This is primarily a materials-supply and fabrication trade, not a licensing-heavy one — the regulatory burden falls mainly on product conformity, consultant approval, and project-level permits held by the main contractor.

GOVERNING AUTHORITY & APPROVALS: Products must comply with UAE conformity requirements — ESMA/Emirates Conformity (ECAS/EQM marking) applies to steel products placed on the UAE market. Dubai Municipality (and Dubai Central Laboratory) governs material approval, mill test certificate acceptance, and independent testing for projects under Dubai Municipality jurisdiction. In free zones/ports areas, Trakhees acts as the authority. Steel enters project approval via the structural consultant and the building permit rather than a supplier-specific NOC. Import clearance runs through UAE Customs; RTA permits apply for oversize/heavy transport and abnormal loads.

STANDARDS: Reinforcing steel is typically specified to BS 4449 (grade B500B / B500C weldable rebar) or ASTM A615/A706; couplers to relevant ISO/ACI mechanical splice criteria. Structural sections to BS EN 10025 / ASTM A36/A992, welding to AWS D1.1 or EN ISO 3834, galvanizing to relevant ASTM/EN standards, and testing (tensile, bend, rebend, chemical) per ISO/BS methods. Mill certificates must be EN 10204 3.1 type. QMS to ISO 9001.

SCOPE & SPECS: Rebar diameters (8–40mm), grades B500B/B500C, cut-and-bend per BS 8666 schedules, stirrups, links, mesh (A142–A393), couplers, dowels, spacers/chairs, tie wire, structural I/H sections, plates, hollow sections, and epoxy-coated/galvanized rebar for marine/coast

Order against an approved BS 8666 bar bending schedule rather than a drawing take-off, and show the 3-5% lap and waste allowance as a separate line so it is not double-counted. Fix grade, standard and acceptable mills in the enquiry, otherwise the quotes are not comparable. Weighbridge every inbound load and reconcile theoretical against actual mass in the first week, not at final account. Store bundles on timber sleepers clear of sabkha and salt spray, and collect MTCs before the pour, never after. Common mistakes: buying on the lowest AED per tonne without checking whether the origin is DM-listed; accepting a quote with no validity date when the mill reprices monthly; ordering straight bar to bend on site because it prints cheaper; omitting the delivery emirate and who offloads; treating a free-zone ex-works price as landed; mixing B500B and B500C in one cage; releasing cut-and-bend before the consultant approves the schedule; and comparing an ex-works quote against a delivered one.

Price builds as mill base plus processing plus logistics plus duty and tax. Rebar trades per metric tonne and the UAE band has recently run roughly AED 2,450-3,200/t. EMSTEEL circulars have issued around AED 2,660/t CPT Abu Dhabi and AED 2,668/t CPT Dubai and the Northern Emirates (January 2025), against AED 2,744 and 2,752/t in earlier cycles - all quoted excluding VAT, with 5% VAT added. Imported rebar, rebar-in-coil and wire rod carry 10% customs duty, raised from 5% in 2019 and extended to 12 October 2026, so landed imports rarely undercut local mills. Cut-and-bend adds a bending rate per tonne but drops site wastage from about 8-12% to 3-5% and removes cutting labour.
